Although this grammar book is currently more than 100,000 words long, it truly only scratches the surface of this beautiful language. Moloko grammar is interesting and complex; we encourage further study to demonstrate its genius in more detail.

The notable features of the language include the following:

Linguistic classification, language use, and previous research are outlined in Sections sec:1.1 to sec:1.3. The four texts that follow in Sections sec:1.4 -- sec:1.7 are chosen from among many that were recorded while the first author lived in the Moloko region from 1999 to 2008. They are used with permission. These stories belong to the community because they represent their collective knowledge and culture. As such, no individual will be named as 'author' of any particular story. Many of the examples from the grammar sections in this book are taken from these stories. The sentence numbers are given in the examples so that the reader can refer to the complete texts and locate the example in its context. The first line in each sentence is the orthographic form. The second is the phonetic form (slow speech) with morpheme breaks. The third line is the gloss and the fourth is the translation.

text:
Moloko (or Melokwo, Molkore, Molkore is the Fulfulde Fulfulde name for Moloko. Məloko Məloko is the spelling for this name using the Moloko orthography. The orthography, described in, is being used by the Moloko (more than a dozen titles are listed in the reference section). ) is classified by classify it as [154] Chadic family, Biu Mandara branch, center-west sub-branch, Wandala-Mafa group, Mafa-south sub-group (A5). as Central Chadic Biu-Mandara A5, as seen in fig:1.1. A more detailed discussion of the classification of Moloko is found in.

The Ethnologue reports 8,500 speakers of Moloko in 1992. A survey by estimated 10,000--12,000 speakers. Most live near Moloko mountain, 30km north of Maroua in the district of Tokombere, department of Mayo-Sava in the Far North Province of the Republic of Cameroon. Local oral history indicates that the Moloko people actually are not a single people group historically, but that people from at least three ethnic groups sought refuge on Moloko mountain during the Fulani invasions of the 19 th century. Eventually they all came to speak the same language.

Moloko mountain remains the center of Moloko culture. There are three villages on the summit itself. Moloko villages are organised by clan, each village being the male descendants of a particular clan and their families. Since the 1960’s, some of the Moloko language group have moved to the plains between the mountain and Maroua, and have settled in Moloko or Giziga-Moloko villages. Others have moved further away and live in small communities in and around the cities of Maroua, Garoua, Toubouro, Kousseri, and Yaounde. Minor dialectal differences exist in pronunciation and vocabulary but all speakers can understand one another without difficulty.
summary:
Moloko (also called Melokwo/Molkore) is a Chadic language of the Biu-Mandara branch, specifically classified in the Central Chadic A5 group. It had an estimated 8,500 speakers in 1992, with later surveys suggesting 10,000–12,000 speakers, most of whom live around Moloko mountain in northern Cameroon.

The Moloko people are said to have formed historically from at least three ethnic groups that took refuge on the mountain during 19th-century Fulani invasions and gradually came to share one language. Moloko remains centered on the mountain, though some speakers have moved to nearby plains and cities; dialect differences are minor and mutually intelligible.

section: Language use, language contact, and multilingualism
text:
A minority of Moloko speakers are monolingual. Most speak three to five other languages. Men and most women have at least a market level knowledge of Fulfulde Fulfulde, the language of wider communication, and also speak at least one of the neighboring languages: Giziga Giziga, Muyang Muyang, Gemzek Gemzek, Mbuko Mbuko, or Dugwor Dugwor. Those with several years of education also speak French.

Men often marry women from neighboring language groups, so homes can be multilingual, but the spoken language at home tends to be the language of the father. Friends will often switch languages as they are conversing, perhaps when talking in different domains, but also simply to bond. Dealings in the market can be done in the trade language, but people prefer to bargain in the language of the seller, if possible.

Language viability for Moloko is only at risk in communities where Moloko is not the primary language, especially in cities like Maroua or Yaounde. In the city, children grow up in neighborhoods where many different languages are spoken and so they tend to speak Fulfulde Fulfulde (as well as learn French at school). In such places, Moloko is at risk to be lost in the next generation. Otherwise, in areas where Moloko people are together, Moloko language use is strong among people of every age and in every domain of home life.
summary: Most Moloko speakers are multilingual, usually speaking three to five other languages in addition to Moloko, especially Fulfulde and at least one neighboring language; those with schooling also speak French. In multilingual homes the father’s language typically dominates, friends commonly switch languages in conversation, and market dealings often use the trade language or the seller’s language. Moloko is endangered mainly in cities or other communities where it is not the primary language, but it remains strong across ages and home domains where Moloko speakers live together.

The vowel system of Moloko is noteworthy in its simplicity - it can be analysed as having only one underlying phoneme with ten phonetic representations (see sec:2.3 ).

The phonology of Moloko has been fully discussed by. The following is a summary of the aspects that are necessary to understand the grammar, with focus on the new work that has been done since her manuscript was initially published.

based her phonological outline of Moloko on a database she compiled consisting of around 1500 words, including some 400 verbs and 1000 nouns. Bow’s database was modified and extended by with a focus on nouns. Later, Mamalis built on their work to describe the tone on verbs, and Friesen discussed phonological word structure of the verb word.

Three inter-related phonological factors must be touched on before a discussion of any of them can be fully understood. The first is that Moloko words are built on a consonantal skeleton with only one underlying vowel /a/ (phonetically expressed as the full vowels [a, o, œ,, ɛ], see sec:2.3 ) that occurs between only some of the consonants. used the distinction +/- Low, which focused on one phonetic feature, however we have found that the most salient issue in discussing the vowel patterns of this language is the concept of full vs. epenthetic vowels. For clarity, therefore, this work will use the terms full and epenthetic to distinguish between the two sets of vowel phones, with full referring to /a/ and its prosodically conditioned allophones, and epenthetic referring to schwa and its allophones. Some consonant clusters (caused by the absence of an underlying vowel between them) are broken up by epenthetic schwa insertion when they are pronounced (and phonetically expressed as [ə, ʊ, u, ø, ɪ, i]). Likewise in Muyang Muyang, another Central Chadic language closely related to Moloko, it can be shown that syllables are built postlexically from the consonant skeleton by regular rules. Only the low vowel /a/ is phonemic, and all high vowels can be accounted for by means of epenthesis. Although syllable structure will be mentioned in this work, attention will be focussed on the underlying consonantal skeleton. notes for Central Chadic languages,

quote
[because] “the consonant skeleton is all-important to the phonological structure, the traditional unit of the syllable is much less useful in the description of Central Chadic languages since at the core of every syllable must be a vowel (or some syllabic segment, at least). And in fact, it can be shown for most of these languages that the syllable is a very superficial phenomenon.”
quote

And further on p. 16,

quote
“We conclude then that the syllable is not a unit that can be exploited as it is in other languages to elucidate the phonological structure. It is a surface structure phenomenon whose character is completely predictable from other phonological aspects of lexemes. On the other hand, an underlying structure that is more worthy of study in Central Chadic languages is that of the consonant skeleton that can take up lexical roots; to this core are added other peripheral phonological elements such as vowels, prosodies, and tones.”
quote

The second basic phonological factor for Moloko is that all of the vowels (both full and epenthetic) and some of the consonants are affected by word-level labialisation or palatalisation prosodies Prosodies in Chadic languages are word-level suprasegmental processes that labialise or palatalise the entire word and affect all vowels and some consonants. See for a fuller discussion. (see sec:2.1 ). These prosodies account for most of the vowel and consonant allophones in the language. Palatalisation can be part of certain morphemes, but Moloko is unlike other Chadic languages where palatalisation and labialisation alone can have morphemic status (for example in Muyang where the application of the palatalisation prosody on a noun produces a diminutive, and application of the labialisation prosody produces an augmentative, Smith, personal communication).

The third basic factor is that the final syllable before a pause is stressed in pronunciation. The stressed syllable necessitates a full vowel, meaning that any epenthetic vowel in that syllable will be changed to its full counterpart. The following two example pairs each show the same word in unstressed and stressed environments. Compare [zij] (non-stressed with epenthetic vowel) with [zaj] (stressed with full vowel) in ex:2:1 and ex:2:2, and [nɔ-zʊm] (non-stressed with epenthetic vowel in final syllable) with [nɔ-zɔm] (stressed with full vowel) in ex:2:3 and ex:2:4.

‘I ate millet loaf.’

Due to these interrelated factors, much of the phonological discussion will require representation of both the underlying and surface forms of lexemes. The underlying form consists of the consonant and vowel phonemes (written between slashes) and the word prosody (written as a superscripted e for palatalisation, o for labialisation at the right of the morphemes). A neutral prosody has no superscript. The following examples illustrate the phonetic forms (between square brackets) and underlying forms (between slashes) of nouns that are palatalised ex:2:5, labialised ex:2:6, and neutral with respect to prosody ex:2:7. All of the examples in this work will be presented in the phonetic form unless otherwise indicated.

The phonetic forms of the examples given in this paper are all in citation form (the form of the word when it is pronounced in isolation), and therefore show each word with a stressed final syllable. In each case, the final syllable (whether open or closed) always contains a full vowel, regardless of whether the underlying form has a full vowel or not.
summary: Moloko is described as having a highly simple vowel system with only one underlying vowel phoneme, /a/, plus epenthetic vowels inserted in pronunciation. Its phonology is organized around an underlying consonantal skeleton, word-level labialisation and palatalisation prosodies, and final-syllable stress, which forces a full vowel in citation forms and makes both underlying and surface forms important for analysis.

Prosody (labialisation or palatalization)|(

One of the most basic phonological processes in Moloko is prosody. Chadic linguists refer to prosody as a suprasegmental process where a labialisation or palatalisation feature is applied to a phonological word. refers to prosodies as suprasegmental sources of palatalisation and labiovelarisation.

has discovered that labialisation and palatalisation work at the morpheme level in Moloko. Both prosodies are attached to a particular morpheme and spread leftward over the entire phonological word. Labialisation affects the back consonants (k, g, ŋg, and h) and vowels; palatalisation affects alveolar fricatives (s and z), affricates (ts and dz, see sec:2.2 ), and vowels (see sec:2.3 ). All Moloko words are either labialised, palatalised, or are neutral with respect to prosody. Recent work demonstrates that some syllables can be affected by both labialisation and palatalisation (see sec:2.3.1 and sec:2.3.2 ).

As stated above, in this work prosody is indicated in the underlying form using superscript symbols included at the right edge of the word: / o / to represent labialisation and / e / to represent palatalisation. In the phonetic form, the prosody is indicated by the quality of the full vowel in the word ([ɔ] for labialisation, [ɛ] for palatalisation, and [a] for no prosody (see sec:2.3 ). The examples ( ex:2:8 -- ex:2:10 ) from give evidence of contrast between the prosodies in a minimal triplet:

/k ra/ 17pt [kəra]\\
‘dog’

/k ra o / 10pt [kʷʊrɔ] \\
‘ten'

/k ra e / 10pt [kɪrɛ]\\
‘stake/post’

The effects of both prosodies on a single underlying form can be seen in the paradigm for the verb /mnzar/ ‘see’ shown in tab:2.1 (adapted from ). The verb stem is bolded in the table. The imperative is neutral with respect to prosody, while the imperative form involves a labialisation prosody and the addition of a suffix /-am o / (see sec:7.3.1 ). The nominalised form carries a palatalisation prosody, and involves the addition of both a prefix /m-/ and suffix /-a e /. Note that vowels and some consonants are affected by the prosodies. As previously stated, the vowel /a/ is realised as [ɔ] in labialised forms, and [ɛ] in palatalised forms, while [ə] is realised as [ʊ] in labialised forms and [ɪ] in palatalised forms (see sec:2.3.2 ). The consonant /nz/ is realised as [nʒ] in palatalised forms (see sec:2.2.3 ).

Labialisation and palatalisation prosodies are lexical features that are applied to a morpheme, and can spread over an entire word. A prosody in the root will spread to a prefix. Compare the prosody in the subject prefixes of the following verbs. In ex:2:11, the root is labialised, in ex:2:12, the root is palatalised, and in ex:2:13, the root is neutral. The underlying forms are given in the examples.

When initiated by a suffix carrying a prosody, the prosody spreads leftwards, affecting all morphemes within the word including prefixes. When the prosody of the suffix is neutral, the prosody on the root is neutralised (compare examples ex:2:16 and ex:2:17 ). The effect of the prosody is shown by comparing the vowels and consonants in ex:2:14 and ex:2:15, both forms of [kaɬ] ‘wait,’ a verb root with no underlying prosody. The prosody of the second person singular verb form remains neutral ex:2:14. The second person plural contains the labialised suffix /-ak o / ex:2:15 and the prosody of the suffix spreads over the entire word. The underlying forms are given in each example. Note that the prosody does not spread to the right across word boundaries since na, a separate word, is not affected by the prosody of the verb stem (nor does it neutralise the prosody on the verb).

Palatalised verbs almost always have a palatalised suffix [-ɛ] (see sec:6.6 ). With the exception of verb stems whose final consonant is /n/, e.g., [tʃɛŋ], /tsan e /, ‘know’. Whenever there is another suffix or enclitic attached to the verb stem, the [-ɛ] is deleted, taking with it the palatalisation prosody (see sec:6.3 ). The verb becomes neutral with respect to prosody, as is shown by ( ex:2:16 -- ex:2:17 ). In ex:2:16, the verb ends with [-ɛ] and the entire verb form is palatalised. summary:
The passage explains that Moloko has two lexical prosodies, labialisation and palatalisation, which are attached to a morpheme and spread leftward across the whole phonological word. Labialisation affects back consonants and vowels, while palatalisation affects alveolar fricatives, affricates, and vowels; words are either labialised, palatalised, or neutral, though some syllables may show both prosodies.

It also shows that prosody can spread from roots or suffixes to prefixes, but not across word boundaries. Palatalised verbs typically have a palatalised suffix [-ɛ] that is deleted when another suffix or enclitic is added, making the form neutral, and vowel-initial syllables are often least affected, especially in labialised words.

Moloko has three sets of sequences which interpreted as single units (C) rather than sequences of two consonants (CC). These are prenasalised consonants /mb/, /nd/, /ŋg/, /nz/, affricates /ts/, /dz/, and labialised consonants /kʷ/, /gʷ/, /ŋgʷ/, /hʷ/. In the case of prenasalised consonants, the nasal is always homorganic with the following consonant. Note that the phoneme /n/ assimilates to the point of articulation of a following consonant throughout the language. Only voiced consonants are prenasalised.

Allophonic variation for consonants occurs in Moloko due to prosodic conditioning ( sec:2.2.3 ) and word-final variations ( sec:2.2.4 ). There is a relationship between consonants and tone which is considered in sec:2.4.1.

summary:
Moloko is described as having 32 consonant phonemes, including a labiodental flap / / that was later identified and occurs in ideophones. The language also has several consonant sequences treated as single units rather than clusters, including prenasalised consonants, affricates, and labialised consonants, with prenasalisation only occurring on voiced consonants and the nasal assimilating to the following consonant.  

Consonants in Moloko also show allophonic variation conditioned by prosody and word-final position, and there is a relationship between consonants and tone.

She showed them to be phonemes even though each of these consonants is also the realisation in labialised words of their non-labialised counterpart (see sec:2.2.3 ). At the surface phonetic level, Bow showed that a labialised velar can have two possible sources, either a labialisation prosody across the whole word ex:2:24, or the presence of an underlyingly labialised consonant ex:2:25. Example ex:2:24 shows consistently labialised vowels indicating labialisation across whole word, while the palatalised vowels in ex:2:25 indicate that there is a palatalisation prosody across the whole word; with the presence of an underlyingly labialised velar consonant.

found underlyingly labialised consonants in words which do not have a labialisation prosody across the whole word. She concluded that the labialisation feature was attached only to these velar consonants within a word since the prosody only affected those particular consonants and the vowels immediately adjacent to them, while other consonants and vowels within the word were unaffected by the labialisation prosody. Another interpretive option could be positing that the labialisation prosody touches down on the velar consonant but something prevents it from spreading to the rest of the word (Smith, personal communication). For the purposes of this work, we will consider the labialised velar to be a separate phoneme rather than a supra-segmental phenomenon.

tab:2.5 illustrates words containing each of the labialised velar phonemes. The labialised velars may occur as the word-initial consonant, medial consonant in palatalised words or words of neutral prosody. Only voiceless labialised velars can occur in word-final position (see sec:2.2.4 ). It is interesting that there are no words of neutral prosody which can have a labialised velar in word-final position. Note that only the vowels that immediately surround a labialised velar consonant are affected by the prosody of the velar consonant (see Section sec:2.3.3 ).

summary:
Bow posited a set of underlyingly labialised velar phonemes, [kʷ, gʷ, ŋgʷ, hʷ], arguing that they are distinct phonemes even though they can also surface as the labialised realization of non-labialised consonants. She showed that a labialised velar may come either from a labialisation prosody affecting the whole word or from an underlyingly labialised consonant, but only the vowels immediately adjacent to the consonant are affected when the labialisation is tied to the consonant itself.  

The passage also notes that labialised velars can occur in several word positions, though only voiceless ones appear word-finally, and that some cases are ambiguous until further morphological evidence clarifies them; in one such case, later verb data showed that the word contained an underlying labialised velar rather than just a word-level labialisation prosody.

text: Word-final position influences the distribution of certain phonemes as well as the production of allophones. The following phonemes do not occur in word-final position: voiced stops (including prenasalised stops but excluding /m/ and the implosives), voiced affricates, and the labiodental flap i.e., [b, mb, d, nd, g, gʷ, ŋg, ŋgʷ, dz, dʒ, nz, nʒ, ]. Also, [x] and [ŋ] are the word-final allophones of /h/ and /n/, respectively ( sec:2.2.4.1 ). In some contexts, word-final /r/ can be realised as [l] ( sec:2.2.4.2 ). tab:2.7 (adapted from ) shows the distribution of each consonant phone (reading down) in different positions within the word (reading across).

In this position, /h/ and /n/ surface as [x] and [ŋ], respectively, and /r/ may be realized as [l] in some contexts.

text:
There are ten surface phonetic vowels in Moloko ( tab:2.10 ) but the vowel system can be analysed as having one underlying vowel /a/. An analysis by using Optimality Theory allowed both a single underlying vowel system (/a/) or a two underlying vowel system (/a/ and /ə/). For the purposes of this work, the schwa is considered as epenthetic since its presence is predictable, and /a/ is considered the only underlying vowel phoneme. This vowel may be either present or absent between any two consonants in the underlying form of a morpheme. found that the absence of a vowel requires an epenthetic vowel to break up some consonant clusters in the surface form. Certain consonants do not require epenthetic schwa insertion ( sec:2.5.1 ). Different environments acting on the underlying vowel and the epenthetic [ə] result in the ten allophones in Moloko (four from /a/: [a, ɛ, ɔ, œ] reported ten surface vowel forms including [æ] which she did not consider as a distinct allophone since not all speakers distinguish between [a] and [æ], leaving nine allophones. added [ø]. and six from the epenthetic schwa: [ə, ɪ, ʊ, ø, i, u]). Note the addition of the vowel [ø] not in Bow’s analysis. Bow noted “a phonetic gap left by the absence of a high vowel with both palatalisation and labialisation.” This work reports the presence of this vowel in environments affected by both prosodies (see sec:2.3.3 ).

distinguished the vowels in Moloko using four features: height, tense (or ATR), palatalisation, and labialisation. In this work, the conditioning environments that affect the phonetic expression of a full or epenthetic vowel include the labialisation and palatalisation prosodies ( sec:2.3.2 ) and adjacency of the epenthetic vowel to particular consonants ( sec:2.3.3 ).
summary: Moloko has ten surface phonetic vowels, but they are analyzed here as deriving from a single underlying vowel /a/, with schwa treated as epenthetic because its appearance is predictable. The absence of a vowel can require epenthetic schwa to break up consonant clusters, and different phonological environments produce the various vowel allophones, including [ø], which this work reports as occurring where both palatalisation and labialisation are present. The vowels are described in terms of height, tense/ATR, palatalisation, and labialisation, with these prosodies and adjacency to certain consonants conditioning their surface realization.

text:
tab:2.10 is a summary table showing the sources of allophonic variation and the resulting phonetic realisations and orthographic representations. In the table, the orthographic representation of each of these phonetic vowels is bolded and follows each vowel or example in the table. The orthographic representation is not employed elsewhere in the chapter, since it is important that the reader appreciate the phonetic expression. However, in the grammar chapters, the orthography is given for each example. For each source of allophonic variation, an example is also given. In a word which is neutral with respect to prosody (line 1), the underlying vowel is pronounced [a] and epenthetic schwa [ə]. In labialised words, (line 2), /a/ becomes [ɔ] and the epenthetic schwa becomes [ʊ]. In palatalised words (line 3), /a/ is pronounced [ɛ] and the epenthetic schwa is pronounced [ɪ]. The epenthetic vowel can also be assimilated to a neighbouring approximant: it is realised as [i] when it occurs beside [j] (line 4) and as [u] when it occurs beside a labialised velar [w, kʷ, gʷ, ŋgʷ, hʷ] (line 5). Under the influence of labialised velars and an adjacent /j/, the /a/ becomes [œ] and the epenthetic schwa becomes [ø] (line 6).

The working orthography for Moloko indicates the word-level processes by the three full vowel graphemes in the word pronounced in isolation: <e> in palatalised words, <o> in labialised words, and ‘a’ in words with neutral prosody. Even if the palatalisation or labialisation is incomplete in a word beginning with /a/, that first vowel is written <e> or <o>, respectively, in the orthography. Epenthetic vowels are written as <ə> in the orthographic representation regardless of the word prosody, because their pronunciation is predictable from the word prosody (discernable from the full vowel in the word) and the surrounding consonants. This results in four orthographic vowel symbols (a, e, o, ə).
summary: The passage explains that Moloko vowels show systematic allophonic variation based on prosody and surrounding consonants: neutral words pronounce /a/ as [a] and epenthetic schwa as [ə], while labialized and palatalized words shift these to [ɔ]/[ʊ] and [ɛ]/[ɪ], respectively. It also notes further assimilation of epenthetic vowels next to approximants or labialized velars, and describes the orthography, which uses four vowel symbols: <a> for neutral words, <e> for palatalized words, <o> for labialized words, and <ə> for epenthetic vowels regardless of pronunciation.

The passage describes how epenthetic vowels in the language are conditioned by adjacent semi-vowels /j/ and /w/ and by underlyingly labialised consonants. Bow found that the epenthetic vowel assimilates to the palatal or labial features of nearby /j/ or /w/, but that these semi-vowels themselves do not trigger word-level palatalisation or labialisation prosodies, and /a/ is unaffected by semi-vowels.

It also notes special vowel outcomes such as [œ] and [ø]: /a/ becomes [œ] before labialised velar /kʷ/ in a palatalised word, and epenthetic schwa between /j/ and a labialised velar can surface as [ø]. The data further suggest that underlyingly labialised velars influence adjacent vowels without spreading labialisation across the whole word.

text:
In addition to published manuscripts and a thesis, Bow produced a database and an extensive series of observations relating to lexical and grammatical tone in Moloko nouns and verbs. This database was later expanded and modified, leading to an initial analysis of tone in noun phrases by and later to tone in verbs by.

describes three phonetic tones (H, M, and L) but only two phonemic tones. In this work, lexical tone and grammatical tone are marked when relevant. Some data was transcribed without tone. The phonetic tone patterns will be indicated on the words using accent marks for H ( \' ), M ( \= ) when necessary, or L tone ( \` ). Because phonetic M can occur due to two causes (see below), this work carefully distinguishes underlying tones (H or L) from phonetic tones (H, M, and L).

tab:2.12 (adapted from with additional data) shows minimal pairs which illustrate the underlying two tone system in Moloko. Tone does not carry a high lexical load, and so there are only a limited number of lexical items distinguished by tone. One of each in these minimal pairs are marked in the orthography with a diacritic so that the pairs can be distinguished. The examples in tab:2.12 are divided into grammatical categories. Some of the minimal pairs are from different grammatical categories.

From an underlying two-tone system, with the influence of depressor consonants, certain melodies can be derived. There are different melodies for nouns and verbs. These melodies will be discussed in the noun and verb sections (see Sections sec:4.1 and sec:6.7 ). Bow described three different categories of verbs, those with underlying high tone, those with underlying low tone, and those with no underlying tone at all (toneless). A list of verbs showing their underlying tone is in Appendix sec:13.1.

Lexical tone itself is not marked in the orthography (or in examples in the morphosyntax part of this work) since there are only a few minimal pairs which are distinguished by a diacritic on one of the words in each pair. Imperfective and Perfective aspect Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfective aspect on verbs Tense, mood, and aspect!Imperfective aspect (indicated by grammatical tone) are distinguished by a diacritic on the subject pronominal verb prefix (see sec:7.4 ).
summary:
Bow’s work on Moloko tone builds on a database and observations of lexical and grammatical tone in nouns and verbs, which were later expanded into analyses of tone in noun phrases and verbs. The language is described as having three phonetic tones (H, M, L) but only two underlying phonemic tones, with lexical tone marked only sparingly because tone distinguishes only a small number of minimal pairs.

The passage also notes that phonetic tone patterns are written with accent marks, while underlying tones are distinguished from surface tones because phonetic mid tone can arise in more than one way. Moloko tone is organized into different melodies for nouns and verbs, and Bow distinguished three verb types: underlying high-tone, low-tone, and toneless verbs; grammatical tone is also used to contrast imperfective and perfective aspects.

text:
There are certain consonants which affect tone in Moloko. discovered that the voiced obstruents [b, d, g, mb, nd, ŋg, v, z, dz, nz, ɮ] notes that the phonemes /h, w, r, l/ can appear to function as depressors. have the effect of lowering the phonetic tone of the syllable in which they occur. notes that:

quote
“The most frequent form of interaction between tone and laryngeal features in African languages is the presence of ‘depressor' consonants. This term describes a subset of consonants, usually voiced, which lower the tone of neighbouring high tones, and may also block high spreading across them. This is a departure from the usual inertness of consonants in tonal systems[…]The set of depressor consonants may include all voiced consonants, or often only non-glottalized, non-implosive voiced obstruents. In some languages, such as Ewe, we find a three-way split, with voiced obstruents most active as depressors, voiceless obstruents as non-depressors, and voiced sonorants having some depressor effects, but fewer than the obstruents.
quote

Depressor consonants do not affect words that have an underlying high tone in Moloko. Words that are underlyingly low tone and contain no depressor consonants have phonetic mid tone, and words that are underlyingly low tone and contain depressor consonants have phonetic low tone. The phonetic low tone is triggered by the presence of depressor consonants. tab:2.13 demonstrates the effect of depressor consonants on the tone of the verb root in Moloko. The table shows minimal pairs of verb roots with phonetic mid and low tone with and without depressor consonants.
summary:
In Moloko, certain consonants—especially voiced obstruents such as [b, d, g, mb, nd, ŋg, v, z, dz, nz, ɮ], and possibly /h, w, r, l/—act as depressors that lower the phonetic tone of the syllable they occur in. The passage explains that depressor consonants are a common phenomenon in African tone systems, where they lower neighboring high tones or block high-tone spreading.

In Moloko specifically, depressor consonants do not affect words with underlying high tone. For underlying low-tone words, those without depressors surface with phonetic mid tone, while those with depressors surface with phonetic low tone, and the table cited shows minimal pairs illustrating this contrast in verb roots.

text: At the phrase level, found that a surface mid tone can have two sources: either an underlying low tone with no depressor consonants (see sec:2.4.1 ), or a surface high tone lowered by a preceding low. Bow found no LH melodies within words, and illustrated that a noun whose final syllable is low will lower a high tone on the first syllable of any word that follows. tab:2.14 (from ) illustrates high tone lowering. Bow also describes a spreading rule which is optional across word boundaries where the mid or high final tone of a noun optionally spreads over a low tone on the first syllable of an adjective.
summary: At the phrase level, Bow found that a surface mid tone can arise either from an underlying low tone without depressor consonants or from a surface high tone lowered by a preceding low tone. He reported no LH tone melodies within words, and showed that a noun with a final low syllable lowers the high tone on the first syllable of a following word. Bow also describes an optional spreading rule across word boundaries, in which a noun’s final mid or high tone may spread over a low tone on the first syllable of an adjective.

text: The syllable in Moloko is a somewhat fluid entity that makes a flexible relation between the underlying structure (consonantal skeleton with optional vowels) and the phonetic surface structure (see introduction to chap:2 ). has discussed the syllable in Moloko in detail. This section deals with aspects of syllable structure that pertain to the grammar ( sec:2.5.1 ) and syllable restructuring when words combine in speech ( sec:2.5.2 ).
summary: In Moloko, the syllable is a flexible unit linking the underlying consonantal skeleton, with optional vowels, to the phonetic surface form. The passage says that the section will discuss syllable structure as it relates to grammar and how syllables are restructured when words are combined in speech.

Bow notes that “[t]he basic syllable in Moloko has a consonantal onset, a vocalic nucleus and an optional consonant coda: CV(C), and carries tone”. She found three syllable types in Moloko: CV, CVC, and initial V. Both CV and CVC syllables can appear anywhere within the word. V syllables occur only in word-initial position and are most likely to have come from what was once a separate morpheme -- the / a- / prefix in nouns (see sec:4.1 ), the third singular prefix in verbs (see sec:7.3.1 ), and an adposition (see Sections sec:5.4.1 and sec:5.6.1 ).

Bow notes no restrictions on consonantal onsets. also discovered that although there are no restrictions on consonantal onsets for nouns, verb stems beginning with /n/ or /r/ are rare. noted that although nouns ending in CV can have any prosody (see sec:4.1 ), almost all verb stems phonetically ending in CV are palatalised ( ex:2:48 -- ex:2:49 ), where the V is the [ -ɛ] suffix discussed in sec:6.3. The only non-palatalised verb stems ending in CV end with the pluractional clitic =aya or =iya, e.g., [h=aja] ‘grind.’ [s=ija] ‘cut.’ see sec:7.5.2. These verbs do not occur without the clitic so we do not know if they carry an underlying prosody or /-j/ suffix.

Bow reported that liquids can function as the coda to a non-word-final syllable. also reports that liquids can function as the nucleus of a syllable and also as the second component of a consonantal onset. Further research has also shown that a semivowel /w/, /j/ or nasal /m, n/ can also function as the coda of a non word-final closed syllable ( ex:2:50 -- ex:2:52 ).

In fast speech, changes may happen within words or at word boundaries affecting adjacent syllables. At word boundaries, certain word-final consonants are lost and there may be vowel elision and reduction of vowels. Within the word, the segments may be restructured into new syllables, vowels may be reduced or deleted, and certain consonants may be deleted.

Specific phonological aspects of nouns and verbs will be discussed in their respective chapters (Chapters chap:4 and chap:6 ).

Word boundaries are established using both phonological and grammatical criteria, which allow the author to distinguish affixes, clitics, and extensions from separate words; these categories are discussed further for Moloko in later sections.

text:
Clitics!Criteria for|(

Five criteria are used to categorise affixes, clitics, and extensions in Moloko. The first is whether the morpheme can occur in discourse without being bound to some other morpheme. Affixes, clitics, and extensions in Moloko are bound morphemes -- they cannot occur alone in discourse. The second criterion is whether prosodies will spread freely between the stem and morpheme in question. Prosodies will always spread between affix and stem, and sometimes between clitic or extension and stem, but prosodies never spread across word boundaries. The third criterion is whether word-final alternations are found in the final consonant of the stem when a morpheme is attached. Suffixes, clitics, and extensions will always block word-final changes in the stem. The fourth and fifth criteria are to distinguish clitics from affixes. Clitics can attach to words of different syntactic categories; whereas no separate word can be inserted between an affix and its stem. Finally, clitics function at the phrase or clause level with grammatical rather than lexical meaning.. In contrast, affixes may have grammatical meaning but their meaning is applied to the word they modify.

What we have classified as an affix in Moloko is tightly bound to the stem. No morpheme known to be a separate word can occur between the affix and its stem. Prosodies spread freely between affix and stem. There are no word-final alternations in the final consonant of the stem when a suffix is attached. Examples of affixes in this section include the /a-/ prefix in nouns and subject pronominal prefixes and suffixes in verbs.

A clitic carries some of the characteristics of an affix and some of an independent word, and different clitics in Moloko fulfil the above criteria differently. A clitic is similar to an affix in that it is phonologically bound to the stem to which it is attached. However the nature of that phonological bondedness is different than for an affix and its stem. Grammatically, a clitic is different from an affix because a known separate word can occur in between the relevant stem and the clitic, and the clitic will then attach itself phonologically to the inserted word.

The verbal extensions are a special class of clitics which are something between a prototypical affix and a prototypical clitic. They form a close phonological unit with the verb stem. The phonological structure of the verb word is more fully discussed with examples in sec:7.1, but a few summary statements are included here. When there is no suffix on the verb, extensions will cliticise to the verb stem. Prosodies on verb clitics always spread to the verb stem (see sec:7.5 ). When there is a suffix on the verb, extensions form a separate phonological word and they cliticise to each other. In addition, the direct object pronominal extension is a separate word from the verb stem, but will be embedded amongst any other extensions that occur. In the presence of the direct object extension, the other extensions will cliticise to the direct object extension. The Perfect extension Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfect is a special enclitic in Moloko. It can occur at the end of the verb word or the end of the verb phrase (see sec:7.5.3 ). The Perfect extension appears to have a stronger phonological connection with the verb stem than the other extensions because the neutral prosody of the extension will neutralise the prosody of the verb word even if the Perfect is phrase-final with intervening words (see sec:7.5.3 ).

The adverbiser /Ca/ (see sec:3.5.2 ) is an interesting clitic in the way it is phonologically bound to its noun. The noun displays word-final changes, which would normally indicate a word break. However, initial consonant of the adverbiser enclitic is a reduplication of the final consonant of the noun (see sec:2.6.1.2 ) which indicates that the reduplication occurs after phonological word-final alterations are made to the noun.

We consider both the plural marker (see sec:4.2.2 ) and possessive (see sec:3.1.2 ) to be clitics even though neither the plural nor the possessive will affect the prosody of the stem (see sec:2.6.1 ). However, there are no word-final changes that indicate a word break on the stem when the plural or possessive is added. Both plural marker and possessive are phonologically bound to a stem yet modify a larger structure (a noun phrase). They are clitics and not affixes since they bind to elements of different grammatical classes (noun or noun phrase in the case of the possessive; noun, noun phrase, numeral, or pronoun in the case of the plural). Clitics!Criteria for|)
summary:
The passage sets out five criteria used in Moloko to distinguish affixes, clitics, and extensions, based on whether a morpheme can stand alone, how prosodies spread, whether stem-final alternations occur, whether other words can intervene, and whether the morpheme has word-level or phrase/clause-level function. Affixes are tightly bound to the stem, allow prosody to spread, and block stem-final alternations; clitics are also phonologically bound but can attach across grammatical categories and may have a separate word inserted before them.  

Verbal extensions are described as special clitics intermediate between affixes and prototypical clitics, with the Perfect extension having an especially strong phonological link to the verb. The adverbiser /Ca/, the plural marker, and the possessive are treated as clitics because they are phonologically bound without triggering stem-final word-break alternations and modify larger structures rather than just the stem.

text:
Moloko has the following grammatical classes, each described in the referenced sections or chapters below:

Note the absence of adjectives as a word class, since all adjectives in Moloko are derived from nouns ( sec:5.3 ).

In the following sections, a detailed treatment will be given for each of these word classes and the morphological structure of each class. An operational definition will be given for each class, so that any word in the language can be readily classified.

The first line in the examples is written in the orthography. The second line is the phonetic form for slow speech with morpheme breaks. All consonantal and vowel allophones are indicated. Palatisation and labialisation prosodies are discernible from the quality of the vowels and the consonants. When an underlying form (typically identified by / / brackets) is cited, only the consonants and the full vowels are written (i.e. not the epenthetic schwas) and the palatalisation or labialisation prosody on the form is marked by a superscripted ‘e’ or ‘o,’ respectively, after the morpheme.
summary: Moloko is described as having a set of grammatical word classes, with no separate adjective class because all adjectives are derived from nouns. The text says that each class will be treated in detail with an operational definition so words can be classified, and it also explains the notation used in examples, including orthographic and phonetic lines, morpheme breaks, allophones, and how palatalisation and labialisation are marked in underlying forms.

text:
Pronouns stand in the place of a noun phrase in a clause. Pronouns are deictic elements -- their reference changes according to the context of the utterance. The role of the speaker furnishes the basic point of reference (first person). The addressee is defined with respect to the speaker (second person). The third person pronouns refer to people or things being talked about by the first and second persons. There are definite and indefinite third person pronouns. Definite pronouns can be used anaphorically Cohesion!Anaphoric referencing, and their reference is determined by linguistic or pragmatic elements in the textual or extratextual environment. Indefinite pronouns have a non-identified referent.

Moloko personal pronouns and proforms are illustrated in tab:3.15. Moloko has one set of free personal pronouns (regular, see sec:3.1.1.1 ), one set of bound pronouns (possessive, see sec:3.1.2 ), and three sets of pronominals within the verb complex for subject, direct object, and indirect object (see sec:7.3 ). All personal pronouns and pronominals are shown in tab:3.15. The regular free pronouns can refer to any of the subject or direct object or indirect object. An emphatic subset of free pronouns exists, formed by adding the adjectiviser ga to the regular personal pronouns. Possessive pronouns always occur within a noun phrase or a relative clause. Special vocative pronouns that attach to nouns are honorific ( sec:3.1.3 ). There are also interrogative pronouns ( sec:3.1.4 ) and unspecified pronouns ( sec:3.1.5 ).

In some of the pronoun sets, there is an inclusive/exclusive distinction in the first person plural. There are no dual nor gender-specific forms, nor are there logophoric pronouns. describes the types of logophoric systems found in some Chadic languages. No logophoric pronouns are described for Biu-Mandara.
summary:
Pronouns replace noun phrases in a clause and are deictic, with reference depending on context: first person refers to the speaker, second person to the addressee, and third person to what is being talked about. Third person pronouns may be definite and used anaphorically, or indefinite with non-identified referents.

In Moloko, there are free personal pronouns, bound possessive pronouns, and pronominal forms inside the verb complex for subject, direct object, and indirect object. The language also has emphatic, vocative, interrogative, and unspecified pronouns, with an inclusive/exclusive distinction in some first-person plural forms, but no dual, gender-specific, or logophoric pronouns.

text: Free pronouns express subject, direct object, and indirect object. They are relatively rare in texts since participants are generally tracked by the bound verbal pronominals. Free pronouns are found in cases of switch reference, at the peak Focus and prominence!Discourse peak of a story where the verbal pronominals disappear, or in cases of emphasis (see sec:3.1.1.2 ).
summary: Free pronouns can function as subjects, direct objects, and indirect objects, but they are relatively uncommon in texts because participants are usually tracked by bound verbal pronominals. They appear mainly in switch-reference contexts, at discourse peaks where the verbal pronominals disappear, and when emphasis is needed.

text:
When free subject, direct object, or indirect object pronouns do occur, they are in the same place within a clause or noun phrase where one would expect the full noun phrase to be (see Sections sec:5.1 and sec:10.1 ).

Note that the subject is also indicated on the verb by the subject pronominal a- and the indirect object is indicated on the verb by the indirect object pronominal enclitic =an (see sec:7.3.2 ). The noun phrase representing the indirect object is embedded in a prepositional phrase (see sec:5.6.1 ). The first line in each example is the orthographic form. The second is the phonetic form (slow speech) with morpheme breaks.

When the subject is replaced by a free pronoun ex:3:2, the pronoun must be marked as presupposed in the clause (see sec:11.2 ). In the examples, the subject is also marked on the verb, the direct object pronoun replaces the object NP in the usual object slot, and the indirect object pronoun appears in a prepositional phrase while the verb also carries an indirect object enclitic. The enclitic can even replace the entire prepositional phrase expressing the indirect object.

Clitics!Possessive pronoun

Another set of Moloko pronouns occurs only within noun phrases and among its primary uses, indicates a possessive relationship, i.e. these pronouns relate the possessor referent to the person or thing that is possessed. Possessive pronouns immediately follow the noun or noun phrase they modify ( ex:3:9 -- ex:3:11 ) and occur before the plural clitic ex:3:12. postulated that the set of possessive pronouns does not include the plural possessive pronouns. Rather, she proposed that the plural possessive is actually an associative noun phrase formed by the preposition /a/ and the free pronoun ( a loko, a ləme, a ləkwəye, and a təta ). We found that possessives are viewed as a set in the minds of speakers, and that there is no difference in distribution between singular and plural possessives. Therefore we will treat the possessive pronouns as a set in Moloko ( aloko, aləme, aləkwəye, and atəta ).

We consider the possessive pronouns to be noun clitics. They are phonologically bound to the noun. Even though prosodies on the possessive pronouns do not spread to the noun ( ex:3:9 -- ex:3:10 ), demonstrated that word-final changes indicating a word break do not occur ( tab:3.16 ). They are clitics, not affixes, since they bind to the right edge of the head of the noun phrase, binding to the final noun where the head is composed of more than one noun, yet modifying the entire structure ( ex:3:11 ) (see sec:5.4.2 ).
summary:
Moloko possessive pronouns occur only inside noun phrases and indicate a possessive relation between a possessor and the possessed noun. They immediately follow the noun or noun phrase they modify, and the plural forms are treated as part of the same possessive pronoun set because their distribution does not differ from the singular forms.

The passage argues that these possessive pronouns are noun clitics: they are phonologically bound to the noun, but they are not affixes because they attach to the right edge of the noun phrase’s head while modifying the whole structure.

concluded that the underlying tone melody for possessive pronouns is HLH. tab:3.17 (from ) shows the surface tonal melodies and underlying tone pattern for all the possessive pronouns with the noun [ ɗ\=af] ‘loaf.’ In Moloko, ɗaf is the basic starch form consumed by the people, a millet porridge eaten with various sauces. summary: The passage argues that possessive pronouns in Moloko have an underlying HLH tone melody, even though their surface forms vary depending on the noun and phonological environment. Singular forms with only two syllables lose the final high tone, most forms show an HM(H) pattern, and the pronoun with the depressor consonant /ŋg/ has a low second syllable; nevertheless, the possessive pronoun keeps its tonal melody across environments. It also notes that a noun with a low surface tone from a depressor consonant can lower the first high tone of certain possessive pronouns.

Deixis!Demonstratives and demonstrationals|(

Moloko has three main types of demonstratives: nominal demonstratives ( sec:3.2.1 ), which point to a person or object and modify a noun in a noun phrase, local adverbial demonstratives ( sec:3.2.2 ), which point to a place and modify a noun in a noun phrase, and manner adverbal demonstratives ( sec:3.2.3 ), which point to an action and modify a verb. describes three types of demonstratives: nominal, local adverbial, and verbal. Verbal demonstratives do not occur in Moloko. Dixon considers manner adverbial demonstratives to be a subtype of nominal demonstratives. Manner adverbials are derived from local adverbial denonstratives.

tab:3.20 shows a complete list of demonstratives in Moloko. All demonstratives have the same form for both singular and plural referents. All are anaphoric in their basic use in that the referent must be known from the preceding context. For comparison, place/time adverbs are also shown. The proximal demonstratives are morphologically similar to the locational adverb ehe ‘here/now’ (shown for comparison in tab:3.20 ).

It can be seen that the near speaker and distant from speaker demonstratives are morphologically derived from the corresponding adverbs. Note that there are no non-visible demonstratives or place/time adverbs.

summary:
Moloko has three main types of demonstratives: nominal demonstratives that modify nouns, local adverbial demonstratives that point to places, and manner adverbial demonstratives that modify verbs, though verbal demonstratives do not actually occur in the language. All demonstratives have the same form in singular and plural and are anaphoric in basic use, requiring a referent known from prior context.  

The proximal forms are morphologically similar to the locational adverb *ehe* ‘here/now’, and the near-speaker and distant-from-speaker demonstratives are derived from the corresponding adverbs. There are no non-visible demonstratives or place/time adverbs.

Nominal demonstratives ( ex:3:46 -- ex:3:48 ) have a referent that is a person or object. They modify a noun within a noun phrase to specify or point out the referent. Moloko has two nominal demonstratives: proximal (near the speaker) and distal (away from the speaker). There is no nominal demonstrative to indicate a referent that is far away from the speaker. In the examples in this section, the demonstrative is bolded and the noun phrase is marked by square brackets. In ex:3:55 from sec:3.2.2.1, the demonstrative is head of the noun phrase, suggesting that it can act as a demonstrative pronoun.

At the conclusion of the Disobedient Girl story, nominal demonstratives are used anaphorically to mark two different referents -- the suffering brought to the Moloko people and the young girl whose disobedience resulted in the suffering. Both are shown in ex:3:50. The beginning of the Disobedient Girl story describes the blessing -- that Moloko people could make an entire meal for a whole family from one grain of millet. The blessing occurred because the millet would multiply during its grinding. The story describes how a young, newly-married non-Moloko girl hears how to handle the millet yet disobeys the rules on how to handle it. As a result, the disobedient girl was killed by the millet. The story tells how the Creator was offended by her act and withdrew his blessing from the Moloko people such that millet would not multiply any more and the Moloko had to work hard to even get enough food to feed their families. The suffering that the Moloko people experienced as a result of the withdrawal of God’s blessing is described in lines 33-37 but it is not named as such until line S. 38. In that line, the particular suffering of the Moloko people that was brought on by the girl is marked by the proximal nominal demonstrative avəya nengehe ‘this particular previously mentioned suffering.' Also, the young woman who, by her disobedience, brought suffering to the entire Moloko population is marked in lines 33 and 38 by the distal nominal demonstrative. text: Local adverbial demonstratives point to a referent that is a place (physical or metaphorical). They commonly occur with a noun but can also occur as the only element in a noun phrase. Moloko has four local adverbial demonstratives: proximal (near the speaker), distal (away from the speaker) ( sec:3.2.2.1 ), far away from the speaker, and an anaphoric demonstrative used only in discourse ( sec:3.2.2.2 ).
summary: Local adverbial demonstratives refer to places, either physical or metaphorical, and typically occur with a noun, though they can also stand alone as the only element in a noun phrase. Moloko has four such demonstratives: proximal, distal, far away from the speaker, and an anaphoric form used only in discourse.

Sometimes local adverbial demonstratives Focus and prominence!Local adverbial demonstratives|( have a highlighting function for new information in a narrative, drawing attention to their referent. mentions that demonstratives can function to introduce new information. Note that in Moloko, all new information need not be marked with a demonstrative. In the ‘Cows in the Field’ story (not illustrated in its entirety in this work), ɗerəywel nendəge ‘this paper here’ ex:3:60 was not with the speaker when he told the story; neither was it previously mentioned in the discourse. According to the discourse, the paper should have helped to bring justice to the men whose cotton was destroyed, but it didn’t. Its marking with a demonstrative therefore has the function to highlight the paper at that moment of the event line.

Alala na, ta anaw [ɗerəywel nendəge ].\\

In the Values exhortation ( ex:3:61, shown in its entirety in sec:1.7 ) the local adverbial demonstrative nehe ‘this here’ is used to draw attention to new information. In the exhortation, the phrase ele nehe ‘these things here’ introduces information not previously mentioned in the discourse. Note that the local adverbial demonstrative nəndəye ‘here’ in the same example functions to simply point out a place in the phrase təta a məsəyon na ava nəndəye ‘the ones in church there’. Also, compare the function of the proximal local adverbial demonstrative nehe with that of the proximal nominal demonstrative nəngehe in the same example. The nominal demonstrative ( sec:3.2.1 ) in the phrase ele=ahay aməgəye bay nəngehe ‘these particular things that one shouldn’t do’ points out particular things which are previously mentioned. This information -- the things that people are not supposed to do -- is the main topic of the entire discourse. The demonstrative notifies the reader of the importance of the new information. Note that the demonstrative is not functioning cataphorically here. It is the narrator who specifies the things that people are not supposed to do in the discourse which follows (S. 4--5 in ex:3:61 ), not the pastor in his speech.
summary:
Proximal and distal local adverbial demonstratives refer to places like ‘here’ and ‘there,’ and in noun phrases they occur as a separate final element rather than in the position used by nominal demonstratives. They can also head a noun phrase, and for distant locations the locative adverb toho is used in possessive or genitive constructions with the noun.  

The passage also shows that local adverbial demonstratives may be used to point out a location in discourse and sometimes to highlight new or prominent information, while nominal demonstratives refer to previously mentioned or already topical information.

Manner adverbial demonstratives have been described by to function as non-inflecting modifiers to verbs. There are two types in Moloko, depending on how they are derived. notes that manner adverbial demonstratives are morphologically derived from nominal demonstratives. In Moloko they are derived from the nominal demonstrative.

The first type in Moloko is derived from the demonstrative by the addition of ka ‘like.’ The adverbial demonstrative ka nehe ‘like this’ ex:3:69 is used when the speaker indicates with hand or body movements how a particular action is carried out. It is derived from the proximal nominal demonstrative nehe ‘this here’ (see sec:3.2.2.1 ).

summary:
The passage says that Moloko has two types of manner adverbial demonstratives, both functioning as non-inflecting verb modifiers and both morphologically derived from other forms. One type is built from nominal demonstratives with **ka** ‘like’ (e.g. **ka nehe** ‘like this’ for a visible manner, and **ka ndana** ‘like what was just said,’ which can also be negated), while the second type is formed from the adverb **ehe** with the tag **kəyga**, yielding forms such as **kəygehe** ‘like this/that way.’  

These forms are used to indicate manner or direction, often accompanied by gestures showing how an action is performed or where it takes place.

tab:3.21 shows that the numbers one to ten are unique. The numbers eleven through nineteen are composites of ten plus one, ten plus two, etc. The word to indicate ‘plus’ is hər, which has no other meaning in the language. Twenty is kokər cew, which is some kind of derivitave of kəro ‘ten.’ After 100, numbers are made of a coordinate noun phrase composed of səkat ‘one hundred,’ the adposition nə ‘with,’ and a second number. One thousand is dəbo, and higher numbers are seen as multiples of dəbo.

There is a culturally governed exception to the use of cardinal numbers in Moloko. To give the age of a one year old child, a Moloko speaker will say məvəye daz (not * məvəye bəlen ‘year one’). Məvəye daz means that the child has lived through one Moloko New Year (celebrated in September). We found no other meaning for the word daz apart from its use here.
summary: Moloko cardinal numbers follow a base-ten system: one to ten are unique, eleven to nineteen are formed as ten plus another numeral using the word hər ‘plus,’ twenty is a derived form of ‘ten,’ and larger numbers are built with “one hundred + with + number” or as multiples of ‘one thousand.’ When used with nouns, numerals follow the noun, but they can also stand alone as the head of a noun phrase if the context makes the referent clear. An exception is the expression for a one-year-old child’s age, which uses məvəye daz rather than the expected numeral form.

text:
Money is counted using two different systems which overlap (see tab:3.22 ). A base-five system is used for amounts under about 250 Central African Francs (Fcfa). Many languages in Cameroon use a base five system for counting money. The reason for its use is probably based on the fact that the smallest coin was worth 5 Fcfa, and it became the basic unit for monetary transactions. The generic term for money in Moloko is dala, possibly a borrowed term from the American dollar. Ten francs, being two of these coins, is dal cew ‘two coins,’ fifteen francs is dal makar ‘three coins,’ and so on (the values for the other coins that were available are indicated in the left column of tab:3.22 ). The system becomes awkward for higher amounts (above 50 coins, or 250 Fcfa) because of the high numbers, and a base ten system is superimposed (right column of tab:3.22 ). Between 100 Fcfa and 250 Fcfa, both the base five and base ten are used, although within the Moloko mountain region, the base five system predominates.

The basic unit for the monitary base ten system is the 100 Fcfa coin ( səloy səkat ‘coin 100’). This system uses the same number for one hundred as the system for counting items ( səkat ). Ten of these coins make the 1000 Fcfa bill, so not unexpectedly, the term for the 1000 Fcfa bill is not the same as the number ‘1000’ for counting non-money items ( dəbo see tab:3.21 ), but rather is a term specific to money -- ombolo.

When larger amounts of money are counted, both base ten and base five systems are used. For example, 13,250 Fcfa is ombolo kəro hər makar nə səloy kokər zlom ‘thirteen thousand Fcfa (base ten) and fifty 5 Fcfa coins (base five)’ (lit. 13 thousand with 50 5Fcfa coins).

It is interesting that recently, a one franc coin has been made available in Cameroon. The term for this coin wasn’t in the original counting system where the 5 Fcfa coin was the basic unit. It is now called el\'e bəlen literally ‘one eye.’
summary: Money in Moloko is counted with two overlapping systems: a base-five system for amounts below about 250 Fcfa, and a superimposed base-ten system for larger amounts. The base-five system likely developed because the smallest coin was worth 5 Fcfa, while the base-ten system uses the 100 Fcfa coin as its basic unit and has a special term, *ombolo*, for the 1000 Fcfa bill. Recently introduced 1 Fcfa coins were not part of the original system and are now called *el'e bəlen* ‘one eye.’

text:
Moloko has three positive existentials and one negative existential. The prototypical existential aba ‘there exists’ ex:3:85. carries the most basic idea of existence. Its negative is abay ‘there does not exist.’ Historically, this existential is perhaps a compound of the existential aba and the negative bay. The locational existential ava ‘there exists in a particular place,’ and the possessive existential aka ‘there exists associated with’ each carry the concept of existence along with their own specific meaning. The possessive existential must be accompanied by a indirect object pronominal.

Existentials are verb-like and fill the verb slot in a clause, but are not conjugated for aspect or mood and do not take subject or direct object pronominals. Some of the existentials can carry verbal extensions or indirect object pronominals. The existential clause contains few elements -- most commonly just a subject and the existential. The existential clause can be in a presupposition construction ( chap:11 ) or an interrogative construction ( sec:10.3 ).

The prototypical existential is aba ‘there is’ ( ex:3:85 -- ex:3:86 ) and its negative is abay ‘there is none’ ( ex:3:87 -- ex:3:88 ). A clause with one of these existentials requires a subject but there are no other core participants or obliques. The existential is bolded in the examples.

Existentials are verb-like clause heads but are not inflected for aspect or mood and do not take subject or direct object pronominals; existential clauses are typically very simple, often containing only a subject and the existential.  

The prototypical existential **aba** and its negative **abay** are used both for ordinary existence/possession and for greetings or health questions, and **aba** also introduces participants in presentational narrative clauses. The locational existential **ava** expresses existence in a specific place and can co-occur with **aba** in presentational contexts; the possessive existential **aka** requires an indirect object pronominal.

The possessive existential **aka** ‘there is on’ expresses existence on a person, indicating possession or accompaniment, and is formally the same element used for the adpositional verbal extension and the locational postposition meaning ‘on.’ In possessive constructions, the possessed noun is followed by the indirect object pronominal cliticized to **an-**, then **aka**, in the same order as in the verb complex.

text: Some adverbs modify verbs within the verb phrase (simple or derived, Sections sec:3.5.1 and sec:3.5.2, respectively), others modify the clause as a whole (temporal adverbs, sec:3.5.3 ), and yet others function at the discourse level ( sec:3.5.4 ). Note that ideophones can function adverbially to give pictoral vividness to a clause. Because they pattern differently than adverbs, they are considered in their own section ( sec:3.6 ).
summary: Adverbs may modify a verb within the verb phrase, modify the clause as a whole, or operate at the discourse level. Ideophones can also function adverbially to add vivid, pictorial force to a clause, but since they behave differently from adverbs, they are treated separately.

text:
Derivational processes!Noun to adverb

Verb phrase adverbs can be derived from nouns by reduplicating the final consonant of the noun and adding [a] (i.e. Ca where the C is the final consonant of the noun). The reduplicated syllable is labelled ‘adverbiser’  We have not found the term ‘adverbiser’ in the literature. Adverbiser in this work is defined as a derivational morpheme whose presence changes the grammatical class of a stem to become an adverb. in ( ex:3:116 -- ex:3:117 ). Compare the noun and its derived adverb in ex:3:116 and ex:3:117. Note that the reduplicated consonant in the derived adverb in example ex:3:116 is the word-final allophone [x] rather than word-medial [h]. Likewise, example ex:3:117 shows [ŋ] rather than [n]. These word-final changes (see sec:2.6.1 ) in the reduplicated consonant indicate that the reduplication occurs after phonological word-final changes are made and that the reduplicated segment is phonologically bound to the noun (see sec:2.6.2 ).

Discourse adverbs occur at the clause-combining level and are grammatically placed in verb-final position. Semantically, they relate the clause to the preceding discourse, and they cannot be negated or intensified by reduplication.

text:
Ideophone|(

Ideophones are a “vivid representation of an idea in sound”. They evoke the ``idea'' of a sensation or sensory perception (action, movement, colour, sound, smell, or shape). As such they are often onomatopoeic.

Ideophones are found in strategic places in narratives (both in legends and in true stories) and add vividness to major points in exhortations. At the peak moment of a story, ideophones can present the entire event expressed in a sentence. In such cases the clause may have no expressed subject or object – a transitivity of zero.

suggests that ideophones do not comprise a grammatical class of their own, but rather are words from several different classes (including nouns, adjectives, and adverbs) which are grouped together based on phonological and semantic similarities rather than syntax. Ideophones are treated as a separate grammatical class in Moloko since although they may fill the noun, verb, or adverb slot in a clause, ideophones do not pattern as typical nouns, verbs, or adverbs. sec:3.6.1 describes the semantic and phonological features of ideophones, sec:3.6.2 discusses their syntax and their role in discourse, and sec:3.6.3 discusses the fact that a clause where an ideophone fills the verb slot can carry zero transitivity.
summary:
Ideophones are vivid sound-symbolic expressions that evoke sensory experiences such as action, movement, colour, sound, smell, or shape, and are often onomatopoeic. They are used especially at key points in narratives and exhortations, where they can compress an entire event into a clause with no expressed subject or object, resulting in zero transitivity.

The passage also contrasts two analyses: one treats ideophones as a collection of words from different grammatical classes grouped by phonological and semantic similarities, while in Moloko they are treated as a separate class because they do not behave like typical nouns, verbs, or adverbs even when they fill those clause positions.

subsection: Semantic and phonological features of ideophones
text:
Ideophones carry an idea of a particular state or event -- Moloko speakers can imagine the particular situation and the sensation of it when they hear a particular ideophone. The sensation may be a sound ex:3:131, vision ex:3:132, taste ex:3:133, feeling ex:3:134, or even an abstract idea (for example, an insult, ex:3:135 ).

gəɗəgəzl\\
g\`əɗ\`əg\`əɮ\\
‘the noise of something closing or being set down’

danjəw\\
dànzúw\\
‘sight of someone walking balancing something on their head’

poɗococo\\
p\`ɔɗ\'ɔts\'ɔts\'ɔ\\
‘taste of sweetness’

pəyecece\\

‘feeling of coldness’

kekəf kəf kekəf kəf\\
k\`ɛk\'ɪf k\'ɪf k\`ɛk\'ɪf k\'ɪf\\
‘imagination of someone who hasn’t any weight’ (an insult)

Ideophones have specific meanings; compare the following three ideophones in ( ex:3:136 -- ex:3:138 ). The ideophones differ in only their final syllable.

‘sound of a whip’

‘sight of the start of a race’

Ideophones do not follow the stress rules for the language ( chap:2 ). Some ideophones are stressed on the initial syllable (shown by full vowels in ex:3:135 ) while others have no full vowel ( ex:3:131, ex:3:139, ex:3:142 ).

jəɓ jəɓ\\
dʒɪɓ dʒɪɓ\\
‘completely wet’

Moloko ideophones sometimes contain unusual sounds, including the labiodental flap [ ], marked as vb in the orthography. The labiodental flap is found only in ideophones that carry a neutral prosody.

vbaɓ\\
àɓ\\
‘sound of something soft hitting the ground’ (a snake, or a mud wall collapsing)

Ideophones often have reduplicated segments as shown in ex:3:141 (see also ex:3:133, ex:3:134, ex:3:135 for additional examples).

həɓek həɓek\\
hìɓ\'ɛk hìɓ\'ɛk\\
‘hardly breathing’ (almost dead)

Some ideophones require a context in order for their meaning to be understood clearly; others give a clear meaning even if they are spoken in isolation. Ideophones which carry a distinctive lexical meaning even when spoken in isolation are exemplified by ex:3:142. If a Moloko speaker hears someone say njəw njəw, they know that the speaker is talking about someone grinding something on a grinding stone. Likewise see also ex:3:131, ( ex:3:133 -- ex:3:135 ), ex:3:141, ex:3:143, and ex:3:160.

njəw njəw\\
nzùw nzùw\\
‘the sound of someone grinding something on a grinding stone’

pəcəkəɗək\\
p\'ʊts\'ʊk\'ʊɗ\'ʊk\\
‘the sight of a toad hopping’

In contrast, a Moloko speaker will need to understand a wider context to determine the meaning of dergwejek ex:3:144, which requires a context for the listener to understand the detail of the picture. In the same way, ex:3:140 also requires a context to specify its exact meaning (snake falling or wall collapsing).

dergwecek\\
dɛrgʷɛtʃɛk\\
‘sight of someone lifting something onto their head’
summary:
Moloko ideophones evoke a particular state or event so vividly that speakers can imagine the associated sensation, which may involve sound, sight, taste, feeling, or even an abstract idea like an insult. They have highly specific meanings, may differ by only a small phonological change, do not follow normal stress patterns, and can include unusual sounds and reduplicated segments.

Some ideophones have a clear lexical meaning even in isolation, while others need a wider context to be fully interpreted. The passage also notes that certain forms use distinctive sounds such as the labiodental flap and that context may be necessary to distinguish closely related meanings.

text:
Attribution!Ideophones

In a sentence, an ideophone can function as a noun, adverb, or verb. As a noun, the ideophone carries a descriptive picture with certain features. Ideophones that are lexical nouns ( ex:3:145 -- ex:3:147, see also ex:3:133 and ex:3:134 ) can function as the head of a noun phrase, but they cannot be pluralised or modified by noun phrase constituents except with the adjectiviser ga. In example ex:3:147, the ideophone mbajak mbajak mbajak ‘something big and reflective’ is the direct object of the clause. The ideophones are bolded in the examples.

summary: Ideophones in this language can function as nouns, adverbs, or verbs. As nouns, they may head a noun phrase but cannot be pluralized or modified by most noun phrase constituents except with adjectiviser *ga*; as adverbs, they describe both the subject and the manner of the action, usually appearing clause-finally with finite verbs or before non-inflected verb complexes, and they cannot be negated. At discourse peaks and other vivid moments, ideophones may even fill the verb slot, taking verbal extensions and pronominals, and sometimes constitute the entire clause.

Transitivity!Clauses with zero transitivity|(

chap:9 discusses the semantics of Moloko verbs for different numbers of core grammatical relations. Moloko verbs can have from zero to four grammatical relations, three of which can be coded as part of the verb complex. Similarly, in clauses where ideophones fill the verb slot, the clause can have from zero to three explicit grammatical relations. The cases where the ideophone clause requires no explicit grammatical relations presents a most interesting situation. The clause displays a grammatical transitivity of zero, even though it expresses a semantic event with participants. The use of ideophones makes the moment vivid and draws the listener into the story as if it was present before them so that the hearer can see and hear and imagine that they are participating in what is going on. This is a narrative device found in Moloko peak episodes. Focus and prominence!Discourse peak

For example, ideophones make up the entire clause in lines S. 28 and 29 at the peak of the Cicada text (example ex:3:157 above). On hearing the ideophones kəwna and dergwejek, the hearer knows that someone has a hold of something, and then lifts it up onto his head to carry it. Two participants are understood, but the actual number of grammatical relations in the clauses is zero. The hearer must infer from the context that it was the cicada (the unexpected participant) who is doing the lifting and carrying. The cicada being so small, the people actually watching the event would not know for sure who was moving the tree either, since it would look like the tree was moving all by itself. Thus the use of ideophones with zero grammatical relations contributes to the visualisation of the story and makes the listener more of an actual participant in the events of the story.

Likewise, in line S. 21 of the Disobedient Girl story ex:3:159 the clause has no expressed subject, direct or indirect object. The verb /h/ is in nominalised form with no pronominals to indicate participants. If a Moloko person hears the ideophone njəw njəw, he or she knows that someone is grinding something. In the context of the story, the woman is grinding millet, but the millet is expanding to fill the room and eventually will crush the woman. The clause only gives a picture/sound/idea of grinding with gaps in knowledge that the listener must work to fill in for themselves, th thus drawing the listener into the story.

A third example is found in the Snake story. In S. 14 and 15, both the ideophone clause (S.14) and the nominalised form plus ideophone (S.15) have zero grammatical relations ex:3:160. The speaker is making both himself and the snake ‘invisible’ at this peak moment of his story Focus and prominence!Discourse peak. The effect would be to allow the hearer to imagine themselves there right beside the speaker in the darkness, wondering where the snake was, hearing only the sounds of the events.

summary:
The passage explains that Moloko clauses can have zero grammatical transitivity when ideophones occupy the verb slot and no core grammatical relations are expressed, even though participants are understood from context. Such clauses are used in peak narrative moments to make events vivid and immersive, requiring listeners to infer missing participants and thereby feel drawn into the story.

Examples from several stories show ideophone clauses with no explicit subject or object, where the listener understands actions like lifting, grinding, or penetrating from the sound symbolism and narrative context. In each case, the zero-transitivity structure enhances visualization and creates a strong discourse effect of prominence.

The most prototypical nouns are those denoting something temporally stable, compact, physically concrete and made out of durable material, with a number of defining sub-features, but the class extends also to include a range of more abstract concepts.
