Moloko nouns (or noun phrases) carry no overt case markers themselves; the function of the various noun phrases in a clause is indicated by the word order in the clause, pronominal marking in verbs (see sec:7.3 ), and adpositions ( sec:5.6 ).
summary: Moloko nouns head noun phrases, and noun phrases can function as clause arguments. The noun class includes prototypical concrete, stable entities as well as more abstract concepts, and nouns are identified morphosyntactically by patterns such as plural marking, possessive or demonstrative forms, and combinations with numerals and modifiers. Moloko nouns do not take overt case markers; their clause function is shown by word order, pronominal marking on verbs, and adpositions.

There are many Moloko nouns whose first syllable is V. This syllable may be historically an old /a-/ prefix. Nouns with these /a-/ prefixes can only be discovered by comparing Moloko vocabulary with that of other related languages where the nouns do not carry the prefix. tab:4.25 illustrates three nouns in Moloko and in Mbuko Mbuko.,. Judging from the number of nouns in the Moloko database that begin with m, there may be some kind of an old / m- / prefix as well.

discovered that tonal melodies on nouns are different than for verbs (see sec:6.7 for verb tone melodies). tab:4.26 (from ) shows how the underlying tone melodies are realised on the surface in one, two, and three syllable nouns. The left column gives examples with no depressor consonants (see sec:2.4.1 ), and the right column contains nouns with depressor consonants which effect different tone melodies. For one syllable nouns, only two tonal melodies are possible (H or L). For two syllable nouns, H, L, HL, or LH are possible. For three syllable nouns, H, L, HL, LH, HLH, and LHL are possible. Note that a surface mid tone can result from two sources. It can be an underlying high tone that has been lowered by a preceding low tone Therefore there are no surface LH combinations since an underlying LH will be realised as LM. or it can be an underlying low tone in a word with no depressor consonants. There are also very few examples of ML combinations in the surface form. The only example was [ k\`ɪm\=ɛdʒ\`ɛ], an underlying LHL that had depressor consonants.

Tonal melodies on nouns

summary:
The passage describes noun syllable patterns in Moloko, noting that syllable structure is independent of prosody and that CVC nouns are much more common than CV nouns, while many apparent CVCV nouns are actually reduplicated forms. It also observes many nouns beginning with V, possibly from an old /a-/ prefix, and suggests there may be an old /m-/ prefix as well.

The text further explains that noun tone patterns differ from verb tone patterns. One-syllable nouns have only H or L tones, two-syllable nouns can have H, L, HL, or LH, and three-syllable nouns can have H, L, HL, LH, HLH, or LHL, with depressor consonants affecting the surface realization of these tonal melodies.

section: Morphological structure of the noun word
text:
Moloko noun words are morphologically simple compared with verbs. A noun can be comprised of just a noun stem, We refer to the simplest form as a stem because it can be more complex than a root in that it can have an /a-/ prefix. a compound noun, or a nominalised verb.

A noun stem can consist of a simple noun root ex:4:16 or two reduplicated segments ex:4:17. These reduplicated elements actually form two separate phonological words (note the word-final alteration ŋ in both segments) but are lexically one item. Because there are word-final consonant changes for only /n/ and /h/, it is not known whether all similar reduplications necessarily form two separate phonological words.

hay\\
hàj\\
‘house’

ndən nden\\
ndəŋ ndɛŋ\\
‘traditional sword’

Nouns can be derived from verbs Derivational processes!Verb to noun by a potentially complex process where a prefix, a suffix, and palatalisation are added. The prefix is mə- or me-, depending on whether the verb has the /a-/ prefix or not. The suffix is -əye or -e, depending on whether the verb root has one or more consonants. The suffix carries palatalisation which palatalises the whole word. The resulting form is an abstract noun which cannot take the plural =ahay but which otherwise has all the characteristics of a noun. This highly productive process is discussed further in sec:7.6 but two nominalisations are shown here. In ex:4:18 and ex:4:19, the underlying form, the imperative, and the nominalised form are given. A one-syllable verb with no prefix takes the prefix mə- and the suffix -əye ex:4:18. A two consonant root with /a-/ prefix takes the prefix me- and the suffix -e ex:4:19.

Another nominalisation process can be postulated when noun stems and verb roots are compared. This second nominalisation process is irregular and non-productive. tab:4.27 illustrates a few examples and compares verb roots with their counterpart regular and irregular nominalisations. In each case, the consonants in the nouns in both nominalised forms are the same as those for the underlying verb root. Derivational processes!Verb to noun These data show that in the irregular set of nominalisations, there is no set process of nominalisation --- in some cases an / a- / prefix is added (see lines 1 and 2); in other cases the prosody is changed to form the irregular nominalised form (from palatalised to neutral in line 4, from neutral to palatalised in lines 3, 5, and 6).

When the irregular nominalisations are compared with the regular nominalised form in tab:4.27, it can be seen that the two types of nouns relate to the sense of the verbs in different ways. The regular nominalisation refers to the event or the process itself (stealing, carrying, sending, etc.), whereas the irregular nominalisation denotes some kind of a referent involved in the event (thief, work, hand, etc.).

Two processes denominalise nouns; one forms adjectives ( sec:4.3 ) and the other, adverbs (see sec:3.5.2 ). It is not possible to derive a verb from a noun root or stem in Moloko.
summary: Moloko noun words are relatively simple morphologically: they may be just a noun stem, a compound noun, or a nominalised verb, and stems may consist of a simple root or reduplicated segments. Nouns can be derived from verbs by a productive process involving a prefix, a suffix, and palatalisation, producing abstract nouns that cannot pluralize, and there is also an irregular, non-productive nominalisation that yields nouns referring to participants or entities involved in the event rather than the event itself. The passage also notes that nouns can be denominalised into adjectives or adverbs, but verbs cannot be derived from noun roots or stems.

section: Morphological structure of the noun word
text:
Noun class!Sub-classes of nouns|(

There are no distinct morphological noun classes in Moloko. Those nouns with an /a-/ prefix Noun class!A-prefix could perhaps be considered a separate class (see sec:4.1 ), but this phenomenon is more of an interesting historical linguistic phenomenon rather than a marker of synchronically different Moloko noun classes. There appears to be no phonological, grammatical or semantic reason for the prefix or other consequences of the presence versus absence of /a-/.

The plural construction is discussed in sec:4.2.2. Moloko has four subclasses of nouns that are distinguished by whether and how they become pluralised. These are concrete nouns ( sec:4.2.3 ), mass nouns ( sec:4.2.4 ), abstract nouns ( sec:4.2.5 ), and irregular nouns ( sec:4.2.6 ).
summary: Moloko does not have distinct morphological noun classes, though some nouns with an /a-/ prefix may reflect a historical pattern rather than a synchronically meaningful class. Instead, nouns are grouped into four subclasses based on how they form plurals: concrete, mass, abstract, and irregular nouns.

section: Morphological structure of the noun word
text:
Noun plurals Plurality!Noun plurals|( are formed by the addition of the clitic ahay which follows the noun or the possessive pronoun. The plural clitic carries some features of a separate phonological word and some of a phonologically bound morpheme. The neutral prosody of [= ahaj ] does not neutralise the prosody of the word to which it cliticises ( ex:4:20, ex:4:21 ), which would indicate a separate phonological word (see sec:2.6.1 ).

Two types of word-final changes indicate that the plural is phonologically bound to the noun. First, word-final changes for /h/ that demonstrate a word break do not occur between a noun and the plural ex:4:2.

Second, the stem-final deletion of /n/ before the /=ahj/ (shown in tab:28. adapted from ) indicates that the plural is phonologically bound to the noun ( sec:2.6.1.5 ).

We consider the plural marker to be a type of clitic and not an affix considered the plural marker to be an affix. because it does show some evidence of phonological attachment and because it binds to words of different grammatical classes in order to maintain its position at the right edge of the noun phrase permanent attribution construction (see sec:5.4.2 ). The plural [= ahaj ] will cliticise to a noun ex:4:22, possessive pronoun ( ex:4:23, ex:4:24 ), or pronoun. The plural modifies the entire construction in a permanent attribution construction ( sec:5.1 example ex:4:10 ).

summary:
Plural nouns are formed by adding the clitic **ahay**, which follows the noun or possessive pronoun. Although it has some properties of a separate phonological word, it is also phonologically bound to the noun, as shown by noun-final changes such as the lack of word-break /h/ effects and stem-final /n/ deletion before the plural marker.

The plural marker is treated as a **clitic rather than an affix** because it shows phonological attachment and can attach to different grammatical classes, including nouns, possessive pronouns, and pronouns, while marking the right edge of the noun phrase. In adjectivised noun phrases, other constituents must also be pluralized.

section: Morphological structure of the noun word
text:
Clitics!Plural

Concrete nouns (see tab:29 ) occur in both singular and plural constructions. The plural of these nouns is formed by the addition of the plural clitic =ahay within the noun phrase Plurality!Pluralisation within the noun phrase, following the head noun (further discussed in sec:5.1 ). Concrete nouns can also take numerals.
summary: Concrete nouns can appear in both singular and plural forms. Their plural is marked by adding the plural clitic =ahay after the head noun within the noun phrase, and these nouns can also combine with numerals.

section: Morphological structure of the noun word
text: Mass nouns (shown in tab:30.) are non-countable --- the singular form refers to a collective or a mass, e.g. yam ‘water.’ These nouns, when pluralised, refer to different kinds or varieties of that noun referent. These nouns cannot take numerals but they can be quantified (see sec:3.3.4 ).
summary: Mass nouns are non-countable nouns whose singular form refers to a collective substance or mass, such as *yam* ‘water.’ When pluralized, they refer to different kinds or varieties of the noun’s referent. They cannot take numerals, but they can be quantified.

section: Morphological structure of the noun word
text: Abstract nouns are ideas or concepts and as such they are not ``singular'' or ``plural.'' In Moloko they do not take =ahay, e.g., fama ‘intelligence, cleverness,’ slərele ‘work.’ Although they cannot be pluralised, they can be quantified (see sec:3.3.4 ).
summary: Abstract nouns denote ideas or concepts, so they are not inherently singular or plural. In Moloko, they do not take the plural marker =ahay, as in *fama* ‘intelligence, cleverness’ and *slərele* ‘work,’ though they can still be quantified.

section: Morphological structure of the noun word
text:
Three nouns, all of which refer to basic categories of human beings, have irregular plural forms in that the noun changes in some way when it is pluralised. The singular and plural forms for these nouns are shown in tab:31. For hor ‘woman’ and zar ‘man,’ the plural forms resemble the singular but involve insertion of the consonant w ( hawər and zawər, respectively). For war ‘child’ the plural form is completely suppletive ( babəza ). For each of these three items, there is an alternate plural form which is formed by reduplicating the entire plural root. This alternate form is interchangeable with the corresponding irregular plural form.

Noun class!Sub-classes of nouns|) Plurality!Noun plurals|)
summary: Three nouns referring to basic human categories have irregular plurals: hor ‘woman’ becomes hawər, zar ‘man’ becomes zawər, and war ‘child’ has the suppletive plural babəza. Each of these nouns also has an alternate plural formed by reduplicating the entire plural root, and this alternate form can be used interchangeably with the irregular plural.

text:
In a language like Moloko where words meld together in normal speech, real compounds are difficult to identify, since two separate nouns can occur together juxtaposed within a noun phrase without a connecting particle (see sec:5.4.2 ). In general, if what might seem to be a compound phonologically can be analysed as separate words in a productive syntactic construction, we interpret them as such. We have found some genuine compound noun stems in Moloko, and proper names are often lexicalised compounds that in terms of their internal structure are structurally like phrases or clauses ( sec:4.4 ).

The grammatical and phonological criteria used to identify a compound are fourfold:

tab:32 shows several compounds made from ele ‘thing,’ placed both before and after another root. The compounds in the table illustrate that compounds can be made from a noun plus another noun root (lines 1--3), or a noun plus a verb root (line 4). Note that when ele ‘thing’ is the leftmost root in a compound (lines 1--2), ele loses its own palatalisation prosody, an indication that the roots comprise a phonological compound. When it is the rightmost root in the compound, its palatalisation prosody spreads leftwards, affecting the whole word.

summary:
The passage explains that in Moloko, genuine compounds are hard to distinguish from adjacent nouns in ordinary speech, so analysis relies on grammatical and phonological criteria; if a form can be understood as a productive syntactic phrase, it is treated as separate words rather than a compound. It notes that Moloko does have some true compound noun stems and many lexicalized proper names, and gives examples showing compounds formed from noun+noun or noun+verb roots, with prosodic effects such as loss or spreading of palatalisation.

A more complex example, *ayva* ‘inside-house,’ might look like a locative phrase but behaves like a noun because it can be possessed and can function as the subject of a verb. This supports its analysis as a lexical compound rather than a syntactic adpositional phrase.

Moloko proper nouns Deixis!Proper Names (names of people, tribes, and places) can be morphologically simple but often are compounds. In the case of names for people, the names often indicate something that happened around the time of the baby’s birth. Names can also be compounds that encode proverbs. Thus, proper names can be simple nouns, compounds, prepositional phrases, verbs, or complete clauses. tab:34. illustrates some proper names that are compounds, and shows the components of the name where necessary. Lines 1--5 show simple proper names and lines 6--11 show proper names that are compounds.

sidewaystable

Proper names
sidewaystable

Twins are usually given special names according to their birth order, Masay ‘first twin,’ Aləwa ‘second twin.’ A single child after a twin birth is named Aban.
summary: Moloko proper names for people, tribes, and places may be morphologically simple, but they are often compounds. Personal names frequently refer to events around a child’s birth or encode proverbs, and proper names may take the form of simple nouns, compounds, prepositional phrases, verbs, or full clauses. Twins receive special names based on birth order, with *Masay* for the first twin, *Aləwa* for the second, and *Aban* for a single child born after twins.

In this chapter, noun phrase modifiers and the order of constituents are discussed ( sec:5.1 ), using simple noun heads as examples. Then, noun heads are discussed ( sec:5.2 ). Next, derived adjectives are discussed, which consist of a noun plus the adjectiviser ( sec:5.3 ). After that, four kinds of noun plus noun constructions are discussed, the genitive construction ( sec:5.4.1 ), the permanent attribution construction ( sec:5.4.2 ), relative clauses ( sec:5.4.3 ), and coordinated noun phrases ( sec:5.5 ). Finally, adpositional phrases are treated in sec:5.6.

Some things one might expect to see in a noun phrase are not found in Moloko noun phrases, but are accomplished by other constructions. For example, some attributions are expressed at the clause level using an intransitive clause (see sec:9.2.4.2 ) or transitive verb with indirect object (see sec:9.2.3 ), and comparison is done through an oblique construction (see sec:5.6.1 ).
summary:
Moloko is an SVO language with head-initial noun phrases, and the head of the NP can be a noun, multiple nouns, or a free pronoun. The chapter first describes noun phrase modifiers and constituent order, then discusses noun heads, derived adjectives, noun-plus-noun constructions, coordinated noun phrases, and adpositional phrases.

It also notes that some meanings often expressed inside noun phrases are instead conveyed by other constructions in Moloko, including clause-level attributions and oblique constructions for comparison.

subsection: Noun phrases with nominalised verb heads
text:
When the head noun is a nominalised verb, the other elements in the noun phrase represent clausal arguments of the nominalised verb. The modifying noun represents the direct object Theme of the nominalised verb and the possessive pronoun or noun in a modifying genitive construction represents the subject of the verb. In ex:5:34, the noun modifier ɗaf ‘millet loaf’ represents the direct object of the nominalised verb məzəme ‘eating’ and the 3 p possessive pronoun ata represents the subject of the nominalised verb, i.e., ‘they are eating millet loaf.’

A [məzəme ɗaf ata] ava na, tázlapay bay.\\

at -eat- millet loaf= 3 p. in 3 p + -talk- \\
‘While eating (lit. in the eating of their millet loaf), they don’t talk to each other.’

In ex:5:35, məndəye ango literally ‘your lying down’ indicates that ‘you are lying.’ The possessive pronoun ango is the subject of the nominalised verb məndəye. In ex:5:36, both subject and direct object of the nominalised verb are present. Mana, the noun in the genitive construction (see sec:5.4.1 ) codes the subject of the nominalised verb and the ‘body-part’ verbal extension va is the direct object, i.e., ‘Mana is resting his body.’

They may be modified only by the adjectiviser, or by a possessive pronoun in emphatic contexts, and noun phrases with pronoun heads cannot take plural, numeral, demonstrative, adjective, or relative-clause modifiers. However, pronouns themselves can serve as the subject of a relative clause.

All adjectives in Moloko are derived from nouns -- there is no separate grammatical class of adjectives. There are no comparative adjectives in Moloko -- comparison is done by means of a clause construction using a prepositional phrase described in sec:5.6.1. Adjectives are derived from nouns Derivational processes!Noun to adjective by a very productive process in which the morpheme ga follows the noun. tab:35. illustrates this process for simple nouns.

Nominalised verbs (see sec:7.6 ) can be further derived into adjectives by the adjectiviser. The process is illustrated in tab:36.

We consider that the adjectiviser is a separate phonological word with semantic scope over the preceding noun phrase. called this morpheme a noun affix. Also, for simple adjectivised noun constructions, speakers consider the adjectiviser to be part of the same word as the noun that is modified. However, in the absence of evidence for phonological bondedness, we consider ga to be a separate phonological word. The adjectiviser maintains its position at the right edge of a noun phrase regardless of the noun phrase components ( ex:5:44 -- ex:5:49 ). This fact indicates that it might be a clitic. However, we find no undisputable evidence that it is phonologically bound to the noun. Example ex:5:42 shows noun-final changes /n/ → [ŋ] before ga. These changes might be due to assimilation of /n/ to point of articulation of /g/ within a word (see sec:2.2 ). However, the same change would occur at a word break, with word-final changes to /n/ (see sec:2.2.4 and sec:2.6.1.2 ). We have not no examples of word-final alterations of /h/ before ga. Also, the prosody of ga does not neutralise any prosody on the word to which it is bound.

Functions of noun phrases containing ga
summary:
In Moloko, there is no separate class of adjectives and no comparative adjectives; instead, adjectives are derived from nouns, and comparison is expressed by a clause construction. A highly productive process adds the morpheme **ga** after a noun or nominalised verb, and this element occurs at the right edge of the noun phrase, where it appears to scope over the whole phrase rather than just the head noun.

The text argues that **ga** behaves like a separate phonological word or possibly a clitic, since there is no decisive evidence that it is phonologically bound to the noun, even though some noun-final alternations may occur before it. When the noun phrase is pluralised, both the head noun and the modifier are pluralised, showing that the entire noun phrase is adjectivised, and derived adjectives can be negated by placing **bay** after them.

text:
The morpheme ga has two other functions besides adjectiviser. These two functions for ga do not indicate homophones. We interpret all cases of ga as the same morpheme since all instances pattern in exactly the same way even when their function is different. We conclude that the same morpheme is functioning at the noun phrase level as an adjectiviser and at the discourse level in definiteness and emphasis. Ga can also function as a discourse demonstrative Deixis!Demonstrative function of ga |( to make the noun definite Focus and prominence!Definiteness and even sometimes emphatic. Its function to render a pronoun emphatic is discussed in sec:3.1.1.2. A set of examples from the Cicada story illustrates the discourse function. Examples ( ex:5:52 -- ex:5:54 ) are from lines 5, 12 and 18 respectively (the Cicada story is found in its entirety in sec:1.6 ). The first mention in the narrative of agwazla ‘tree of a particular species’ is shown in ex:5:52. summary:
The passage describes the Moloko genitive construction, in which the genitive phrase follows the head noun and consists of the particle **a** plus the possessor phrase. The particle is homophonous with an adposition, carries tonal effects including a floating low tone that lowers the tone of the preceding noun, and may elide with adjacent vowels while still preserving those tone effects.

Semantically, the genitive expresses a temporary relationship to the head noun and covers ownership, kinship, part-whole relations, and looser associations. The passage also notes that other modifiers in the genitive phrase modify the genitive noun rather than the head noun, and it gives idiomatic examples where body-part nouns serve as the head of figurative genitive expressions.

In a ‘permanent attribution construction,’ the noun phrase has a head composed of two (or even three) nouns, which acts as a unit within a larger noun phrase ( ex:5:85 -- ex:5:91 ). The nouns in a permanent attribution construction do not comprise a compound made of phonologically bound words, but are separate words (prosodies do not spread from one noun to the other, ex:5:87, ex:5:88, ex:5:91, and there are word-final changes in the first noun). Semantically, the second noun in the noun phrase indicates something about the identity of the first noun or gives a permanent attribute of the head noun. As compared with the genitive construction which gives a more temporary attribute sec:5.4.1. The glosses in each of the examples below confirm this observation.

It is interesting that when dependent and nominalised clauses (see sec:7.6 and sec:7.7 ) are within permanent attribution and genitive constructions, the same modal differences seen in sec:12.1.1 still apply. The nominalised form of the verb functions to give a particular situation a finished idea, with an event that has been accomplished before the point of reference, almost as a state. In contrast, the dependent form of the verb is employed in situations which have an incomplete idea, one that is not yet achieved. Compare ex:5:94 and ex:5:95. Example ex:5:94 refers to someone whose identity is a shepherd Tense, mood, and aspect!Mood in noun phrase -- he is a man who makes his living caring for sheep or other animals. He probably is hired. This more permanent identity or state is expressed through the nominalised form of the verb in a permanent attribution construction. In contrast, ex:5:95 (a relative clause, see sec:5.4.3 ) reflects a man who cares for sheep but being a shepherd isn’t his identity -- he has sheep now but may not always have them. It is an incomplete or not completely realised situation expressed through the dependent form of the verb (a relative clause, but similar to the genitive).

summary:
A permanent attribution construction is a noun phrase with a head made of two or three separate nouns that function together as a single unit. Semantically, the second noun gives a permanent identity or characteristic of the first noun, unlike the genitive construction, which expresses a more temporary relation.

Other elements in the noun phrase, such as numerals, demonstratives, and relative clauses, modify the whole multi-noun head rather than just one noun inside it. The passage also contrasts nominalised and dependent verb forms in these constructions: nominalised forms express a completed, identity-like state, while dependent forms express an incomplete or non-permanent situation.

text:
Relative clauses are one of the final elements in a noun phrase. The structure of relative clauses in Moloko is shown in fig:9. and consists of a pronoun (when necessary), a verb in dependent form (see sec:7.7 ) and a complement. A relative clause has no pronoun when the head of the relative clause is the subject of the relative clause. If the head of the relative clause has a grammatical role other than subject, then a pronoun is used.

The head noun of the relative clause can be either the subject or the direct object of the relative clause. When the head noun is the subject of the relative clause ( ex:5:99 -- ex:5:102 ), there is a gap for subject in the relative clause (marked by Ø in the examples). For example, the understood subject of the relative clause in ex:5:99 is the same as war dalay ‘the girl’ in the noun phrase. In the example, the Ø is a zero marking where the subject of the clause would otherwise be. There is a gap for subject because the subject of the relative clause is the same as the head of the noun phrase that is being modified. The relative clause is bolded and the noun phrase is delimited by square brackets in the examples in this section.

Any information inside a relative clause must be known or presupposed information expected to be shared by the hearer. Relative clauses function in two ways. Firstly, relative clauses may specify the head noun among others. Secondly, in a narrative, relative clauses identify their content as carrying information concerning a key participant in the discourse and may allude to the moral of the story.
summary:
The passage explains that in Moloko, relative clauses can modify head nouns or stand alone as the entire noun phrase, but headless relative clauses occur only in limited constructions, especially as predicates in predicate nominal clauses. It also shows that relative-clause noun phrases can be complex, with embedded clauses and ambiguous plural marking, and that the end of a relative clause may be marked by the presupposition marker *na*.

It further notes that relative clauses contain presupposed, shared information and serve two main functions: identifying one noun among others and highlighting key participants or important narrative content in discourse.

Consider the Disobedient Girl text (see sec:1.5 for the full narrative). The moral of the story is to instruct children (especially girls) to be obedient. There are relative clauses in S. 13 ex:5:115, S. 29 ex:5:109, S. 33 ex:5:101, and S. 38 ex:5:114. Note that all but one ex:5:115 of the relative clauses in this narrative concern the moral of the story. The Disobedient girl story involves suffering of a particular nature that was brought on by a particular girl who disobeyed specific instructions. The instructions that she disobeyed are in a relative clause within the husband’s lament when he finds her ( ex:5:109 ). The disobedient girl is the head of two relative clauses at the end of the story, one citing her as the reason that God got angry ( ex:5:101 ) and the other stating that she brought suffering to the Moloko people ( ex:5:114 ). The only relative clause that does not concern information relevant to the moral of the story ex:5:115 is from a section in the narrative where the man instructs his wife on how much millet to grind. The man tells her to take one grain of millet. Then he specifies with a relative clause ‘that one grain of millet you have taken.’ This relative clause specifies the one grain of millet (from the other grains in the sack) that will be multiplied for them.

In the Disobedient Girl narrative, almost all relative clauses appear at the end of the story and support the moral that children, especially girls, should be obedient. They identify the girl as the cause of God’s anger and the suffering of the Moloko people, while the one exception merely specifies the single grain of millet the man tells his wife to grind.  

The passage also notes that in the Snake narrative there is only one relative clause, and it introduces the snake indirectly by describing it as the thing that caused the mouse to fall.

text: Adpositional phrases function to relate noun phrases to the clause, expressing physical, grammatical, or logical relationships. found two types of adpositional phrases in Moloko; simple and complex. Simple adpositional phrases ( sec:5.6.1 ) consist of an adposition followed by the noun phrase. Complex adpositional phrases ( sec:5.6.2 ) consist of a noun phrase framed by a preposition and a postposition.
summary: Adpositional phrases relate noun phrases to the clause by expressing physical, grammatical, or logical relations. In Moloko, two types are identified: simple adpositional phrases, which consist of an adposition followed by a noun phrase, and complex adpositional phrases, which consist of a noun phrase framed by a preposition and a postposition.

The passage describes two complex adpositional phrases formed by a preposition and a postposition surrounding a noun phrase. The first, **kə…aka** ‘on,’ marks a noun phrase as the destination or target of an event and can be used both physically and figuratively, while the second, **a…ava** ‘in,’ marks a physical location into which the action is directed.

text:
In addition to analysing the phonology of Moloko, studied verb morphology and also produced notes on the grammar of Moloko which were expanded by; is an analysis of the Moloko verb and verb phrase. The next four chapters are based on, but the data and analysis have been re-worked, reorganised, and expanded.

The verb is the centre of the clause in Moloko. It expresses the action of an event, or a situation or state. It may be the only element in a clause, or it may be accompanied by noun phrases or pronouns expressing the subject, the direct object, and the indirect object of the verb, adpositional phrases expressing location, and/or discourse markers. Ideophones Ideophone ( sec:3.6 ) figure greatly in the expression of the action, both when they function as adverbs and when they fill the verb slot in a clause.

Typical of a Chadic language, Moloko has a variety of extensions that modify the sense of the verb stem. Note that the term ‘extension’ for Chadic languages has a different use than for Bantu languages. In Chadic languages, ‘extension’ refers to particles or clitics in the verb word or verb phrase. It has 6 extensions which specify location of the event, direction with respect to centre of reference, and the Perfect. An underspecified valence system ( chap:9 ) allows variable transitivity usage for a given verb. In Moloko, valence-changing operations are not achieved through morphological modifications of the verb (for example with causative, applicative, and passive affixes). Transitivity is a clause-level property that carries a grammatical function.

Because of its complexity, the Moloko verb and verb phrase are treated in four separate chapters. We distinguish verb root, stem (both described in chap:6 ), verb word -- renamed ‘verb complex’ for Moloko (verb stem plus affixes and extensions, chap:7 ), verb phrase ( chap:8 ), and finally verb and transitivity types ( chap:9 ).
summary:
The passage explains that the Moloko verb is the core of the clause and can appear alone or with noun phrases, pronouns, adpositional phrases, and discourse markers. It also notes that ideophones are important in expressing action, and that Moloko has six verb extensions marking location, direction, and the Perfect, while transitivity is a clause-level property rather than being changed by verbal morphology.  

Because the Moloko verb and verb phrase are complex, they are analyzed in four chapters that separate the verb root, stem, verb complex, verb phrase, and verb/transitivity types.

section: The basic verb root and stem
text:
Verb classification|(

found that the verb root in Moloko consists of one to four consonants and perhaps a vowel. The verb root by itself never occurs in the language. In discussing the verb in Moloko it is more profitable to consider the verb stem as the most basic lexical unit. The Moloko verb stem itself is already complex. determined that in order to pronounce a verb stem in Moloko, a speaker needs to know the following six features:

summary: The passage says that Moloko verb roots consist of one to four consonants and possibly a vowel, but the root never occurs independently in the language. Instead, the verb stem is treated as the basic lexical unit, and it is already complex: to pronounce it, a speaker must know six structural features arranged in a specific pattern.

section: The consonantal skeleton of the root
text:
Moloko verb roots are like those of other Afroasiatic languages in that they are built on a consonantal skeleton. found that the verb root consists of one to four consonants, although a skeleton of two consonants is most common. Bow’s database includes 26 one-consonant verbs, 231 two-consonant verbs, 83 three-consonant verbs, and 10 four-consonant verbs. That Moloko verb roots are based on a consonantal skeleton can be evidenced by two facts, both of which are illustrated in tab:37. (adapted from ). Firstly, the consonants display a unique stability when the verb is inflected. Note there are consonantal allophones in palatalised and labialised words. The vowels, on the other hand, change with the prosody of the inflection and whether or not the word carries stress. Since stress is phrase-final, the final syllable of these elicited examples will always carry a ‘full’ vowel. Secondly, there are verb roots that consist simply of one consonant and a prosody. These have no underlying root vowel, but they will acquire their vowels in the inflections.

The underlying form of a verb stem is defined as the consonantal skeleton plus the optional presence of an underlying vowel, /-j/ suffix, and a- prefix, potential prosody, and tone (see Sections sec:6.3 -- sec:6.7 ). In the examples in tab:37 and in the rest of this section, the underlying form will be given when necessary in addition to the phonetic pronunciation. The tone class is not shown.

Mamalis found that the underlying consonants in a verb root can most easily be identified from the imperative form ( tab:38 from ). Note that palatalisation will cause an underlying /s/ to be expressed as [ʃ] (see sec:2.2.3 ). The same verb stems are included as were in tab:37 as well as a few more. Prosody, underlying vowels (lines 12, 15), and the /-j/ suffix (lines 4-7, 15) can also be seen in the imperative form; these features will be discussed in the sections below.

The consonants in a verb stem in Moloko are remarkably constant. We have found only two irregular verbs where there are changes in the verb consonants. Firstly, the irregular verb /l o / adds an epenthetic [h] in some conjugations to break up vowels (the full conjugation of /l o / is in Appendix sec:13.2 ). Secondly, the root-final ɗ of the verb /z ɗ/ ‘take’ drops off when affixes and clitics are added ( ex:6:1, ex:6:2 ). This process does not happen with the phonologically similar verb /f ɗ/ ‘put’ ( ex:6:3, ex:6:4 ).

take[. ] =. =to 25pt ‘give to me’\\

take[. ] =on 50pt ‘give again’ (on top of what you gave before)

summary:
Moloko verb roots are built on a consonantal skeleton, typically of two consonants, though roots may contain one to four consonants. This is shown by the stability of consonants under inflection, the variation of vowels with prosody and stress, and the existence of roots with only a consonant plus prosody that acquire vowels in inflected forms.  

The underlying verb stem consists of the consonantal skeleton plus optional vowel, suffix, prefix, prosody, and tone, and the consonants are most easily identified from the imperative form. Verbal consonants are highly stable, with only two irregular verbs noted: one adds an epenthetic [h] in some conjugations, and another loses root-final ɗ when affixes and clitics are added.

text:
Moloko verb stems can be divided into two subclasses based on whether an underlying suffix is present or not. Slightly over 70% of the verb stems in Bow’s ( Bow1997c) data take the suffix /-j/, which can have different surface variants depending on the prosody of the stem.

FriesenMamalis2008 found that although the /-j/ suffix appears to have no semantic value, it does allow certain consonants to be verb root final which would otherwise not be permitted. I.e., [ b, mb, d, nd, dz, nz, g, ŋg, gʷ, ŋgʷ, ts, w, j ]. See discussion on word-final consonants in sec:2.5.1. However, for many verb stems, it appears to be at least synchronically simply a place-holding suffix that drops off whenever other suffixes or extensions are attached to the verb (compare columns 3 and 4 in tab:37 ). Examples ex:6:5 and ex:6:6 show the same verb complex with ex:6:5 and without ex:6:6 the /-j/ suffix. The first line in each example is the orthographic form. The second is the phonetic form (slow speech) with morpheme breaks.

Apay.\\
a-p-aj\\
3 s -open- \\
‘It opens.’

Apala.\\
a-p=ala\\
3 s -open=to\\
‘It opens towards.’

Verb stems with the underlying suffix but no underlying (i.\,e. neutral) prosody take the surface suffix form [-aj]; verb stems that are labialised carry the surface form suffix [-ɔj]. Prosody is applied to the verb stem since the - aj suffix takes on the prosody of the stem (prosodies spread leftwards, sec:2.1 ). With the exception of verbs with the root-final consonant /n/, Stems ending in n are all palatalised, e.g., cen ‘understand’, cəjen ‘lose’, njeren ‘groan’, mbesen ‘relax’, ndeslen ‘make cold’, ɓərzlen ‘count’, mbeten ‘put out’, and mbezen ‘spoil’. We interpret these verbs as having /n/ as final consonant because the n cannot be interpreted as direct or indirect object and also there are no other stems which end in n. verb stems that are palatalised carry the surface form suffix [ɛ]. We interpret the [-ɛ] in palatalised verbs as the palatalised variant of the /-j/ suffix for two reasons. First, [-ɛ] patterns the same way as the /-j/ suffix (dropping off with its prosody whenever another suffix or extension is added). Second, the same rules of restriction of final stem consonants apply for palatalised verb stems as for other verb stems (see sec:2.5.1 ), and so the presence of [-ɛ] allows root-final consonants which would otherwise be restricted. For example, /d/ and /g/ are both not permitted as word-final consonants ( sec:2.2.4 ), but the presence of [-ɛ] allows verbs like [d-ɛ] and [g-ɛ]. Examples from verb roots of one, two, and three consonants are shown in tab:39. We found no three-consonant palatalised verb stems in the data. Labialised verb stems without the / -j/ suffix were rare.

Because the suffix surfaces only word-finally, whenever the relevant verb is pronounced in isolation (and is thus phrase-final), the suffix syllable takes the phrase-final stress, necessitating a full vowel. It is therefore pronounced [aj] (see example ex:6:7 ) in verbs with neutral prosody, [ɔj] in labialised verb stems, and [ɛ] in palatalised verb stems). Whenever the verb is not phrase-final, the vowel drops and an epenthetic schwa occurs, rendering the pronunciation [i] for labialised and neutral prosody verbs ex:6:8 and [ɪ] for palatalised verbs.

[a-paɗ-aj]\\
3 s -crunch- \\
‘It crunches.’

[a-paɗ-ij ʃɛʃɛ]\\
3 s -crunch- meat\\
‘He eats meat.’

tab:40 (adapted from and ) illustrates the phonetic pronunciation including tone of pairs of verb stems that have the same consonantal shape but with and without the /-j/ suffix.
summary: Moloko verb stems are divided into two subclasses depending on whether they contain an underlying suffix /-j/, which occurs in over 70% of the stems in Bow’s data and has no clear semantic meaning. The suffix appears to function partly as a place-holding element that can permit otherwise restricted final consonants, and it surfaces differently according to stem prosody: [aj] with neutral prosody, [ɔj] with labialisation, and [ɛ] with palatalisation. When a verb is not phrase-final, the suffix vowel drops and is realized with an epenthetic schwa, and the suffix itself disappears when other suffixes or extensions are attached.

noted that no Moloko verb root has more than one underlying internal vowel and many Moloko verb roots have no underlying vowels (see tab:38 )., page 24. Her database of 350 verb stems has 189 with the internal vowel. The presence of an underlying internal vowel in the verb stem (if any) can be determined by studying the second plural imperative. Bow illustrates the following minimal pair. The verb stems /ts r/ ‘climb’ and /tsar/ ‘taste good’ have identical surface forms in the second person singular imperative ( ex:6:9 -- ex:6:10 ) due to stress on the final syllable, which necessitates a full vowel. However, the presence of the underlying vowel can be seen in the second person plural imperative ( ex:6:11 -- ex:6:12 ). The imperative is formed by adding the suffix - om and labialisation prosody. The verb root for ‘climb’ does not have an underlying vowel, so a schwa is inserted and labialised to become [ʊ] ex:6:11. On the other hand, the verb root for ‘taste good’ has an internal vowel which becomes [ɔ] when labialised ex:6:12.

‘climb!’

tab:41 (from ) shows several other examples. Single consonant roots have no internal vowel (line 1). Two and three-consonant roots may have no internal vowel (lines 2-4) or an internal vowel (lines 5-7). All four-consonant roots have an internal vowel (line 8).

Bow discovered that when an underlying vowel exists in the root, it always immediately precedes the final root consonant, so possible verb roots could take the following forms (disregarding affixes): C, CC, CaC, CCC, CCaC, CCCaC. These ‘full’ vowels will remain full in all inflections of the verb, and will be affected by the prosodies of the forms, resulting in surface [a, ɛ, ɔ, œ]. In syllables where there are no underlying vowels, an epenthetic schwa is inserted between certain consonant clusters to facilitate pronunciation in the inflected forms. On stressed syllables, the schwa will become its full vowel counterpart (see ex:6:9 ).
summary: Bow reports that Moloko verb roots may have at most one underlying internal vowel, and many have none; in a database of 350 verb stems, 189 contain such a vowel. The presence of the vowel is revealed in the second plural imperative, where roots without an underlying vowel insert schwa, while roots with one show a full vowel that changes under labialisation, and in all cases the vowel—if present—immediately precedes the final root consonant.

The verb stems in one class of bi-consonantal verbal stems take subject prefixes with the full vowel /a/ instead of the epenthetic schwa. called this a historical a- prefix on the verb stem. She reported that 83 out of 231 bi-consonantal verb stems that she studied have the (now frozen) a- prefix. Whether a verb stem has this prefix or not can be determined from the nominalised form. Bow illustrates the presence of this prefix with the minimal pair /a-ndaw/ ‘swallow’ and /ndaw/ ‘insult.’ ex:6:13 and ex:6:14 show the nominalised form of the two verb stems. The nominalised form has a mə- or me- prefix, an -e suffix, and is palatalised ( sec:7.6 ). The verb stem məndewe ‘swallow’ does not have the a- prefix. The verb stem mendewe ‘insult’ has the a- prefix (shown by the full vowel e in the prefix).

Bow treats stems with and without this prefix as synchronically belonging to different classes, illustrated by the minimal pair for ‘swallow’ and ‘insult’ and their nominalised forms with **mɪ-** versus **mɛ-**. The prefix appears to have little lexical or semantic significance, and the contrast between prefixed and non-prefixed verbs is lost in the irrealis mood, where the potential forms are identical.

found that in their underlying lexical form, Moloko verb stems are either labialised, palatalised, or without a prosody. The database in Appendix sec:13.1 shows that 83 out of 350 verb stems carry a prosody (61 are palatalised and 22 are labialised). The effects of labialisation and palatisation are discussed in sec:2.1. Note that there are also some morphological processes where palatalisation or labialisation is a part of the morpheme, for example, palatalisation is part of the formation of the nominalised form ( sec:7.6 ), and labialisation is a part of the 1P and subject forms sec:7.3.1. Although prosodies can carry predictable lexical weight in some other related languages, All causatives in Muyang Muyang involve the palatalisation of the root. text:
concluded that verb stems in Moloko belong to one of three underlying tone classes: high (H), low (L), or toneless (Ø). She discovered that the underlying tone of a verb stem can be identified by comparing the imperative with the Potential form. The Potential form has a high tone on a lengthened subject prefix (see sec:7.4.3 ). If the tone melody of the stem is high on both imperative and Potential forms, then that stem has an underlying high tone. If the tone melody is mid or low on both forms due to the presence of depressor consonants (see sec:2.4.1 ), then the stem has underlying low tone. If the tone melody of the stem syllable is low in the imperative but high following the high tone of the subject prefix in the Potential form, that verb stem is toneless. The high tone of the Potential form of the subject prefix spreads to the toneless stem. For the imperative form of a toneless stem, a default low tone is applied to the stem.

A minimal triplet is shown in tab:44 (from ). Line 1 shows a High tone verb stem. The tone on the verb stem is high in both the imperative and Potential forms Tense, mood, and aspect!Irrealis mood|(. Line 2 shows a low tone verb stem with low tone in the imperative form and mid in the Potential form. Line 3 shows a toneless verb stem. This verb stem carries no inherent tone of its own and its surface tone is low in the imperative form and takes the high tone of the prefix in the Potential form.

Mamalis  studied tone patterns in Moloko verbs. tab:45 (adapted from ) shows the imperative and Potential forms and the underlying tone patterns for different verb stems.

Tense, mood, and aspect!Irrealis mood|)
Tone patterns in Moloko verbs are summarised in tab:46 (from ), which shows the tone pattern on the stem for the imperative and Potential forms for the three underlying tone forms. All verb stems in each class have the same pattern, as follows (note that the tone in parentheses is the tone on the /-j/ suffix, if there is one). Tone patterns are influenced by the presence of depressor consonants (see sec:6.7.1 ) and the underlying structure of the verb stem (see sec:6.7.2 ).
summary: Mamalis concluded that Moloko verb stems fall into three underlying tone classes: high (H), low (L), and toneless (Ø). The underlying tone can be identified by comparing imperative and Potential forms, because the Potential adds a high tone to the lengthened subject prefix, which spreads to toneless stems; imperatives of toneless stems receive a default low tone. The tone patterns of these classes are consistent across verb stems, though they are affected by depressor consonants and stem structure.

text: subdivided the low tone verb stem category phonetically into mid and low surface forms by the presence or absence of one or more of the class of consonants known as depressor consonants (see sec:2.4.1 ). Depressor consonants in Moloko include all voiced obstruents except implosives and nasals (i.e. [b, d, g, dz, v, ɮ, z, mb, nd, ŋg]). demonstrated that an underlyingly low tone verb with no depressors has a mid tone surface form; with depressors it has a low tone surface form. For verb stems of underlying high tone or toneless verb stems, the presence or absence of depressor consonants makes no difference to the surface form of the melody. Toneless verb stems take low tone as the default surface form, regardless of depressors. tab:47 (from ) shows the realisations of surface tone with and without depressor consonants for the most common verb type (underlying form /CaC/ with high tone /-j/ suffix in the. form).
summary: The passage explains that in Moloko, low-tone verb stems are phonetically split into mid and low surface forms depending on whether they contain depressor consonants, which are voiced obstruents excluding implosives and nasals. An underlyingly low-tone verb without depressors surfaces as mid tone, while one with depressors surfaces as low tone; however, depressors do not affect underlying high-tone or toneless stems, and toneless stems default to low tone.

text:
Moloko does not have a simple verb word. Rather, named this structure the ‘verb complex’ since affixes and extensions attach to the verb stem that comprises a close phonological unit that is not always one phonological word. The verb complex may be made up of from one to three phonological words as defined by prosody spread and word-final allophones ( sec:2.6.1 and sec:2.6.2 ).

There are two fundamental aspects of Moloko grammar that are expressed in the verb complex. The first is the concept of the point of reference. The point of reference involves both place and time. Actions in Moloko are usually placed with respect to a set locational point of reference, which in normal speech is usually the speaker. In a narrative or other discourse, the speaker can set the point of reference. Verbs are aligned with respect to the locational point of reference by means of directional Directionals verbal extensions ( sec:7.5.2 ). These extensions determine the direction of the event with respect to the point of reference, and can be towards the speaker, away from the speaker, or back and forth. Directionals are different from adpositionals ( sec:7.5.1 ), since adpositionals Adpositionals align the action with respect to other elements in the immediate context. The temporal point of reference Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfect is set in Moloko by mood and the Perfect. Mood involves what is real or not yet experienced in the world shared by the speaker and his or her audience (realis and irrealis, sec:7.4.3 ). The speaker and audience are, as it were, walking backwards into the future. I first heard this image at a First Nations languages conference in Canada in 2011 to express an Indigenous view of time. What has happened and is happening is ‘visible’ to them (realis) and they move together into the ‘invisible’ world behind them (irrealis). The point of reference will be the time of communication in normal speech. However, again in a narrative or other type of discourse, the speaker can set the point of reference (usually to the time the events took place). The Perfect extension is employed whenever the speaker needs to make sure that the hearer understands that an event is already completed before the point of reference, with ongoing effects to that point.

Another fundamental concept in Moloko verbs expressed in the verb complex is expectation, accomplished through mood Tense, mood, and aspect!Irrealis mood|(. The realis world is the realm of the visible or real; it includes the past and what is present as it happens before the speaker and audience and what is shared knowledge or expectations about the world and how it works. It is presented by the speaker as being real or known -- events and states that happened, are happening, or which are part of the expected ‘frame’ of a situation. Within the realis world, the distinctions coded in verbs are for events that are complete/accomplished (Perfective, sec:7.4.1 ), incomplete/unachieved (Imperfective Tense, mood, and aspect!Imperfective aspect, sec:7.4.2 ), in progress ( sec:8.2.1 ), repeated (three types, sec:7.4.4, sec:7.4.5, sec:7.5.2 ). The irrealis world is the realm of desire and will and the unknown world of the future. Within that world, verbs in Moloko are marked as to the degree of desire and perhaps the control the speaker has over the accomplishment of the event. Tense, mood, and aspect!Irrealis mood|)

There is no system of tense as such in Moloko. considered tense and mood. Perfective versus Imperfective aspect is expressed through Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfective aspect changes in the tone of the subject prefix ( sec:7.4.1 and sec:7.4.2 ). Irrealis mood is differentiated from realis mood by vowel changes in the subject prefix ( sec:7.4.3 ). For the imperative ( sec:7.4.2 ), the subject prefix is absent.

The verb stem as defined in chap:6 can take up to two prefixes and only one suffix. Morphemes on the stem include the subject pronominal affixes (a prefix and a suffix for and subjects, sec:7.3.1 ) and an indirect object pronominal enclitic ( sec:7.3.1.1 ). Two prefixes are derivational -- one prefix nominalises the verb ( sec:7.6 ) and the other subordinates the entire clause in which it occurs ( sec:7.7 ).

Another noteworthy feature is that Moloko has three ways to indicate repeated actions. Reduplication in the root is one of the ways that pluractionals are formed in other Chadic languages. Contrary to many Chadic languages, Moloko does not have a productive pluractional. Only a few verb stems take the pluractional extension (used for actions that are made up of repetitive motions, sec:7.5.2 ). The only stems which take the pluractional which we have so far identified are a-h=aya ‘he/she grinds,’ a-s=əya ‘he/she cuts,’ and d=əya ‘take many’. However, two kinds of reduplication of the verb stem in Moloko express iterative aspect. Reduplication of a consonant in the stem indicates an iterative action that is habitual ( sec:7.4.4 ) and reduplication of the entire verb word indicates an iterative action that is intermittent ( sec:7.4.5 ).

The verbal extensions, which include locational and directional information and Perfect aspect, are also described in this chapter ( sec:7.5 ). They and the indirect object pronominal enclitic are discussed as part of the verb complex because they form a close phonological unit with the verb stem, even though they may sometimes be part of a separate phonological word.
summary:
Moloko does not have a simple verb word; instead, verbs occur in a “verb complex” of one to three phonological words with affixes and extensions attached to the verb stem. This complex encodes key grammatical distinctions, especially point of reference in space and time, mood and aspect rather than tense, and repeated actions, with categories such as realis/irrealis, perfective/imperfective, perfect, and several iterative patterns marked by tone, vowel change, or reduplication.

The verb stem can take up to two prefixes and one suffix, including subject pronominal markers, an indirect object enclitic, and two derivational prefixes for nominalization and subordination. Moloko has only a limited pluractional, but it does distinguish habitual and intermittent iteration through different kinds of reduplication, while locational and directional extensions also form part of the verb complex.

section: The phonological structure of the verb word
text:
The phonological structure of the Moloko verb word is interesting in that, although its elements can each be part of a phonological unit with the verb stem, combinations of different elements can cause the entity to be broken into up to three phonological words. Its complexity is especially located in the post-verbal elements of the verb complex. The subject prefix and verb stem are the only necessary parts of the basic inflected verb complex. The structure of the nominalised or dependent forms of the verb is similar. The derivational prefixes are in the same location as the subject prefix. All other affixes and extensions are possible with the exception of the Perfect extension. All other affixes and extensions are structurally optional and are determined by the context and the lexical requirements of the particular verb.

discovered that Moloko has three types of verb complexes. The first type of verb complex is one phonological word ( fig:7.1 ), and occurs when there is no plural suffix (see sec:7.3.1 ), no indirect object pronominal enclitic (see sec:7.3.1.1 ), and no direct object pronominal (see sec:7.3.2 ). In this case, the extensions (see sec:7.5 ) cliticise directly to the verb stem.

In the examples, the verb word is delineated by square brackets.

do[. ]=on=to\\

The second type necessitates two phonological words -- a verb word and an ‘extension word’ – because of the presence of either a direct or indirect object pronominal (or both). The verb word may have either a subject suffix or an indirect object pronominal enclitic (but not both). The structure of this second verb complex is illustrated in fig:7.2.

The word break is initiated by both the direct and indirect object pronominals such that when either is present, there will be a word break. The word break after the 3 s indirect object pronominal enclitic is indicated by word-final changes in /n/; in slow speech the 3 s indirect object pronominal enclitic /= an / is pronounced [aŋ] (showing word-final changes) even when there are other clitics following the verb word ( ex:7:3, see sec:7.3.1.1 ). The word break before the 3 s pronominal is indicated by the fact that the 3 s pronominal does not neutralise the prosody on the verb stem, and does not cause the /-j/ suffix to drop ( ex:7:4 -- ex:7:5, see sec:7.3.2 ). The third type of verb complex consists of three phonological words (a verb word, an ‘indirect object word,’ and an ‘extension word’). This type occurs when the verb complex has both a subject suffix and an indirect object pronominal enclitic. Phonological rules will not allow two morphemes suffixed or cliticised to the verb; nor can the indirect object pronominal enclitic commence another word. So, the morpheme an is inserted and the indirect object pronominal clitic attaches to the inserted morpheme. The overall structure is then as shown in fig:7.3.

In ex:7:9 and ex:7:10, the verb kəslom has the imperative suffix attached ( -om ). The indirect object pronominal enclitic and the inserted morpheme an. Other extensions must make a third phonological word since there is a word break following the indirect object pronominal enclitic.

‘You (p) kill another goat for him.’ (lit. you slay a goat for him on top of [another time a goat was slain]

summary: Moloko verb complexes can be realized as one, two, or three phonological words depending on which pronominal clitics and extensions are present. The basic inflected verb needs only a subject prefix and verb stem, while the presence of direct and/or indirect object pronominals determines where extensions cliticize and whether an extra phonological word must be inserted.

text:
showed that the verb complex can carry pronominals that indicate the subject, direct object, and indirect object. These markers in the verb complex are all bound forms. They are called pronominals and not just agreement markers because all of them can be the only indication of their referent in the clause. Because the pronominals are present, there is no need for a noun phrase or free pronoun in the clause. Participants are tracked Cohesion!Participant tracking in discourse solely by pronominals, and free pronouns and noun phrases only occur in discourse to introduce a participant or to switch the referent.

tab:55 lists all the pronominals. Subject is indicated by a verbal prefix for singular subjects and third person plural. Plural subjects for first and second person are indicated by a combination of a prefix and a suffix. These subject pronominals (discussed in sec:7.3.1 ) are given in their underlying form because the surface vowel and tone on the prefix is determined by mood and aspect, respectively. Also, the underlying form is given to show the prosody, because the labialisation prosody in the plural subject suffixes will spread over the entire verb stem. The direct object pronominal ( sec:7.3.2 ) only occurs for third person singular and plural. The indirect object pronominal ( sec:7.3.1.1 ) cliticises to the right edge of the verb stem and the direct object pronominal follows it. In tab:55, the independent pronouns are also given for comparison since there are similarities between the free pronoun and its corresponding pronominal.
summary:
The verb complex can encode subject, direct object, and indirect object through bound pronominals, which are treated as pronominals rather than simple agreement markers because they can be the sole expression of a referent in the clause. As a result, noun phrases and free pronouns are generally unnecessary and are used mainly to introduce a participant or switch reference in discourse.  

The passage also describes the pronominal system: subjects are marked by prefixes, with plural first and second person using both a prefix and suffix, direct objects occur only in third person singular and plural, and indirect objects cliticize to the right edge of the verb stem before the direct object marker.

The subject is always marked on the finite form of the verb, regardless of whether there is a free subject phrase in the clause. The presence of both subject pronominal and corresponding noun phrase occurs for pragmatic reasons. In fact, the subject pronominal marker in the verb can be the only indication of subject in the entire clause. In a non-finite verb form, the subject pronominal is absent and the subject of the clause is either understood from the context or indicated by a free pronoun or noun phrase in the clause (Sections sec:7.6.2, sec:7.7, and sec:8.2.3 ). As noted in tab:56 and tab:57 (adapted from ), subject is marked by a prefix or combination of prefix and suffix. In the examples below, the pronominal affixes are bolded. The prefix carries aspectual tone (see sec:7.4 ), and the vowel quality is influenced by the prosody on the verb stem (see sec:6.6 ), the presence of the /a-/ prefix (see sec:6.5 ), and the mood of the verb (see sec:7.4.3 ). The and suffixes are labialised. This prosody will spread over the entire verb stem.

found that a prosody on the verb stem will spread leftwards from the verb stem over the singular subject prefixes. The fact that palatalisation and labialisation spread over the subject prefixes indicates that the subject markers are fully bound to the verb stem and are not separate words. ex:7:11 presents the palatalised verb /g e / ‘do,’ and ex:7:12 presents the labialised verb /l o / ‘go.’

Nege.\\
[nɛ -g-ɛ]\\
-do- \\
‘I did.’

Olo.\\
[ɔ -lɔ]\\
3 s -go\\
‘he/she went.’

also discovered that labialisation on the and subject suffixes will spread leftwards from the suffix onto the entire verb word. This fact indicates that these morphemes are fully bound to the verb stem and are not separate words. The verb /ts k-j e / ‘stand’, shown in example ex:7:13 in its form, loses its palatalisation and becomes labialised when the (labialised) plural Plurality!Verb plurals|) suffixes are added ex:7:14:

Necəke.\\
nɛ -tʃɪk-ɛ\\
-stand- \\

Nəcəkom. \\
nʊ -tsʊkʷ-ɔm\\
-stand- 1 Pex \\
‘We (exclusive) stand.’

also determined that the subject pronominal prefixes in Moloko appear to be toneless. The aspect of the verbal construction will allocate tone to the pronoun. In the Imperfective aspect Tense, mood, and aspect!Imperfective aspect, the pronoun always takes high tone (see sec:7.4.2 ). In the Perfective aspect Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfective aspect, the pronoun copies the first tone of the root if it is low or mid. If the first tone of the root is high, the pronoun takes on mid tone.
summary: The passage states that subject agreement is always marked on the finite verb in Moloko, even when an independent subject noun phrase is present, and that in non-finite forms the subject marker is absent and the subject must be inferred or expressed separately. It also argues that the subject pronominal affixes are tightly bound to the verb stem because prosodic features such as palatalization and labialization spread across them, and that these prefixes are toneless, receiving tone from the aspectual system.

An indirect object pronominal enclitic can attach to the verb word to express the indirect object, which is a core argument of the verb. The indirect object in Moloko is the participant that represents the place where the direct object is directed to – the recipient or beneficiary of the action. Employing the Agent-Theme-Location analysis developed by, the indirect object in Moloko expresses the semantic (see chap:9 ). The direct object pronominal expresses the semantic Theme -- the participant that changes position or state (see sec:7.3.2 ). In ex:7:15, the verb /dz -j/ ‘help’ takes the indirect object. The indirect object represents the participant who receives the help.

Ajənaw.\\
a-dzən=aw\\
3 s -help=. \\
‘He/she helped me.’

The indirect object pronominal enclitic allows the core indirect object argument to be expressed in a prepositional phrase ana Mana ‘to Mana’ ex:7:16.

Ajənan ana Mana.\\
a-dzən=aŋ ana Mana\\
3 s -help= 3 s. Mana\\
‘He/she helped Mana.’

The indirect object pronominal enclitic can also stand in the place of the prepositional phrase ex:7:17.

Ajən an.\\
a-dzən =aŋ \\
3 s -help= 3 s. \\
‘He/she helped him.’

tab:7.58 (adapted from ) shows the verb /v l/ ‘give’ conjugated for the indirect object argument. The indirect object expresses the recipient.

The indirect object pronominal enclitics are phonologically bound to the verb stem and do not comprise separate words. When an indirect object pronominal cliticises to the verb stem, there are no word-final alternations in the verb stem. Compare the following pairs of examples showing verb stems with and without indirect object pronominal enclitics. When the indirect object pronominal enclitic is attached ex:7:19, there is no word-final alternation of /h/ → [x] / _#. See sec:2.6.1, c.f. ex:7:18. Likewise, we do not see the word-final process of n → [ŋ] / _# between the verb stem and the indirect object pronominal.

Aɓah zana.\\
a-ɓax zana\\
3 s -sew clothing\\
‘He/she sews clothing.’

Aɓahaw zana. \\
a-ɓah=aw zana \\
3 s -sew=. clothing \\
‘He/she sews clothing for me.’

Similarly, the example pairs ex:7:20 and ex:7:21 illustrate that the /-j/ suffix is dropped when the indirect object pronominal is present ex:7:21, indicating that the pronominal is phonologically bound to the stem (see sec:6.3 ).

Ajay.\\
a-dz-aj\\
3 s -speak- \\
‘He/she speaks.’

Ajan.\\
a-dz=aŋ\\
3 s -speak= 3 s. \\
‘He/she speaks to him/her.’

The indirect object pronominal enclitic is not phonologically a true suffix, because the prosody of the indirect object pronominal enclitic does not affect the prosody on the verb stem. Compare ex:7:22 and ex:7:23 which illustrate the verb stem /s/ conjugated with second person singular and plural indirect objects. If the prosody of the indirect object pronominal enclitic affected the verb stem, one would expect that the /s/ in example ex:7:23 would be affected by the palatalisation prosody of the plural indirect object pronominal enclitic and be expressed as [ʃ].

Asok aka ɗaf.\\
a-s=ɔk =aka ɗaf\\
3 s -please=. =on millet loaf\\
‘You want to have more millet loaves.’ (lit. millet loaf is pleasing to you)

Asaləkwəye aka ɗaf.\\
a-s=alʊkʷøjɛ =aka ɗaf\\
3 s -please=. =on millet loaf\\
‘You want to have more millet loaves.’ (lit. millet loaf is pleasing to you)

The fact that the indirect object pronominal can attach to verb stems as well as other particles confirms that it is in fact a clitic pronoun. Normally, the indirect object pronominal enclitic attaches directly to the verb stem ex:7:24. However, if the plural subject pronominal suffix is required on the verb ex:7:25, the indirect object pronominal can no longer attach to the verb, because the verb stem can take only one suffix (see sec:7.1 ). Instead, the indirect object pronominal cliticises to the particle an. This particle may be related to ana, the dative preposition ‘to.’

Kasl an awak.\\
ka-ɬ =aŋ awak\\
-slay= 3 s. goat\\
‘You slay the goat for him.’

Kəslom anan awak.\\
kə-ɬ-ɔm an=aŋ awak\\
2-slay- to= 3 s. goat\\
‘You (plural) slay the goat for him.’

There is a word break after the indirect object pronominal enclitic (the phonological words are indicated by square brackets in the examples immediately below). The word break is indicated by the fact that the 3 s indirect object pronominal enclitic /= an / in slow speech is pronounced [aŋ] even when there are other clitics following the verb word (see ex:7:26 -- ex:7:27 ). The word-final [ŋ] will delete in fast speech (see sec:2.5.2 ). These clitics (e.g., the adpositional clitics in these examples, see sec:7.5.1 ) would otherwise attach to the verb (compare with example ex:7:28 ):

As an aka ɗaf.\\
[a-s =aŋ ] [ =aka ] ɗaf\\
3 s -please= 3 s. =on millet loaf\\
‘He/she wants to have more millet loaves.’ (lit. millet loaf is pleasing to him)

Ad an aka ɗaf.\\
[a-d =aŋ ] [ =aka ] ɗaf\\
3 s -prepare= 3 s. =on millet loaf\\
‘She made more loaves of millet for him.’

Ad aka ɗaf.\\
[a-d =aka ] ɗaf\\
3 s -prepare=on millet loaf\\
‘She made more loaves of millet.’
summary: Moloko indirect object pronominal enclitics mark the core recipient/beneficiary argument of the verb, corresponding to the semantic Location/recipient role, while the direct object pronoun marks the Theme. These enclitics are phonologically bound to the verb stem and behave like clitic pronouns rather than true suffixes: they do not trigger stem-final alternations or affect prosody, and when the verb already bears another suffix they attach instead to a following particle such as *an*.

tab:55 (from ) shows the direct object  pronominals. The third person pronominals replace or double a full noun phrase in a discourse -- the na ( 3 s. ) or ta ( 3 p. ) refer back to something in the immediately preceding context. Examples ex:7:29 and ex:7:30 show two clauses that might occur in a discourse. In ex:7:30 the na refers back to sla ‘cow’ in ex:7:29.

Kaslay sla. \\
kà-ɬ-aj ɬa \\
+ -slay- cow \\
‘You slew the cow.’

Kaslay na. \\
kà-ɬ-aj na \\
+ -slay- 3 s. \\
‘You slew it.’

A third person pronominal can be the only expression of direct object in a clause if its identity is known in the discourse ( ex:7:30, ex:7:32, and ex:7:36 ). The only time that a clause will contain both a third person pronominal and a noun phrase that co-refer to the direct object in the clause is when a special focus on the direct object is required (‘all his brothers’ in ex:7:31, ‘that fruit-bearing tree’ in ex:7:38 ).

Race Story.\\
Moktonok na, abək ta aya va məlama ahan ahay jəyga.\\

toad 3 s -invite 3 p = = brothers= 3 p. =Pl all\\
‘The toad, he had already invited all of his brothers.’

We know that the third person pronominals are phonologically separate words (not clitics like the other verbal extensions) because the /-j/ suffix does not drop when the pronominal is added to a clause ex:7:32. Normally the /-j/ suffix drops off when extensions or suffixes are added to the clause ( ex:7:33, see also sec:6.3 ).

Apaɗay na. \\
a-paɗ-aj na \\
3 s -crunch- 3 s. \\
‘He/she crunches it.’

Apaɗaka.\\
a-paɗ=aka\\
3 s -crunch=on\\
‘He/she crunches on.’

Another indication that the pronominal is phonologically a separate word is that the neutral prosody on the pronominal does not affect the prosody of the verb word. Compare ex:7:34 and ex:7:35. In both examples the verb complex is palatalised in spite of the addition of the pronominal. This situation is in contrast to what happens with the Perfect enclitic (see sec:7.5.3 ).

Nese.\\
nɛ-ʃ-ɛ\\
-drink- \\
‘I drink.’

Nese na.\\
nɛ-ʃ-ɛ na\\
-drink- 3 s. \\
‘I drink it.’

A third indication is that word-final changes (like word-final /n/ being realised as [ŋ] (see sec:2.6.1 and example ex:7:36 ) are preserved when followed by na or ta.

Nəvəlan na. \\
nə-vəl=aŋ na \\
-give= 3 s. 3 s. \\
‘I gave it to him.’

The normal slot for the pronominal is within the verb complex between the verb stem and the directional extension. In each example below, the verb complex is delineated by square brackets and the third person pronominal is bolded.

Baba ango avəlan na alay ana məze.\\
baba=aŋgʷɔ [a-vəl=aŋ na =alaj] ana mɪʒɛ\\

‘Your father gave it to that person.’

Any further verbal extensions will cliticise to a third person pronominal. In example ex:7:38, the directional extension =ala ‘toward’ cliticises to na and vowels will elide resulting in the pronunciation [nala]. See also example ex:7:31, where the pluractional and perfect extensions = aya and = va cliticise to the pronominal ta to result in the pronunciation [tajava].

Cicada, S. 12\\
Tolo [təmənjar na ala] mama agwazla nəndəye.\\

3 p -go 3 p -see 3 s. =to mother spp. of tree \\
‘They went and saw that fruit-bearing tree.’

The first and second person direct objects are expressed by free pronouns (see sec:3.1.1.1 ) or noun phrases. The free pronouns are distributionally and phonologically distinct from the third person direct object pronominals. The free pronouns occur after the verb complex. Note that they occur after the directional extensions in ex:7:39 and ex:7:40. In each example, the verb complex is delineated by square brackets and the first or second person independent pronoun is bolded.

[Kazalay] ne a kosoko ava ɗaw?\\

waya aməmbeɗe hor ata.\\
waja amɪ-mbɛɗ-ɛ hʷɔr=atəta\\

The 3 s pronominal is employed in discourse to track participants Cohesion!Participant tracking (along with the subject and indirect object pronominals, see Sections sec:7.3.1 and sec:7.3.1.1, respectively). Examples ex:7:41 and ex:7:42 are from the Snake story (see sec:1.4 ). The snake is introduced with a noun phrase gogolvan ‘snake’ ex:7:41. Further on in the narrative, the snake is referred to by the 3 s pronominal na ex:7:42.

Snake story, S. 4\\
Alala na, gogolvan na, olo alay.\\
a-l=la na gʷɔgʷɔlvaŋ na \`ɔ-lɔ=alaj\\

‘Some time later, the snake went.’
