summary: The passage explains that third person direct-object pronominals (na for singular, ta for plural) refer back to a previously mentioned noun phrase in discourse and can function as the sole expression of a direct object when its referent is already known. They are phonologically separate words rather than clitics, as shown by their failure to trigger expected verbal suffix changes and by the fact that their neutral prosody does not alter the verb word. The passage also notes that these pronominals normally occur within the verb complex, while first- and second-person objects are expressed by free pronouns or noun phrases after the verb complex.

text:
In a clause where the referent is clear, the 3 s pronominal na can sometimes be left out in a clause. Four consecutive lines from a narrative not illustrated in this work are shown in ex:7:43. In the narrative, the head of the household brings home some things he bought at the market. He tells his workers to carry the things into the house. In his instructions horom alay ayva ‘carry [all the things] into the house,’ there is no grammatical indication of ‘those things.’ The absence of the pronominal is indicated in the clause by the symbol Ø. In this case, the referent is clear and is not required in the clause. The pronominal in Moloko does not function in the way Frajzyngier has postulated for some Chadic languages. say that the pronoun codes the definiteness of the referent in some Chadic languages. While it is true in Moloko that when the pronominal (or any other pronoun) is used, then the referent is definite, the converse is not true. For example, the referent in ex:7:43 is definite yet there is no pronominal.

Bahay a hay olo a kosoko ava.\\
bahaj a haj ɔ-lɔ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava \\
chief house 3 s -go at market in\\
‘The head of the house went to the market.’\\

Askomala ele ahay gam.\\
a-sʊkʷɔm=ala ɛlɛ=ahaj gam\\
3 s -buy=to thing=Pl many\\
‘He bought many things.’\\

Awəɗakata ele ngəndəye ana ndam slərele ahan ahay, awəy,\\
a-wuɗak=ata ɛlɛ ŋgɛndijɛ ana ndam ɬɪrɛlɛ=ahaŋ=ahaj awij\\
3 s -divide= 3 p. thing people work= 3 s. =Pl said\\
‘[When he got home], he divided the things among his workmen, saying,’\\

“Horom alay ayva!”\\
hʷɔr-ɔm Ø =alaj ajva\\
carry[ ]- =away inside house\\
‘“Carry [all the things] into the house.”’

Likewise, in the Cicada story, the direct object (the tree that the chief wanted by his door) is not grammatically indicated in the clause in S. 16 ex:7:44. Although the referent is definite, there is no grammatical reference to it in the clause.

Cicada, S. 16\\
Taazala təta bay. \\
tàà-z=ala Ø təta baj \\
3 p + -take=to ability \\
‘They were not able to bring [the tree].’

Participants can be made prominent in a clause by doubling the reference to them. In ex:7:45 from S. 20 of the Cicada story, the tree that the chief desired is indicated twice in a clause, both by the presence of a noun phrase memele ga ndana ‘that tree that you spoke of’ and also the 3 s pronominal (both are bolded in ex:7:45 ). The effect is prominence.

Cicada, S. 20\\
Náamənjar na alay memele ga ndana əwɗe.\\
náá-mənzar na =alaj mɛmɛlɛ ga ndana uwɗɛ\\
+ -see 3 s. =away tree first\\
‘“First I want to see the tree that you spoke of.”’
summary:
In Moloko, the 3rd singular pronominal *na* may be omitted when the referent is already clear from context, even if the referent is definite. Thus definiteness is not simply coded by the presence of the pronominal: when a pronoun is used, the referent is definite, but definite referents can also appear without any pronominal reference.

The passage also shows that participants can be made prominent by doubling their reference, with both a noun phrase and a pronominal appearing in the same clause. In this way, pronominal use is associated with definiteness and prominence, but not obligatorily with all definite referents.

text: showed that Moloko does not mark verb stems for tense, but uses an aspectual system, looking at realis events as complete (Perfective, see sec:7.4.1 ) or incomplete (Imperfective, see sec:7.4.2 ). The vowel in the prefix expresses realis or irrealis mood (see sec:7.4.3 ). The tonal melody on the subject prefix expresses realis events as Perfective or Imperfective aspect, and expresses the various kinds of irrealis events. Reduplication of a consonant in the verb stem indicates habitual iterative aspect (see sec:7.4.4 ). Reduplication of the entire verb stem indicates the intermittent iterative aspect -- the intermittent repetition of the same action, possibly by the same actor, over a period of time (see sec:7.4.5 ). Another repeated aspect is the pluractional. The pluractional extension in Moloko indicates an action is back and forth, for example s=əya ‘sawing’ or h=aya ‘grinding’ ( sec:7.5.2 ).
summary: Moloko does not mark verb stems for tense; instead, it uses aspectual distinctions, treating realis events as perfective or imperfective, while the vowel in the prefix marks realis or irrealis mood. The tonal melody on the subject prefix distinguishes aspect and irrealis events, and reduplication signals iterative aspects: consonant reduplication marks habitual iterative aspect, full stem reduplication marks intermittent iterative aspect, and the pluractional extension indicates back-and-forth action.

Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfective aspect|(

The Perfective  aspect in Moloko is the aspect that presents a realis event as completed. Usually, the term ‘Perfective’ is used to refer to a situation as a whole, whether it is completed at the time of speaking or not. The situation is viewed in its entirety for Perfective, whereas in Imperfective aspect, the situation is viewed ‘from inside.’ as an ongoing process (; ). refers to verbs expressing completed actions as ‘perfect’ and those expressing incomplete actions as ‘imperfect.’ We have used the term ‘Perfective’ for completed actions in Moloko because there is also a morpheme representing Perfect in Moloko ( sec:7.5.3 ) which collocates with both of these other aspects. The Perfective aspect Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfective aspect is indicated by a phonetic low or mid tone on the subject prefix. Verb stems with underlyingly low tone or toneless verb stems have a phonetic low tone if the verb stem begins with a depressor consonant (see sec:6.7.1 ), and phonetic mid tone otherwise. Verb stems with underlyingly high tone are unaffected by depressor consonants and so the phonetic tone of the subject prefix is mid. tab:59 (from ) shows an example from each tone class.

The default verbal aspect for the main event line in a narrative is Perfective. Perfective verb forms are found in the main event line clauses expressing the events immediately following the setting sections of narratives. This is seen in the following examples drawn from three different narratives: ex:7:46 is from lines 4-6 of the Snake story, ex:7:47 is from a story not illustrated in this work, and ex:7:48 is from line 6 of the Cicada story. In Moloko, the Perfective aspect presents a realis event as completed, viewing the situation in its entirety rather than as an ongoing process. It is marked by a low or mid tone on the subject prefix, with the exact tone depending on the verb stem’s tone class and whether the stem begins with a depressor consonant.

Tense, mood, and aspect!Imperfective aspect|(

In contrast with the Perfective, the Imperfective aspect  can refer to a realis event that is incomplete and in the process of happening or to an event that is just about to begin. ‘Imperfective aspect’
usually refers to a situation ‘from the inside’ and is concerned with the internal structure of the situation. Perhaps ‘incomplete’ would be a better name for this aspect in Moloko; however it does not correspond with imperfect as described by in that the action need not begin before the present and be continuing, as notes. The subject prefix for the Imperfective form is always high tone and the tone over the verb stem varies according to the underlying tone of the verb stem. noted that the high tone on the prefix spreads to the first syllable of an underlyingly low tone verb. In the examples, the high tone of the Imperfective and low tone of Perfective are marked on the subject pronominal prefix. Compare ex:7:49 (Imperfective) and ex:7:50 (Perfective). Example ex:7:49 refers to an event in process of happening (going to the market; already en route). Tense, mood, and aspect!Irrealis mood|(

showed how mood influences the vowel features of the subject pronominal prefix. Moloko has two moods: realis and irrealis. The main formal feature of the irrealis mood is that the vowel in the subject prefix is lengthened. There are three subtypes of irrealis mood, indicated by tone along with the lengthened subject prefix. Only two moods were distinguished in previous documents (; ). Tone on the subject prefix has three patterns, and no longer correlates with Perfective or Imperfective aspect in the irrealis mood. Rather, it correlates with the speaker’s desire and will. These three types of mood are called Potential, Hortative, and Possible, respectively. Potential mood expresses an action desired by the speaker that is under his or her influence to perform. It carries a mild hortatory force for second person forms. Hortative mood expresses an action desired by the speaker to be performed by another who is somehow under his or her influence. Possible mood expresses that an action is desired by the speaker but dependent on the will of another.

The difference between the moods is illustrated in the following narrative situations. The first ( ex:7:63 and ex:7:64 ) illustrates a situation where someone says that he wants the chief to come to him, but he is not sure if the chief will actually come. The fact that the chief’s coming is desired by the speaker but dependent on the will of the chief is expressed by the Possible mood in ex:7:63, with falling tone on the lengthened subject prefix (bolded). Compare with the response given in ex:7:64, where the speaker is sure that the chief will come. The surety is expressed by the Potential mood, with high tone on the lengthened subject prefix (bolded).

Within irrealis, tone distinguishes three subtypes—Potential, Hortative, and Possible—which express, respectively, an action the speaker wants and can influence, an action the speaker wants another person to do, and an action the speaker wants but that depends on another person’s will. In these moods, tone on the lengthened subject prefix no longer correlates with perfective or imperfective aspect, but with the speaker’s desire, influence, and degree of certainty.

summary: The passage describes the habitual iterative aspect in Moloko, which expresses that an actor performs an action repeatedly as a usual habit. It is formed by geminating the onset of the final syllable of the verb word; if the root has one consonant, that consonant is doubled, and with CC roots the first consonant of the stem is doubled. The text contrasts this pattern with other repetition-related forms in Moloko, namely the intermittent iterative and the pluractional, which are marked differently.

text:
Tense, mood, and aspect!Intermittent iterative|(

The intermittent iterative called this aspect simply “iterative.” expresses the idea of the intermittent repetition of the same action, possibly by the same actor, over a period of time. Moloko has two other forms that involve repetition of the same actions -- the habitual iterative (marked by reduplication of one consonant in the stem, see sec:7.4.4 ) and the pluractional (marked by a verbal extension =aya or = əya, see sec:7.5.2 ). The intermittent iterative is formed by complete reduplication of the verb. Example ex:7:90 reflects a remark made by a friend concerning a situation where one duck died, then the owner bought another, and it died, and the situation was repeated four times. In the examples, the verb complex is delimited by square brackets.

Andəbaba ango amət amat.\\
andəbaba=aŋgʷɔ [a-mət a-mat]\\
duck=. 3 s -die 3 s -die \\
‘Your ducks keep dying.’ (lit. your duck, it dies it dies)

In the elicited example below, the situation is that a group of people has gone to the market and has bought several items from several different vendors. Note that the directional extension ala occurs only once, following the second verb.

A kosoko ava na, nəskwəmom nəskwəmom ala.\\
a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava na [nʊ-sʊkʷʊm-ɔm nʊ-sʊkʷʊm-ɔm =ala ]\\
at market in -buy- 1 Pex -buy- 1 Pex =to\\
‘At the market, we buy and buy.’ (lit. at the market, we buy we buy)\\

Plurality!Verb plurals|) Tense, mood, and aspect!Intermittent iterative|)
summary: The intermittent iterative in Moloko expresses the repeated occurrence of the same action over a period of time, and it is formed by complete reduplication of the verb. The text contrasts it with other repetition-related forms in the language, namely the habitual iterative, which uses consonant reduplication, and the pluractional, which uses the verbal extensions =aya or =əya.

text:
found that the six verbal extensions in Moloko are a class of morphemes that modify the meaning of the verb. They are clitics which cliticise to the right edge of the verbal complex to form a phonological word. The verb stem and the extensions may be separated syntactically by the indirect object pronominal clitics and third person pronominals (see Sections sec:7.3.1.1 and sec:7.3.2, respectively). The extensions will trigger the loss of any prosody on the verb stem.

In Moloko there are three categories of verbal extensions. Adpositionals (= aka ‘on’ and = ava ‘in’) These locational extensions are the same as the locational clitics on adpositional phrases; see sec:5.6.2. modify the meaning of the verb with particular reference to the location Deixis!Locational of the action. Directionals ( =ala ‘toward,’ =ala ‘away,’ and =aya ‘back and forth’ or pluractional) add the idea of movement with respect to a particular point of reference. The third category is the Perfect = va.
summary: The six verbal extensions in Moloko are clitics that attach to the right edge of the verbal complex and modify the verb’s meaning, forming a phonological word and causing the verb stem to lose its prosody. They belong to three types: adpositional extensions (=aka ‘on’, =ava ‘in’) that specify location, directional extensions (=ala ‘toward’/‘away’, =aya ‘back and forth’ or pluractional) that add movement relative to a reference point, and the Perfect =va.

text:
Clitics!Adpositionals|( Adpositionals|(

There are two adpositional enclitics: called these ``locationals.'' =aka ‘on, on top of’ and =ava ‘in.’ These extensions give the verb an added sense of the location of the action in the discourse. The extension =aka ‘on, on top of’ ex:7:92 resembles the second element of the adposition kə…aka ‘on.’ In like manner, =ava ‘in’ ex:7:93 resembles the adposition a…ava ‘in’ (see sec:5.6.2 ). Even though the verb in this example has verbal extensions, it is not conjugated for subject since it is a climactic point in the story where nominalised forms are often found ( sec:7.6 ). The corresponding adpositional phrases often co-occur with the adpositionals. In the examples, the adpositions and adpositionals are bolded.

Afəɗ aka war elé háy na, kə ver aka.\\
a-fəɗ= aka war ɛlɛ haj na kə vɛr aka \\
3 s -place=on child eye millet on stone on\\
‘She put the grain of millet on the grinding stone.’\\

Məmət ava alay a ver ava.\\
mə-mət= ava =alaj a vɛr ava \\
-die=in=away at room in\\
‘She died in the room.’\\

Adpositional extensions are phonological enclitics at the right edge of the verb. showed them to be phonologically bound to the verb stem because the /-j/ suffix drops off when the clitic attaches ex:7:95 (see also sec:6.3 ). Compare ex:7:94 and ex:7:95 which illustrate the verb /g -j e / ‘do.’ Note that the /-j/ suffix in the stem drops off when the extension =aka is attached ex:7:95. Another piece of evidence that the extension is phonologically bound to the verb stem is that the palatisation of the verb stem is neutralised by the extension. There is no adpositional extension and the verb word is palatalised in ex:7:94, whereas in ex:7:95 the locational extension =aka has neutralised the prosody of the entire verb complex.

Tege cəɗoy.\\
tɛ-g-ɛ tsʊɗɔj\\
3 p -do- trick\\
‘They played a trick.' (lit. they did trick)\\

Tag aka cəɗoy.\\
ta-g= aka tsʊɗɔj\\
3 p -do=on trick\\
‘They played another trick.’ (lit. they did trick ‘on top’ [of when they did it before])\\

Another piece of evidence that the extensions are phonologically attached to the verb stem is that the word-final allophones of /n/ and /h/, that is [ŋ] and [x], respectively, do not occur in the word-final position in the verb word when the locational is attached. When the extension =va cliticises to the verb /r h/ ‘fill,’ word-final alterations of /h/ do not occur ex:7:96. These allophones would be expected if the verb stem and Perfect extension were separate words.

Arah va peɗeɗe.\\
à-rah =va pɛɗɛɗɛ\\
3 s + -fill= id:full\\
‘It had filled right to the rim.’\\

The adpositional does not cliticise to the verb in ex:7:97 and ex:7:98 since the indirect object pronominal enclitic and plural subject suffix both trigger a word-final boundary (see sec:7.1 ), rendering the adpositional in a separate phonological word. In the examples, the boundaries of the phonological words are indicated by square brackets.

Kanjaw aka.\\
[ka-nz=aw] [= aka ]\\
-sit=. [=on\\
‘You are better than me.’ (lit. you sit on me)\\

Nədozlom ava a cəveɗ ava nə məze.\\
[n\`ə-dɔɮ-ɔm] [ =ava ] a tʃɪvɛɗ ava nə mɪʒɛ\\
+ -intersect- 1 Pex [=in in road in with person\\
‘We met a person on the road.’\\

The extension =aka ‘on’ or ‘on top of’ also has the metaphorical meaning of ‘in addition to,’ ‘again,’ or ‘even still’ when the action of the verb occurs ‘on top of’ something that occurred previously; compare the following pair of examples, and note how the =aka in ex:7:100 looks backward to another instance of the same action in ex:7:99.

Dərala.\\
dər=ala\\
move[. ]=to\\
‘Come closer (to me).’\\

Dər aka ala.\\
dər= aka =ala\\
move[. ]=on=to\\
‘Come even still closer.’\\

Using =aka in a context where the addressee is eating renders the meaning ‘do you want any more ‘on top of’ what you have already eaten?’ ex:7:101.

Asok aka ɗaw? \\
a-s=ɔkʷ = aka ɗaw\\
3 s -please=. =on q \\
‘Do you want any more?’ (lit. is it pleasing to you on?)\\

With the verb mbaɗ ‘change,’ =aka gives an idiomatic meaning to mark a change of speaker; that is, he spoke ‘on top of’ what the other person had just said.

Ambaɗaŋ aka. \\
a-mbaɗ=aŋ = aka \\
3 s -change= 3 s. =on\\
‘He/she replied.’ (lit. he changed to him on)\\
Adpositionals|)
summary:
The passage describes two locational adpositional enclitics, =aka ‘on, on top of’ and =ava ‘in,’ which add a sense of location to the verb and often co-occur with corresponding adpositional phrases. It argues that these elements are phonologically bound to the verb stem, based on effects such as suffix loss, neutralization of palatalization, and the behavior of word-final allophones, though they may fail to cliticize when other enclitics or suffixes create a phonological word boundary.  

It also notes that =aka can extend metaphorically to mean ‘in addition to,’ ‘again,’ or ‘even still,’ as in expressions meaning ‘come closer again,’ ‘do you want any more?,’ or ‘he replied.’

found three directional extensions =ala ‘towards’ ( ex:7:103, ex:7:104 ), =alay ‘away from’ ex:7:105, and =aya/=əya ‘back and forth repeated movement’ ex:7:106. These directionals occur after the verb word and, if present, after the adpositional extensions as seen in ex:7:103 and ex:7:104. The directionals precede the Perfect (see sec:7.5.3 ), as seen in ex:7:106.

Kazaka ala hor ese.\\
ka-zaɗ=aka= ala hʷɔr ɛʃɛ\\
-take=on=to woman again\\
‘You take another wife’ (on top of the one you already have). The root-final ɗ of the verb zaɗ ‘take’ drops off when affixes and clitics are added ( sec:6.2 ). (lit. you take a wife on again)\\

Təjapata aka ala ana Məloko enen ahay.\\
tə-dzap=ata =aka= ala ana Mʊlɔkʷɔ ɛnɛŋ=ahaj\\
3 p -group= 3 s. =on=to Moloko another=Pl\\
‘They grouped together again against some of the Molokos.’ (point of reference is the Molokos)\\

Dəraka alay. \\
dər=aka= alaj \\
move[. ]=on=away\\
‘Move further away (from me).’\\

Race story. \\
Moktonok na, abək ta aya va məlama ahan ahay jəyga.\\
mɔkʷtɔnɔkʷ na a-bək ta= aja =va məlama=ahaŋ=ahaj dzijga\\
toad 3 s -invite 3 p = = brothers= 3 p. =Pl all\\
‘The toad, he had already invited all of his brothers.’ (i.e., he went back and forth to all his brothers, inviting each)\\

Like the adpositionals, the directionals are phonological clitics at the right edge of the verbal complex. The presence of the enclitics requires that the /-j/ suffix be dropped off (the verb stem in example ex:7:104 is /dzap -j/ ‘mix’). The neutral prosody of these extensions causes the palatalisation on the verb stem to neutralise. In ex:7:107 the verb stem is / nz -j e / ‘go’ with a 3 s surface form of [ɛnʒɛ].

Anj ala.\\
a-nz= ala \\
3 s -go=to\\
‘He/she is coming.’

Directional extensions orient the event expressed by the verb relative to a centre of reference. In speech, that point of reference is usually the speaker, so actions are seen as going towards the speaker (= ala ), away from the speaker (= alay ), or back and forth repeatedly (= aya ). Compare the following examples of the verb /s kʷ m/ ‘buy/sell’ with a first person subject. When used with the directional =ala ‘toward,’ the verb means ‘buy’ ex:7:108. When it is used with the directional =alay ‘away,’ it means ‘sell’ ex:7:109.

Nəskom ala awak.\\
n\`ə-sʊkʷɔm =ala awak\\
+ -buy/sell=to goat\\
‘I bought a goat.’\\

Nəskom alay awak.\\
n\`ə-sʊkʷɔm =alaj awak\\
+ -buy/sell=away goat\\
‘I sold my goat.’\\

The directional =ala ‘toward’ indicates an action that moves toward the centre of reference (see ex:7:110 and ex:7:112 ). The directional =alay ‘away’ indicates an action that moves away from that centre (see ex:7:111 and ex:7:113 ). Compare the example pairs for /d r/ ‘move’ ( ex:7:110 and ex:7:111 ) and for / z ɗ/ ‘take’ ( ex:7:112 and ex:7:113 ). In each example pair, the first shows an action towards the speaker and the second shows an action away from the speaker.

Dər ala. \\
dər= ala \\
move[. ]=to\\
‘Come closer (to me).’\\

Dər alay.\\
dər= alaj \\
move[. ]=away\\
‘Move away (from me).’\\

Z ala eteme.\\
\ zaɗ= ala ɛtɛmɛ\\
take[. ]=to onion\\
‘Bring the onion (to me).’\\

Z alay eteme.\\
\ zaɗ= alaj ɛtɛmɛ\\
take[. ]=away onion\\
‘Take the onion away (from me).’\\

The third directional =aya or = əya gives the idea of repetitive movement back and forth. This repetitive back and forth movement is called pluractional Tense, mood, and aspect!Pluractional Plurality!Verb plurals. A verbal extension or affix is one way of showing pluractional actions in other Chadic languages. The other is reduplication of the verb root. Such verb root reduplication is also seen in Moloko for habitual iterative aspect sec:7.4.4 and intermittent iterative aspect sec:7.4.5. A few verbs never occur without the pluractional and involve regular back and forth movements like sawing ex:7:114, grinding ex:7:115, or putting many ( d=əya ). For other verbs, adding the directional adds a back and forth movement to the sense. Example ex:7:106 above involves the subject going from person to person to invite them to help.

Zar asəya memele.\\
\ zar a-s=ija mɛmɛlɛ\\
man 3 s -saw= tree\\
‘The man saws the tree.’\\

Aban ahaya háy.\\
Abaŋ a-h=aja haj\\
Abang 3 s -grind= millet\\
‘Abang grinds millet.’\\

Directionals are a device used in Moloko discourse to help provide cohesion. Other discourse devices which function in cohesion include demonstratives ( sec:3.2 ), the adjectiviser ga ( sec:5.3 ), the presupposition marker na ( chap:11 ), and participant tracking ( sec:7.3 ). Directionals keep the hearer oriented to the events of a story and how they relate to a particular spatial point of reference (a place or dominant character). The point of reference may remain constant throughout the whole story or it may change during the story. Selected lines from the Cicada text ex:7:116 illustrate how directionals relate main line events to the point of reference which is the chief (or perhaps the place in his compound where he makes the millet beer). The directionals are bolded in the examples. The presence of the two directionals in ex:7:119 and ex:7:120 is the only way in the story that we know that the cicada brought the tree back to the chief (until the chief thanks him in line 34).

Cicada, S. 6\\
Albaya ahay ndana kəlen təngala ala ma ana bahay.\\
albaja=ahaj ndana kɪlɛŋ t\`ə-ŋgala =ala ma ana bahaj\\
youth=Pl then 3 p + -return=to word chief\\
‘The above-mentioned young men then took the word (response) to the chief.’ (lit they returned the word to the chief)\\

Cicada, S. 12\\
Təlo tamənjar na ala mama agwazla nəndəye.\\
t\`ə-lɔ tà-mənzar na =ala mama agʷaɮa nɪndijɛ\\
3 p + -go 3 p + -see 3 s. =to mother spp. of tree \\
‘They went to see [for the chief] that mother-tree.'\\
summary:
Moloko has three directional verbal extensions: =ala ‘towards’, =alay ‘away from’, and =aya/=əya ‘back and forth repeated movement’. These clitics occur at the right edge of the verbal complex before the Perfect, and they orient events relative to a reference point, usually the speaker, so that =ala indicates motion toward that point, =alay motion away from it, and =aya repetitive back-and-forth movement.

The passage also shows that directionals can change verb meaning, as in ‘buy’ versus ‘sell’ with the same verb stem, and that some verbs are inherently pluractional with repeated movement. Beyond lexical meaning, directionals help maintain discourse cohesion by tracking how events in a story relate to a particular spatial or participant reference point.

‘but they were not able to bring it [to him].'\\

Amag ala ləmes.\\
ama-g =ala lɪmɛʃ\\
-do=to song\\
‘He was singing towards [the chief’s house].' (lit. to do towards a song)\\

Sen ala. \\
ʃɛŋ =ala \\
id:go=to\\
‘Going, [he] came [to the chief’s house].’\\

Sometimes the directional =ala ‘towards’ (see see sec:7.5.2 ) can carry a Perfect kind of idea (an event being completed before a temporal reference point with ongoing effects to that time) but which has a slightly different connotation to the Perfect extension =va. Compare ex:7:121 and ex:7:122. Use of the directional =ala ‘towards’ ex:7:121 with the verb /z m o / indicates that the person has already eaten, but at some other location, since the directional gives the idea that food has come to the speaker. Use of the Perfect itself ex:7:122 indicates that the person has finished eating (at the place where he is sitting). As such, the directional =ala may be in the process of becoming grammaticalised for past tense or a subtype of Perfect.

Nəzəm ala toho.\\
n\`ə-zəm =ala tɔhʷɔ\\
+ -eat=to \\
‘I already ate over there (some other person’s house – before I arrived here).’\\

Nəzəm va pew.\\
n\`ə-zəm =va pɛw\\
+ -eat= enough\\
‘I already ate/ I have eaten enough (here in this place since I arrived here).’\\

Likewise, the verb /s kʷ m/ ‘buy/sell’ is given a Perfect idea when it carries the =ala extension. In ex:7:108, the goat has come to the speaker. There is no Perfect extension =va but the idea is accomplished through the directional =ala.

Nəskom na ala awak.\\
n\`ʊ-sʊkʷʊm na =ala awak \\
+ -buy/sell 3 s. =to goat\\
‘I bought the goat (and it is mine now).’\\

summary: The passage shows that the directional clitic =ala ‘towards’ can express motion toward a goal, as in ‘go to bring back the tree,’ ‘singing towards the chief’s house,’ and ‘going, [he] came to the chief’s house.’ It can also convey a Perfect-like meaning, especially when an action has been completed before a reference point and has present relevance, though this differs slightly from the Perfect extension =va, which more clearly refers to completion in the current location. The author suggests that =ala may be grammaticalizing into a past tense or a subtype of Perfect.

Tense, mood, and aspect!Perfect|( Clitics!Perfect|(

The final extension is = va, the Perfect. The Perfect marks events or states as having occurred prior to a particular point of reference Cohesion!Point of reference, with ongoing effect that continues to that point of reference. The Perfect extension is bolded in the examples.

Tawəy, “Ambəɗə va anga ləme.”\\
tawij à-mbəɗ= va aŋga lɪmɛ\\
3 p +said 3 s + -change= 1 Pex \\
‘They said, “It has become ours!”’ (lit. it has changed; belonging to us)\\

Nasar həraf ɛlɛ nəngehe asabay, \\
nà-sar həraf ɛlɛ nɪŋgɛhɛ asa-baj \\
+ -know medicine thing again- \\
‘I didn’t know how to resolve the problem,’ \\

waya nəl va afa səwpərefe.\\
waja n\`ə-l= va afa suwpɪrɛfɛ\\

‘because I had already been to the sub-prefect [and he didn’t help me].’\\

Təta na, tanjakə va ɛlɛ məzəme.\\
təta na tà-nzak= va ɛlɛ mɪ-ʒɪm-ɛ\\
3 p 3 p + -find= thing -eat- \\
‘And so they had found something to eat.’\\

Arahə va peɗeɗe.\\
à-rah =va pɛɗɛɗɛ\\
3 s + -fill= id:full\\
‘It had filled right to the rim.’\\

Nəzəm va.\\
n\`ə-zəm =va \\
+ -eat= \\

Unlike the other extensions, the Perfect enclitic has two possible positions in the verb phrase. It can either be phonologically bound to the right edge of the verbal complex (see sec:7.1 ) or to the right edge of the clause ( chap:8 ) after the direct object and adpositionals. In ( ex:7:124 -- ex:7:127, ex:7:131 ), = va follows the adpositional and directional extensions in the verb complex and precedes other elements in the verb phrase. In ex:7:129 and ex:7:132, = va occurs at the end of the clause, a rarer construction that presumably occurs to underscore the idea that the event is already finished.

Disobedient Girl, S. 17\\
Azləna, hor na, asərkala afa təta va na, \\
aɮəna hʷɔr na à-sərk=ala afa təta =va na\\
but woman 3 s + -habitually=to at house of 3 p = \\
‘Now, that woman, she was in the habit at their place’\\

aməhaya háy na, gam.\\
amə-h=aja haj na gam\\
-grind= millet a lot\\
‘[of] grinding a lot of millet.’\\

The Perfect extension has neutral prosody itself and causes the loss of palatalisation of the verb stem (compare ex:7:130 -- ex:7:131 where the stem is /s-j e /). Also, verb stems drop their /-j/ suffix when this extension is present. These features all confirm that =va is an enclitic. In ex:7:130 without the Perfect, the verb stem is palatalised. When the verb carries the Perfect extension ex:7:131, the stem loses its palatalisation.

n\`ɛ-ʃ-ɛ gʊzɔm\\
+ -drink- millet beer\\
‘I drank millet beer.’\\

Nasa va gəzom.\\
n\`a-sa= va gʊzɔm\\

‘I drank millet beer already.’\\

Notably, palatalisation is lost even when there are intervening words ex:7:132, even though the prosody of these words is unaffected.

Nasa gəzom va.\\

‘It is the cool of the day (after three o’clock).’ (lit. late afternoon has done)\\

[n\'ə-bál-áj háj]\\

When the Perfect co-occurs with Imperfective aspect ( ex:7:139 -- ex:7:142 ), the verb is resultative, referring to an ongoing state that is the result of a previous completed event (filling, becoming tired, ripening, or becoming angry).

summary:
The Perfect enclitic =va marks an event or state as already occurring before a reference point and still relevant to that point. It can occur either inside the verbal complex or at the end of the clause, where it is used more emphatically, and it also causes loss of verb palatalisation and /-j/ suffixes, showing that it is an enclitic with a floating HL tone.  

When combined with Perfective aspect, =va indicates that the event happened before the discourse reference point, while with Imperfective aspect it yields a resultative meaning, referring to an ongoing state resulting from a completed event. It can also mark relative-clause information as completed before the main clause event.

The nominalised verb form called this form the ‘infinitive.’ is derived from a verb Derivational processes!Verb to noun stem by the addition of the prefix / m- / plus a palatalised suffix [-ɛ]. There is also an irregular nominalisation process that has already been discussed ( sec:4.2 ). Syntactically, the nominalised form can pattern as a noun (see sec:7.6.1 ), and in certain cases it can pattern as a verb, taking some inflectional components such as object suffixes and extensions (see sec:7.6.2 ). In the examples below, both underlying and nominalised forms are given. The nominalised form indicates an event (race, ex:7:145; betrayal, ex:7:146 ) or state (beauty, ex:7:147; coldness, ex:7:148 ).

In the case where a verb stem consists of one single consonant, the nominalised form receives an additional syllable [-ijɛ].

The prefix vowel in an a- prefix verb is full; in ex:7:152 and ex:7:153, this full vowel is realised as [ɛ] due to the palatalisation prosody which is part of the nominalising morphology. summary:
The passage explains that the nominalised verb form, sometimes called the “infinitive,” is derived from a verb stem by adding the prefix **m-** and a palatalised suffix **[-ɛ]**, though there is also an irregular nominalisation process. This nominalised form can behave syntactically like a noun and, in some cases, like a verb by taking inflectional material such as object suffixes and extensions.

It typically denotes events or states, and when the verb stem is a single consonant, an extra syllable **[-ijɛ]** is added. The form also reflects the underlying vowel of any **a-** prefix in the verb stem, and its tone pattern follows the tone of the original verb stem.

summary: Nominalised verb forms function like abstract nouns: they can take quantifiers, numerals, possessives, demonstratives, and adjectivisers, but not plural marking, and any clause argument may be expressed in the nominalisation. When modified by a noun, the nominalised verb can act as the head of constructions such as genitives or attributional phrases, where the following noun may represent either the subject or the direct object depending on the construction. Adjectives derived from nominalised verbs with *ga* express resultant states, such as already-ground peanuts, a beautiful girl, or someone who is already seated.

The nominalised form can take verbal extensions ( 3 p indirect object =ata, adpositional =aka and Perfect =va in ex:7:165; the adpositional =ava and the directional =alay in ex:7:166 ).

summary: The nominalised form can function as the verb in a full clause, and such clauses occur on the main event line, especially at narrative inciting moments and peaks, where they add focus and prominence. Although the nominalised form is not inflected for subject or direct object, the clause may still include them as well as verbal extensions such as indirect objects, adpositional markers, perfect, and directional elements.

text:
Focus and prominence!Verb focus construction

The nominalised form of a verb is used in an idiomatic construction that functions to bring focus on the verb. The verb focus construction is composed of an inflected verb followed by an adpositional phrase (see sec:5.6.1 ) containing the same verb in nominalised form. ex:7:167 shows the construction nəskom nə məskwəme ‘I really did buy it’ (lit. I bought [it] with buying). This construction specifies that the action is done ‘by means of’ or ‘by actually’ doing something (to the exclusion of all other possibilities). It is used by the speaker to contest a real or implied challenge of the validity of what has been said. In ex:7:167, the speaker is saying that he actually bought a particular item, i.e. he didn’t steal it and nobody gave it to him. Likewise, ( ex:7:168 -- ex:7:170 ) illustrate other verbs in this construction.

summary: The passage describes a verb focus construction in which an inflected verb is followed by an adpositional phrase containing the same verb in nominalised form. This idiomatic pattern highlights the action as being done “by means of” or “by actually” performing that verb, often to counter an implied challenge or denial of what was said. Examples show it being used to insist that something was truly bought or to specify the exact manner of killing or slaying.

A dependent verb form is formed by prefixing am- to the verb stem, palatalisation, and the suffix -e (or -əye for verb roots of one syllable). Historically, this construction may involve the nominalised form (see sec:7.6 ) preceded by the preposition a ‘to.’ Crosslinguistic studies reveal that locatives can give rise to Imperfectives (;; ). In any case it acts as a single unit now. tab:69 shows examples of the dependent verb form for stems of each underlying prosody. There are no subject inflections on the dependent verb form; the subject is determined either by the subject of the matrix clause (a gap for subject is marked as Ø in ex:7:171, ex:7:173, and ex:7:174 ) or a pronoun within the dependent clause indicating subject ( ex:7:172 -- ex:7:176 ). The dependent form of the verb may receive object suffixes and extensions. The dependent verb form is used when clauses that carry an imperfective or unfinished idea are embedded in other constructions. The clause structure is illustrated in fig:14.

The dependent verb form is built with am- plus palatalisation and the suffix -e, or -əye with one-syllable roots, and it may historically derive from a nominalised form preceded by a preposition. It has no subject inflection, though the subject is recovered from the matrix clause or a pronoun in the dependent clause, and it can take object suffixes and extensions.

This form is used for embedded clauses expressing an imperfective or unfinished idea, including relative clauses, temporal adverbial clauses, and complement clauses functioning as subjects or direct objects.

text: The verb phrase is the third of four chapters that concern the Moloko verb. chap:6 explores the structural features of the verb root and stem. chap:7 discusses what we have called the verb complex, which is a phonological unit consisting of the verb stem plus the pronominal affixes and enclitics, aspect/mood markings, and verbal extensions. These components are closely phonologically bound even though they may comprise from one to three phonological words. The chapter also covers derived forms. chap:9 describes verb types and transitivity. Moloko has a flexible valence system which allows variations in the transitivity of a given verb with no morphological marking. This chapter This chapter is adapted from. concerns the structure and functions of the verb phrase. sec:8.1 describes the constituents of the verb phrase and their order. sec:8.2 shows auxiliary verb constructions where two verbs form a syntactic unit.
summary: This chapter on the Moloko verb phrase follows earlier chapters on the verb root and stem, the verb complex, and verb types and transitivity. It focuses on the structure and functions of the verb phrase, including the order of its constituents and auxiliary verb constructions in which two verbs form a syntactic unit.

text:
The verb phrase in Moloko is centred around the verb complex (bolded in fig:15, cf. chap:7 ). Other elements are all optional and occur in the order diagrammed in fig:15.

The auxiliary verbs include the progressive (see sec:8.2.1 ), the verb l o ‘go’ when used as an auxiliary (see sec:8.2.2 ), and the verb stem or ideophone Ideophone|( in its construction (see sec:8.2.3 ).

Direct objects follow immediately after the verb complex and are expressed as noun phrases (bolded in ex:8:1 and ex:8:5 ) or ‘body-part’ incorporated nouns (bolded in ex:8:2; see sec:9.2.5 ). Adpositional phrases (underlined in ex:8:2 -- ex:8:6, see sec:5.6 ) and then adverbs (italicised in ex:8:4 and ex:8:5; see sec:3.5 ) or ideophone (italicised in ex:8:1 and ex:8:6; see sec:3.6 ) follow after the direct object. Following these criteria, all of the above elements are part of the verb phrase as a constituent of the clause. The elements of the verb phrase behave distributionally as a single structural unit that does not permit intrusion of parenthetical elements internally, but rather only at the boundaries. For Moloko, the distribution of adverbs, emphatic interrogative pronouns, ideophones, the Perfect enclitic, and the manner of fronting all attest to the unity of the verb phrase as described above. It also states that these elements form a single constituent that generally does not allow internal interruption, a fact supported by the distribution of temporal adverbs, emphatic interrogative pronouns, ideophones, and the Perfect enclitic =va. Only the presupposition marker can intrude into the verb phrase, and only in a specific construction.

text:
In an auxiliary verb construction in Moloko, two verbs (or a verb plus an ideophone) form a syntactic unit and, consequently, have the same subject. The second verb is the main verb in the construction. Together the two verbs comprise the head of just one clause, with only one set of core participants and obliques that semantically are related to the second (main) verb.

This section presents three auxiliary verb constructions. In the first two constructions, both main and auxiliary verbs are inflected. These constructions express progressive aspect ( sec:8.2.1 ) and movement from one place to another ( sec:8.2.2 ). The third construction consists of a verb stem or ideophone plus the main verb which is in the nominalised form ( sec:8.2.3 ). We consider this third construction to be an auxiliary construction even though the verb stem/ideophone does not carry much of the inflectional information normally associated with auxiliaries (stems and ideophones carry neither subject and object agreement nor aspect and mode marking). These criteria for verb auxiliaries are given by. However, the verb stem/ideophone Ideophone construction demonstrates the same structure as the progressive and movement auxiliary constructions and the stem/ideophone functions as an auxiliary in that it adds grammatical information to the main verb.
summary: In Moloko auxiliary verb constructions, two verbs or a verb plus an ideophone form a single syntactic unit with one subject, and the second verb is the main verb that determines the clause’s core participants and obliques. The section describes three such constructions: two with both verbs inflected, expressing progressive aspect and motion, and a third where a verb stem or ideophone combines with a nominalized main verb; although the stem/ideophone lacks normal auxiliary inflection, it is still treated as an auxiliary because it adds grammatical information and has the same overall structure.

Progressives are also found in the peak section Focus and prominence!Discourse peak of a narrative where they function to slow down the events and draw the reader into the action. Example ex:8:30 shows the entire peak section of the Disobedient Girl. In the story (shown in its entirety in sec:1.5 ), there is a battle between the disobedient girl and the millet itself. The millet has a supernatural ability to expand, and eventually triumphs over the girl. Verbs in the progressive form (bolded in the example) mark the ongoing multiplication of the millet (S. 23) while the girl is grinding as well as the girl’s ongoing grinding (S. 25) while the room is filling up with flour.
summary:
The progressive in Moloko is formed with the auxiliary **nday** ‘to be’ plus the main verb, with **nday** appearing first in the verb phrase and the main verb carrying the subject affixes and other inflections. It expresses an action or event in progress, and **nday** can also occur alone as a main verb meaning the subject’s location.  

The progressive does not co-occur with the Perfect enclitic or with the iterative reduplicative construction. In discourse, it is used for ongoing dynamic events, including tail-head links, expository explanations of ongoing states, and narrative peaks where it slows the action and highlights events in progress.

The stem or ideophone plus verb constructions mark significant events Focus and prominence!Discourse peak at the inciting moment and in the peak of a Moloko narrative. Example ex:8:38 is from the inciting moment of the Disobedient Girl story when the man instructs his wife. In the peak, the construction is seen when the woman prepares a lot of millet after having decided to disobey him ex:8:39, when she pours a lot of millet on the grinding stone ex:8:39, and when the millet suffocates her and she dies ex:8:43. In the dénouement there is another ideophone plus nominalised form construction when the husband opens the door and finds her ex:8:40. There are no other nominalised forms that fill the main verb slot in this text.

Because the subject, direct object, and indirect object are optional for this construction, the construction can be used in Moloko discourse as a narrative device to reduce the number of explicit grammatical relations in a clause (cf. Sections sec:3.6.3 and sec:9.4 ). The participants become indefinite in the construction and must be inferred from the context. The effect is to draw the hearer into the action of the moment. In ex:8:35, ex:8:39, and ex:8:40, Transitivity!Clauses with zero transitivity|( the construction is completely non-inflected for subject and has zero grammatical relations Transitivity!Clauses with zero transitivity. The narrative effect is that in ex:8:35 and ex:8:39, the hearer only knows that someone is pouring something onto the grinding stone. In ex:8:40, it is as if the hearer is with the husband, looking into the house to find the woman. Likewise, in ex:8:44, the verb mələye ‘bury’ is non-conjugated for subject, making those who buried the dead woman ‘out of sight’ in the narrative.

summary:
The passage describes a Moloko verb phrase construction used to mark discourse peaks and other pivotal narrative events. In this construction, either a verb stem or an ideophone precedes the main verb in nominalised form; neither verb is inflected for subject, and explicit subject noun phrases are usually absent or limited to full free pronouns.

This construction often reduces the number of overt grammatical relations, making participants indefinite and inferred from context, which heightens the immediacy of the action. The examples show it being used at the inciting moment, the climax, and the dénouement of a narrative, especially in the “Disobedient Girl” text.

text:
The way Moloko expresses transitivity is one of its remarkable features. reported that Moloko verb lexemes are underspecified with respect to transitivity Transitivity|(. This chapter extends and deepens their work. Almost every Moloko verb can occur in clauses which are intransitive, transitive, or bitransitive and therefore cannot be classed as belonging to any one transitivity type. Even clauses with no grammatical arguments exist -- a transitivity of zero Transitivity!Clauses with zero transitivity. The unique way that the semantics of the verb are realised by the affixes and extensions is one of the things that shows the genius of the language.

It is important to understand four important features of Moloko verbs with respect to transitivity. The first is that there are two kinds of transitive constructions in Moloko and an Agent-Theme-Location semantic analysis is necessary to interpret these two constructions ( sec:9.1 ). For transitive clauses, the grammatical relations of Moloko verbs directly and uniformly reflect the semantic picture. Subject expresses Agent. Direct object expresses semantic Theme, the core participant that literally or metaphorically changes state or position. Indirect object expresses semantic Location  which can be (depending on the verb type) either a literal or a metaphorical (recipient or beneficiary). This semantic picture holds for bitransitive clauses (Sections sec:9.2.4 and sec:9.2.5 ). For intransitive clauses, the subject can correspond to a range of semantic roles; it can be any one of Agent, Theme, or (Sections sec:9.2.4.2 and sec:9.2.5 ).

The second feature is that most Moloko verbs are ambitransitive -- the same verb with the same morphology may occur in clauses that are bitransitive, transitive, or intransitive. Moloko verbs are divided into classes based on the type of transitive and ditransitive construction(s) that the verb has ( sec:9.2 ). The third feature of Moloko verbs with respect to transitivity is that some verbs exhibit noun incorporation ( sec:9.3 ). The final feature of Moloko verbs is that there are clauses with zero transitivity ( sec:9.4 ). Transitivity!Clauses with zero transitivity|)

With the exception of the reciprocal (see sec:9.2.5 ), there are no affixes, extensions, or particles that express changes in transitivity as might be expected in a Chadic language. Causative verbal extensions, for example, are widespread in Chadic languages. In Moloko, it is the number and type of grammatical relations that a verb has that reflects the semantics of the construction.
summary:
Moloko verbs are largely underspecified for transitivity: most can occur as intransitive, transitive, or bitransitive, and some clauses even have zero transitivity. The language has two kinds of transitive constructions, best analyzed with an Agent-Theme-Location model, where subjects typically encode agents, direct objects themes, and indirect objects locations/recipients/beneficiaries; intransitive subjects may correspond to agent, theme, or location.

The passage also notes that most Moloko verbs are ambitransitive, with verb classes distinguished by the transitive and ditransitive constructions they allow. Unlike many Chadic languages, Moloko generally does not mark transitivity changes with affixes or particles; instead, the semantics of a construction is reflected in the number and type of grammatical relations.

text:
Moloko has two kinds of transitive clauses -- transitive clauses with subject and direct object ( ex:9:1 -- ex:9:2 ) and transitive clauses with subject and indirect object ( ex:9:3 -- ex:9:4 ). These two grammatically different transitive clauses illustrate that the semantics of Moloko verbs allows three core participants (represented by subject, direct object, and indirect object). Moloko verbs do not have just Agent-Patient semantic frames for events. In this work we follow an Agent-Theme-Location analysis, as developed by, in which ‘Location’  has a particular definition. Indirect object always expresses semantic -- the participant that represents the place where the Theme is directed to. As such the indirect object can express (depending on the verb type, see Sections sec:9.2.3 -- sec:9.2.5 ) the recipient or beneficiary of the event. Direct object always expresses semantic Theme, the core participant that changes position or state because of the event. Subject in transitive clauses expresses the Agent.

It is the verbal pronominals that best illustrate the grammar of the two types of transitive clauses because the grammatical distinction between direct and indirect object is expressed by a core pronominal (the direct object pronominal and the indirect object pronominal enclitic). Note that when the indirect object is a noun phrase, it is inside a prepositional phrase. The indirect object prepositional phrase in Moloko is not a syntactic oblique, however, because the pronominals indicate that it represents a core participant of the event. For this reason, most of the examples are given in pairs in this chapter. The first example in each pair shows full noun phrase arguments for each core participant. The second example in each pair shows the same clause with all core participants represented by verbal pronominals. Pronominals are bolded in the second example in each pair.

Examples ex:9:1 and ex:9:2 show a transitive clause with subject ( Mana ) and direct object ( awak ‘goat’ in ex:9:1, na 3 s direct object pronominal in ex:9:2 ).

Mana aslay awak.\\
Mana a-ɬ-aj awak\\
Mana 3 s -slay- goat\\
‘Mana slays a goat.’

A slay na.\\
a- ɬ-aj na \\
3 s -slay- 3 s. \\
‘He slays it.’

Examples ex:9:3 and ex:9:4 show a transitive clause with subject ( Mana ) and indirect object ( ana kəra ‘to dog’ in ex:9:3, = an ‘to him’ in ex:9:4 ).

Mana aɓan ana kəra. \\
Mana a-ɓ=aŋ ana kəra \\
Mana 3 s -hit= 3 s. dog\\
‘Mana hits a dog.’ (lit. he hits to him to dog)

Aɓan. \\
a-ɓ=aŋ \\
3 s -hit= 3 s. \\
‘He hits him.’ (lit. he hits to him)

Crosslinguistic studies might lead one to expect a verb like ‘hit’ to take a direct object; however verbs in Moloko require an Agent-Theme- semantic model to explain their behaviour. The indirect object kəra ‘dog’ is the semantic \ -- here the recipient of the action -- the participant that represents the place where the Theme (the hit) is directed to. The participant that changes position or state in this event (the hit) is implicit in verbs of this type (see sec:9.2.3 ).

Returning to the transitive clause with subject and direct object ( ex:9:1 and ex:9:2 ), the direct object awak ‘goat’ is the Theme -- the participant that changes position or state because of an event (it is slain).
summary:
Moloko has two kinds of transitive clauses: ones with subject plus direct object, and ones with subject plus indirect object. This shows that Moloko verbs can involve three core participants and are best analyzed with an Agent-Theme-Location model, where the subject is the Agent, the direct object is the Theme, and the indirect object is the Location, which may function as recipient or beneficiary depending on the verb.

The distinction is clearest in verbal pronominals, which mark direct and indirect objects differently and show that the indirect object is a core participant even when expressed as a prepositional phrase. Examples like ‘slay’ take a direct object Theme, while verbs like ‘hit’ pattern with an indirect object expressing the place or recipient toward which the action is directed.

text:
Most Moloko verbs are ambitransitive (i.e., labile) in that they can occur in intransitive, transitive, and sometimes bitransitive clauses with no morphological change in the verb complex (except of course the addition of the appropriate pronominals, sec:7.3 ). Some verbs in related Chadic languages can also be ambitransitive. These include Cuvok Cuvok, Buwal Buwal, and Vame Vame. Nevertheless, they can be divided into classes that exhibit different morphological and syntactic patterns relating/with respect to transitivity. Verbs are classified here as to the maximum number of grammatical relations that the verb can take as well as the type of grammatical relations:

Examples are given in pairs in this chapter, first with full noun phrase arguments and then the same clause is given with the noun phrases replaced by pronominals. Examples with pronominals are necessary because the centrality of the distinction of verb types in Moloko is more apparent from the pronominals, especially for the indirect object. The indirect object can be expressed with a core pronominal within the verb complex, or a full noun phrase within an adpositional phrase.
summary: Most Moloko verbs are ambitransitive, meaning they can appear in intransitive, transitive, or sometimes bitransitive clauses without any morphological change in the verb complex, aside from the appropriate pronominals. The chapter classifies verbs by the maximum number and type of grammatical relations they can take, and notes that pronominal examples are especially important because they make verb-type distinctions clearer, particularly for indirect objects, which may be expressed either as core pronominals in the verb complex or as full noun phrases in an adpositional phrase.

subsection: Group 1: Verbs that can only be intransitive
text:
Tense, mood, and aspect!Progressive|(

Only one verb in Moloko can never take an object (neither direct nor indirect). The locational clause contains the verb nday. It states that the subject is presently located somewhere ( ex:9:5 -- ex:9:6 ). An explicit free noun phrase subject is not required when this verb is the main predicate since the subject is indicated in the verb prefix; however an adpositional phrase giving the location is required and follows the verb. This same verb functions as a progressive aspect auxiliary (see sec:8.2.1 ). It is interesting that the locational extension = aka is also used to express progressive aspect sec:7.5.1.

Hawa anday a mogom.\\
Hawa a-ndaj a mɔgʷɔm\\
Hawa 3 s -be.located at home\\
‘Hawa is at home.’

Anday a Marva.\\
a-ndaj a marva\\
3 s -be at Maroua\\
‘She is in Maroua.’

Tense, mood, and aspect!Progressive|)
summary:
The verb **nday** is the only verb in Moloko that cannot take either a direct or indirect object. In locational clauses, it indicates that the subject is currently located somewhere, with the subject marked by the verb prefix and a following adpositional phrase required to specify the location.

The same verb also serves as a **progressive aspect auxiliary**, and the locational extension **=aka** is likewise used to express progressive aspect.

subsection: Group 2: Verbs that can be transitive with direct object
text:
Clauses with reflexive-causative verbs can have either one core argument (subject) or two core arguments (subject and direct object). We have never found these verbs in a context where they take an indirect object as third core argument.

Verbs from this class express reflexive actions when in an intransitive clause (action is to self; ex:9:7 ) and causative actions when in a transitive clause with a direct object (action is to direct object; ex:9:8 ).

Mana enjé a mogom. \\
Mana \`ɛ-nʒ-\'ɛ a mɔgʷɔm \\
Mana 3 s + -leave- at home\\
‘Mana went home.’ (lit. Mana left to home)

Mana enjé awak a mogom. \\
Mana \`ɛ-nʒ-\'ɛ awak a mɔgʷɔm\\
Mana 3 s + -leave- goat at home\\
‘Mana took the goat home.’ (lit. Mana left goat to home)

summary: Clauses with reflexive-causative verbs may have either one core argument, in intransitive clauses, or two core arguments, in transitive clauses with a direct object. These verbs express reflexive actions when used intransitively and causative actions when used transitively, and they have not been found with an indirect object as a third core argument.

subsection: Group 3: Verbs that can be transitive with indirect object

Attribution!Expressed using verb

Some transitive verbs in Moloko never take a direct object but rather have only what we have been referring to as an indirect object in this work. These verbs express experience, feeling, or emotion. The indirect object expresses the semantic (recipient, beneficiary, experiencer) of the event. A semantic core participant that moves or undergoes a change of state or is in a state (Theme) may be implicit or be lexicalised into the verb.

The verb rəɓ-ay ‘to be beautiful’ involves a thing and its quality ( ex:9:9 -- ex:9:10 ), and the person whose opinion or perception is being cited is coded as the indirect object. In an intransitive clause, the subject ( dalay ‘girl’) is at the state of being beautiful. In a transitive clause (with an indirect object), the subject ( dalay ‘girl’) is felt to be beautiful by the indirect object ( =aw ‘to me’).

Dalay arəɓay.\\
dalaj a-rəɓ-aj\\
girl 3 s -be beautiful- \\
‘The girl is beautiful.’

Dalay arəɓaw.\\
dalaj a-rəɓ=aw\\
girl 3 s -be beautiful=. \\
‘The girl is beautiful to me.’

The experience verb /ts r/ ‘taste good’ is grammatically expressed in ex:9:11 as the subject ɗaf ‘millet loaf' tastes good to the semantic expressed by the indirect object (the pronominal enclitic =aw ‘to me’).

‘Millet loaf tasted good to me.’

The verbs /dz n-j/ ‘help,’ /ɓ-j/ ‘hit,’ and /s/ ‘please' are also in this group of verbs. The receiver of the help or hit is expressed by the indirect object which is affected positively (in the case of help) or negatively (in the case of hit) by the event. For these verbs, the semantic Theme (the hit or the help) never appears as a direct object since it is part of the meaning of these verbs. tab:71 presents examples of verbs of this type.

Note that an intransitive clause appears to be ungrammatical for the verbs /ɓ-j/ ‘hit’ and /s/ ‘please’ ( ex:9:13 -- ex:9:14 ).

This includes verbs of feeling and experience such as ‘be beautiful,’ ‘taste good,’ and ‘fear,’ as well as ‘help,’ ‘hit,’ and ‘please,’ where the affected person is coded as the indirect object and no separate direct object occurs. The passage also notes that for ‘hit’ and ‘please,’ an intransitive clause is ungrammatical.

subsection: Group 4: Verbs that can be bitransitive
text:
Verbs that can occur in bitransitive clauses with subject, direct object, and indirect object can also occur in intransitive clauses (subject only) and transitive clauses (subject and direct object). When present, the indirect object always expresses the benefactive or malefactive.

The semantics of transitive and bitransitive clauses is uniform for these verbs – subject always expresses semantic Agent, direct object always expresses semantic Theme, and indirect object always expresses semantic (typically Beneficiary or Maleficiary). Intransitive clauses are more flexible in that the subject can express either Agent or Theme for some verbs. Transitive and bitransitive clauses are discussed for these verbs in sec:9.2.4.1 and intransitive clauses are discussed in sec:9.2.4.2.
summary: Verbs that appear in bitransitive clauses with subject, direct object, and indirect object can also occur in intransitive and transitive clauses. In bitransitive and transitive uses, the roles are consistent: the subject is an Agent, the direct object is a Theme, and the indirect object, when present, expresses a benefactive or malefactive. Intransitive clauses are more variable, since the subject may function as either Agent or Theme depending on the verb.

subsection: Group 4: Verbs that can be bitransitive
subsubsection: Group 4 verbs in transitive and bitransitive clauses
text:
The verb p-ay ‘open’ illustrates this verb type. In a transitive clause ex:9:15, the subject ( Mana ) performs the action on the direct object ( mahay ‘door’).

Mana apay mahay.\\
Mana à-p-aj mahaj\\
Mana 3 s + -open- door\\
‘He/she opened the door.’

In a bitransitive clause ex:9:16, the action done to the direct object is for the benefit of the indirect object.

Mana apan mahay ana Hawa.\\
Mana à-p=aŋ mahaj ana Hawa\\
Mana 3 s + -open= 3 s. door Hawa\\
‘Mana opened the door for Hawa.’

The verb mənjar ‘see’ occurs in intransitive, transitive, and bitransitive clauses. In a transitive clause ex:9:17, the subject ( Mala ) sees the direct object ( awak ‘goat’). The indirect object ‘goat’ undergoes a change of state from being unseen to being seen at a particular.

Mala ámənjar awak.\\
Mala á-mənzar awak\\
Mala 3 s + -see goat\\
‘Mala sees a goat.’

In a bitransitive clause ex:9:18, the subject ( Mala ) sees the direct object ( awak ‘goat’) on behalf of the indirect object beneficiary ( bahay ‘chief’). The chief is the metaphorical to which the action is directed.

Mala 3 s -go 3 s -see= 3 s. goat chief\\
‘Mala went to see a person’s goat in the chief’s place.’

For the verb /h/ ‘say’ ex:9:19, the subject Mana says the utterance (expressed by the direct object pronominal na ) to Hawa.

Mana à-h=aŋ na ana Hawa\\

‘Mana told it to Hawa.’

For some transitive verbs of this type, the indirect object (when present) marks the malefactive of the event. The indirect object will be negatively affected by the event. For the verb paɗ-ay ‘eat’ in ex:9:20 the subject ( awak ‘goat’) ate the direct object ( háy ‘millet’), incurring a negative effect on the indirect object ( =aw ‘to me’). This phenomenon is also known as possessor raising or external possession. We consider that the semantics for this construction in Moloko are malefactive rather than possessive because a possessive construction can also be employed (without an indirect object): awak a-paɗ-ay na háy əwla =va, ‘the goat ate my millet’. The construction with an indirect object connects the millet to its owner with less precision than the possessive construction, and concentrates on the loss that the owner incurred (due to the damages done to his millet field) rather than the fact that he owned the field.

The literal meaning of ex:9:23 is ‘They are greeting you,’ but this construction is used even when the person greeting is singular and the speaker knows who it is but doesn’t want to say. In intransitive clauses for these verbs, Imperfective aspect indicates that the subject is at the state of being potentially able to do or submit to the action (more of an irrealis idea) while Perfect is a resultative state. In contrast, for transitive and bitransitive clauses, Imperfective aspect expresses an incomplete event (see sec:7.4.2 ) and the Perfect expresses that the event was completed prior to a point of reference (see sec:7.5.3 ). text:
Three transfer verbs in Moloko are notable. They are dəbənay ‘learn/teach,’ skom ‘buy/sell,’ and vəl ‘give.’ These verbs are especially labile in terms of their semantic expression in that a transitive clause can have either a direct or an indirect object.

The verb vəl ‘give’ is shown in a bitransitive clause in ex:9:33. The subject ( bahay ‘chief’) transfers the direct object ( dalay ‘girl’) to the indirect object ( Mana ).

Bahay avəlan dalay ana Mana.\\
bahaj à-vəl=aŋ dalaj ana Mana\\
chief 3 s + -give= 3 s. girl Mana\\
‘The chief gave the girl to Mana (in marriage).’

When vəl ‘give’ occurs in a transitive clause, the second core argument can be either a direct object ex:9:34 or an indirect object ex:9:35. In ex:9:34, the chief is marrying off his daughter to an unspecified suitor. The subject ( bahay ‘chief’) transfers the direct object ( dalay ‘girl’) to someone who is unspecified in the clause.

Bahay ávar dalay.\\
bahaj á-var dalaj\\
chief 3 s + -give girl\\
‘The chief is marrying off his daughter [to someone].’ (lit. chief gives girl)

In ex:9:35, the subject ( bahay ‘chief’) transfers something or someone to the indirect object ( Mana ). What he gave would probably be specified in the immediate context, but is out of sight in this clause.

Bahay avəlan ana Mana.\\
bahaj à-vəl=aŋ ana Mana\\
chief 3 s + -give= 3 s. Mana\\
‘The chief gave [something] to Mana.’

When the verb vəl ‘give’ occurs in an intransitive negative clause (Imperfective Tense, mood, and aspect!Imperfective aspect, ex:9:36 ), it expresses that the subject is in the state of not giving anything to anyone, or not being the giving kind. Note the phonological change of the final consonant ( r becomes l when there is a suffix, see sec:6.2 ). Without the negative marker, the meaning would probably be ‘the chief is the giving kind.’ This is a specific example from a text. We have not seen one-participant clauses for this verb type in Perfective aspect.
The semantics of one-participant clauses for group four verbs is discussed in sec:9.2.4.2.

Bahay ávar bay.\\
bahaj á-var baj\\
chief 3 s + -give \\
‘The chief is not the giving kind.’ (lit. chief doesn’t give)

The verb dəbənay ‘learn’/‘teach’ occurs in transitive and bitransitive clauses. We found no clauses with one core participant for this verb. In bitransitive clauses illustrated by ex:9:37, the subject ( bahay ‘chief’) transfers the direct object ( Məloko ‘Moloko language’) to the indirect object ( ana babəza ahay ‘to the children’). The indirect object is expressed in an adpositional phrase as well as the verbal pronominal extension =ata ‘to them.’ The indirect object expresses the recipient or beneficiary of the event.

Bahay adəbənata Məloko ana babəza ahay. \\

Noun incorporation|(

identified a unique group of verb constructions in Moloko. In these constructions, a special, sometimes phonologically reduced noun form that represents a part of the body is incorporated into the verb phrase. This is a case of noun incorporation where these body-part nouns are closely associated with the verb complex and their incorporation changes the lexical characteristics of the verb. These body-part nouns include ma ‘mouth,’ ( ex:9:45, sec:9.3.1.3 ), elé ‘eye,’ ( ex:9:46, sec:9.3.1.1 ), sləmay ‘ear,’ ( ex:9:47, sec:9.3.1.2 ), and va or har ‘body,’ ( ex:9:48, ex:9:49, Sections sec:9.3.1.4 and sec:9.3.1.5, respectively). These nouns can be incorporated into transitive or bitransitive verbs from the types in Sections sec:9.2.2 and sec:9.2.3.

‘He/she calls the child again.’ (lit. he calls mouth to him to the child again)

‘Mala looks around attentively.’

The body-part noun follows directly after all other elements in the verb complex. It appears to be in the same position as any other noun phrase direct object in the verb phrase (see chap:8 ); however it is in more tightly bound to the verb complex than a noun phrase. The body-part noun does not fill the pronominal slot, because verbal extensions that follow the pronominal in the Moloko verb complex precede the body-part (see ex:9:45 and ex:9:47 which each have an adpositional extension, see sec:7.5.1 ). It is not phonologically bound to the verb since, unlike the Perfect verbal extension =va which is part of the verb complex, the body-part va does not neutralise the prosody on the verb stem ex:9:48. However, the incorporated noun is grammatically closer to the verb complex than a noun phrase direct object would be because the body-part can never be separated from the verb complex. The body-part can never be fronted in the clause (see sec:8.1 ). Nor can the body-part be separated from the verb complex by the presupposition marker. Both of these situations can occur for noun phrase direct objects and are illustrated in sec:11.2 ( ex:9:29 and ex:9:30 ).

Incorporation of the body-part noun never co-occurs with another direct object or with the pronominal na. A transitive clause with subject, indirect object and incorporated body-part noun can occur where the indirect object expresses semantic (sometimes metaphorical).

elé ‘eye’

The body-part noun elé ‘eye’ collocates with some verbs to lexicalise the engagement of the eyes and reduce the focus on what is seen. This body-part word is used in its full form. For example, the verb mənjar normally means ‘see’ (see tab:76 ). With the incorporation of elé ( ex:9:52 -- ex:9:53 ), the verb plus body-part construction has a more active experiential meaning in that the subject of the clause ( Mala ) is looking around attentively. Since there can be no direct object, there is no explicit referential object as stimulus -- the speaker is vague about what exactly Mala will look at.

sləmay ‘ear’

A second body-part noun is sləmay ‘ear’ which collocates with some cognition verbs. This body-part noun is used in its full form. Like elé ‘eye,’ it adds a new, more active lexical meaning to the verb with which it collocates.

For example, the normal lexical meaning of the verb cen is ‘hear’ or ‘understand’ ex:9:55 and the verb is bitransitive (see sec:9.2.4 ). The incorporation of the body-part sləmay ‘ear’ gives a much more active or intensive idea -- not just hear and understand someone, but also listen to them or obey them ex:9:56. The focus is on the fact that the person is benefitting from using his ears to intently listen, rather than on the person speaking or the content of their message.

‘Mana is deaf/disobedient.’

summary:
Moloko has a special type of noun incorporation in which body-part nouns such as ‘mouth,’ ‘eye,’ ‘ear,’ and ‘body’ are incorporated into the verb complex, often in reduced form, and this incorporation can change the verb’s lexical meaning. These incorporated nouns occur with transitive or bitransitive verbs, follow the rest of the verb complex, and are more tightly bound to the verb than ordinary direct objects, since they cannot be fronted or separated by the presupposition marker and do not co-occur with another direct object or with the pronominal na.

The passage also shows that body-part incorporation often creates idiomatic or more intensive meanings: for example, ‘eye’ with ‘see’ can mean looking around attentively, and ‘ear’ with ‘hear/understand’ can mean listening or obeying. It also notes idioms built with the verb ‘do,’ such as ‘do heart’ meaning ‘be angry’ and ‘do brain

The ‘body-part’ noun ma ‘mouth’ (which also means ‘word’ and ‘language’) collocates with some speech verbs. It is found in its full form in the verb plus body-part constructions. Example ex:9:57 shows the verb hay ‘say’ with the body-part noun ma ‘mouth.’

Tahok ma.\\
ta-h=ɔkʷ ma\\
3 p -tell=. mouth\\
‘You are being greeted.’ (lit. they are telling word to you)

The example pairs shown in tab:78 illustrate its use with three speaking verbs; taray ‘call,’ hay ‘say’ and jay ‘speak.’ Examples are shown with the direct object pronominal na (column 1) and with ma ‘mouth’ (column 2). With the body-part incorporation, there can be no other direct object.

A similar creation of new lexical meaning occurs with verbs that are normally not speech verbs but that become speech verbs when they collocate with ma. The verbs sok-oy ‘point,’ zom ‘eat,’ and njakay ‘find’ are shown in tab:79. The incorporation of ma with sok-oy ‘point’ gives a particular manner of communication: sokoy ma ‘whisper.’ Incorporation of ma with the verb zom ‘eat’ gives the idea of helping someone else to eat. Incorporation of ma with njakay ‘find’ yields an expression 'to find trouble.'

va ‘body’

There are two different phonologically reduced forms of the word hərva ‘body’ -- va and har. When collocated with certain verbs, the verb plus incorporated body-part takes on a new lexical meaning. This is a non-productive process found with only a few verbs.

The first reduced form of hərva ‘body’ is va. Note that there are three homophones of va which one must take care to distinguish: [ =va ] ‘perfect,’ [ va ] ‘body,’ and [ ava ] ‘in’. They all can occur immediately following the verb stem. This body-part is used for forming reciprocals with plural subjects of a few verbs in a context of killing and loving ( zləge ‘throw’ ex:9:58 -- ex:9:59, kaɗ ‘kill by clubbing’ ex:9:60, and ndaɗay ‘need,’ ex:9:61 ).
