summary: The passage describes a non-productive process of noun incorporation involving the body-part nouns *ma* ‘mouth/word/language,’ *va* ‘body,’ and *har* ‘body,’ which combine with certain verbs to create new lexical meanings. With *ma*, some speech verbs retain or shift meaning, and even non-speech verbs can become speech-related; with *va*, the resulting constructions can express reciprocity, resemblance, or rest; and with *har*, incorporation yields meanings such as dispersing or pleasing.

text:
Transitivity!Clauses with zero transitivity|(

There are clauses in Moloko with no grammatically explicit arguments - these clauses have a transitivity of zero. The ideophone clause can also have zero transitivity
( sec:3.6.3 ). See also zero transitivity in nominalised forms, sec:8.2.3. Nominalised and dependent verb forms are not inflected for subject (see Sections sec:7.6 and sec:7.7, respectively). When they also carry no or pronominal, the clause has zero transitivity. The use of verb forms with no grammatical relations has a discourse function to temporarily take participants out of sight. In the Disobedient Girl story peak episode S. 22 ex:9:67, the dependent verb aməhaya ‘grinding,’ is unconjugated for subject, direct object, and indirect object. The effect is to keep the participants out of sight as the events unfold and increase vividness as the audience is drawn into the story. All the audience hears is the sound of grinding. The millet is expanding, filling the room and the disobedient girl is lost inside it as she is being suffocated by the millet.

Disobedient Girl, S. 22\\
Njəw njəw njəw aməhaya azla.\\
nzuw nzuw nzuw amə-h=aja aɮa\\
id:grind -grind= now\\
‘ Njəw njəw njəw [she] ground [the millet] now.’

Likewise in line S. 15 of the Snake story ex:9:68, the nominalised form of the verb ‘to penetrate’ occurs with neither nor indirect object pronominals. The climactic moment when the storyteller spears the snake is in a clause with zero transitivity. Focus and prominence!Discourse peak Participants are out of sight in the discourse.

Snake story, S. 15\\
Mecesle mbəraɓ!\\
mɛ-tʃɛɬ-ɛ mbəraɓ\\
-penetrate- id:penetrate \\
‘It penetrated, mbəraɓ!’

Transitivity|) Transitivity!Clauses with zero transitivity|)
summary: Moloko has clauses with zero transitivity, meaning they contain no grammatically explicit arguments. This occurs with ideophone clauses and also with nominalised or dependent verb forms that are not inflected for subject, and may lack object pronominals as well. Such forms are used in discourse to temporarily hide participants from view and increase vividness or focus during climactic story events.

text: Moloko is an SVO language, which means that the default order of clausal constituents in a simple clause is subject, followed by verb (or predicate), and finally object. Elements can be fronted only in a special na construction described in chap:11. Clause types in Moloko are closely related to the verb type and transitivity of the clause (see chap:9 ). In this chapter the basic structure of declarative clauses for all verb types is discussed ( sec:10.1 ). The na construction can be superimposed upon the basic clause structure, changing the word order. Since the na construction is more complex and can involve more than one clause, na constructions are discussed in a separate chapter ( chap:11 ). Negation, interrogative, command, and exclamatory clause structures can be further superimposed on a simple or na -marked clause to add a functional element (Sections sec:10.2 -- sec:10.5 ). Clause combining is discussed in chap:12.
summary: Moloko is an SVO language, with the basic simple clause order subject–verb–object. Fronting is only possible in the special *na* construction, which can alter word order and is treated separately because it is more complex and may involve more than one clause. Declarative clause structure is discussed for all verb types, and negation, questions, commands, and exclamations can be added to either simple or *na*-marked clauses; clause combining is covered in a later chapter.

text:
Moloko has two basic types of declarative clauses, depending on whether the clause contains a verb or not. The verbal clause is described in sec:10.1.1. Clauses where an existential or an ideophone Ideophone is the central element are a subtype of verbal clauses. The special features of the structure of existential and ideophone clauses are discussed in sec:3.4 and sec:3.6, respectively. Non-verbal clauses are described in sec:10.1.2. These include predicate nominal, predicate adjective, and predicate possessive clauses.

There is not a lot of variation in the word order of the elements of the basic clause, but the number of grammatically explicit core participants controls the semantic roles assigned to the subject, direct object, and indirect object (see chap:9 ).
summary:
Moloko has two basic types of declarative clauses: verbal and non-verbal. Verbal clauses include those whose central element is a verb, as well as existential and ideophone clauses, while non-verbal clauses include predicate nominal, predicate adjective, and predicate possessive clauses.  

The basic clause shows little variation in word order, but the number of grammatically explicit core participants determines how semantic roles are assigned to the subject, direct object, and indirect object.

text:
The basic structure of Moloko verbal clauses includes the illustrated elements in the order shown in fig:16. Elements whose inclusion in the clause is optional are in parentheses. The order of clause constituents for all clause types is always SVO (with V and O being within the verb phrase). The verb phrase ( chap:8 ) is the centre of the clause (and also its final element) and can contain information concerning the subject, direct object, indirect object, aspect, mood, direction, location, repetition, and discourse-importance of the event or state expressed by the verb (see Sections sec:7.3 -- sec:7.5 ). All other elements are optional. When present, the temporal adverb gives locational information concerning the event. If a full subject noun phrase is present, it precedes the verb phrase, and any other core clause constituents follow the verb in the verb phrase (direct object, indirect object, obliques). The subject controls the subject inflections on the verb word.

The first element in the clause can be a temporal noun phrase ( ex:10:1 ).

Apazan albaya ahay tolo a ləhe.\\
apazaŋ albaja=ahaj tɔ-lɔ a lɪhɛ\\
yesterday youth=Pl 3 p + -go at bush\\
‘Yesterday the youths went to the bush.’

The subject is expressed by the subject pronominal on the verb ( sec:7.3.1 ). A coreferential noun phrase can be present for discourse functions ( ex:10:2 and ex:10:3 ). The coreferential noun phrase precedes the verb.

Hawa ahəmay.\\
Hawa à-həm-aj\\
Hawa 3 s + -run- \\
‘Hawa ran.’

nɛ =ahaŋ n\'ɔ-zɔm na\\
= 3 s. 3 s + -eat 3 s. \\
‘I myself ate it.’

The simplest form of the verbal clause type consists of a verb complex only. A verb complex can stand alone as a clause because, in addition to the verb stem, it contains information on grammatical relations (subject in the subject prefix, direct object and indirect object in a verb extension or suffix). The verb complex also includes directional and (non-core) locational information and indicates aspect and mood. It is interesting that the SVO order is maintained in the affixes (s-v-o), as seen in fig:7.2. (from sec:7.1 ).

The examples below are clauses consisting of just a verb complex. They all have information on the subject (from subject inflections, ex:10:4, ex:10:6, ex:10:7, ex:10:8 ) or the form of the imperative ( ex:10:5 and ex:10:9 ). Some have information on the direct object ( ex:10:6 -- ex:10:9 ), indirect object ( ex:10:8 and ex:10:9 ), direction of the action ( ex:10:5, ex:10:7, ex:10:9 ), and discourse information ex:10:5.

summary: Moloko verbal clauses have a basic SVO order, with the verb phrase as the central and final element of the clause. The verb phrase can encode subject, object, indirect object, aspect, mood, direction, location, repetition, and discourse information, while all other clause elements are optional. A clause may consist of only a verb complex, since the verb itself can carry grammatical relations and other information through affixes.

subsection: Predicate nominal, predicate adjective, and predicate possessive clauses
text:
Predicate nominal ( ex:10:10 -- ex:10:12 ), predicate adjective ex:10:13, and predicate possessive ( ex:10:14 and ex:10:15 ) clauses lack any verb and consist of a juxtaposition of two noun phrases, in an order shown in fig:17.

Predicate nominal clauses typically express the notions of proper inclusion (i.e., the clause indicates that the subject is a member of the particular class of items indicated by the predicate, ex:10:10 ) or equation (i.e., the clause indicates that the subject is identical to the predicate, ex:10:11 and ex:10:12 ). In the following examples, each noun phrase is delimited by square brackets.

[ɬəmaj=uwla] [Abaŋgaj]\\
name=. Abangay\\
‘My name [is] Abangay.’

[Zar nehe] [baba əwla].\\
[zar nɛhɛ] [baba=uwla]\\
man father=. \\
‘The man [is] my father.’

Predicate adjective clauses consist of a subject noun phrase and a derived adjective
( sec:5.3 ) as the predicate noun phrase. These clauses express an attribute of the subject ex:10:13.

‘He/she [is] big.’

Predicate possessive clauses have a subject noun phrase and a possessive prepositional phrase (see sec:5.6.1 ) as the predicate phrase. The participant named in the possessive phrase is expressed via a full noun phrase. These clauses express that the subject noun phrase is associated with the participant named in the possessive phrase. The semantic range for the predicate possessive clauses is the same as that of any possessive or genitive construction (see Sections sec:3.1.2.1 and sec:5.4.1 ).

[Babəza ahay nəndəye] [ anga bahay].\\
[babəza=ahaj nɪndijɛ] [ aŋga bahaj]\\
children=Pl chief\\
‘The children here belong to the chief.’ / ‘The children here[are] belonging to the chief.’

[Dəray ga] [ anga ləme].\\
[dəraj ga] [ aŋga lɪmɛ]\\
head 1 Pex \\
‘The head belonged to us.’/ ‘The head [was] belonging to us.’

For all three of these clause types, the subject may be marked as presupposed (see sec:11.2 ). For a predicate nominal construction, fronting and marking the predicate with na expresses equation in ( ex:10:16 -- ex:10:18 ).

[Zar mehere na], [Mana].\\
[zar mɛ-hɛr-ɛ] na [Mana]\\
man -build- Mana\\
‘The builder [is] Mana.’

[Bahay a Laway na], [Ajəva].\\
[bahaj a Lawaj na] [Adzəva]\\
chief Lalaway Adzava\\
‘The chief of Lalaway [is] Adzava.’

[Malan ga na], [ndahan].\\
[malaŋ ga] na [ndahaŋ]\\
largeness 3 s \\
‘The biggest one [is] him.’ (lit. big, him)
summary:
Predicate nominal, predicate adjective, and predicate possessive clauses in this language lack an overt verb and consist of two juxtaposed noun phrases in a fixed order. Predicate nominal clauses express either inclusion or equation, predicate adjective clauses express an attribute of the subject, and predicate possessive clauses express association with the participant named in the possessive phrase. 

The subject in all three clause types may be marked as presupposed, and in predicate nominal clauses, fronting the predicate and marking it with **na** expresses equation.

text: Negation constructions are specific constructions superimposed on a clause to create negation of the entire proposition ( sec:10.2.2 ) or negation of one element of the clause ( sec:10.2.3 ). For both, Moloko uses a negative particle baj or compound at the end of the clause or noun phrase ( sec:10.2.1 ).
summary: Negation constructions are added to a clause to negate either the entire proposition or a single element within the clause. In Moloko, both kinds of negation are expressed with the negative particle **baj** or a compound placed at the end of the clause or noun phrase.

text:
The all-purpose negative is the particle bay, which follows the verb phrase and occurs ( ex:10:19 -- ex:10:21 ) before any interrogative word (see sec:10.3 ). In the examples in this section, the negative is bolded and the negation construction is in square brackets.

[Alala bay ].\\
[à-l=ala baj ]\\
3 s + -go=to \\
‘He/she didn’t come.’

[War ga ecen sləmay bay ].\\
[war ga ɛ-tʃɛŋ ɬəmaj baj ]\\
child 3 s -hear ear \\
‘That child did not obey.’ (lit. that child, he hears ear not)

[Táazləgalay avəlo bay ].\\
[táá-ɮəg=alaj avʊlɔ baj ]\\
3 p + -throw=away above \\
‘They should not throw it too high.’

In ( ex:10:22 -- ex:10:24 ) the negative is clause-final and may have sematic scope over the entire proposition (c.f. constituent negation, sec:10.2.3 ). See especially ex:10:23 where it is clear that the entire proposition is being negated, and not just the information within the constituent closest to the negative. The meaning is ‘don’t insult a small person.’ If the information in only one constituent was being negated, the meaning would have been ‘insult a person who is not small.’

[Tagaw ele lala bay ].\\
[ta-g=aw ɛlɛ lala baj ]\\
3 p -do=. thing good \\
‘They do bad things to me.’ / ‘They don’t do good things to me.’

[Kárasay məze cəɗew ga bay ].\\
[ká-ras-aj mɪʒɛ tʃɪɗɛw ga baj ]\\
+ -minimise- person smallness \\
‘Don’t insult one of the little people.’

[Anday dəren bay ].\\
[à-ndaj dɪrɛŋ baj ]\\
3 s + - far \\
‘He/she was not far.’

In ex:10:25, bay is not clause final but is the final element in a noun phrase within the clause. In this case, the information expressed within the noun phrase itself is negated; ele lala bay ‘a bad thing.’

Nde, [ele lala bay ] kə təta aka.\\
ndɛ [ɛlɛ lala baj ] kə təta aka\\
so thing well done on them on\\
‘So, a bad thing [was] upon them.’

When relative clauses are negated, the negative may have semantic scope over the entire relative clause ( ex:10:26, ex:10:27 ).

Values, S. 6\\
Ele ahay [aməgəye bay ] nəngehe pat tahata na va.\\
ɛlɛ=ahaj [amɪ-g-ijɛ baj ] nɪŋgɛhɛ pat ta-h=ata na=va\\
thing=Pl -do- all 3 p -tell= 3 p. 3 s. = \\
‘All these things that [we] are not supposed to do, they have already told them.’

Kəra [aməmənjere elé bay ] táslay na gəraw.\\
kəra [amɪ-mɪndʒɛr-ɛ ɛlɛ baj ] tá-ɬ-aj na gəraw\\
dog -see- eye 3 p + -slay- 3 s. id:cut through middle\\
‘The dog that couldn’t see they slew it through the middle.’

The negative can form a compound with some adverbs. Negated and non-negated clauses with four adverbs are shown in tab:81. The negative asabay ‘never again’ is a compound of the adverb ese ‘again’ and bay. The evidence of phonological binding is that the adverb ese loses its palatalisation when it compounds with bay (line 1 in tab:81 ). Likewise, fabay (line 2 in tab:81 ) is considered phonologically bound since the word-final /n/ in the adverb fan ‘already’ is deleted when the negative is added. These changes occur with some clitics (see sec:2.6.1.5 ). The other adverbs are considered to be separate phonological words since there are no other indications that the negative is phonologically bound to the adverb since the prosody of other adverbs is not affected (e.g., kəlo ‘before,’ line 3 in tab:81 ).
summary: The particle **bay** is the general negative marker; it follows the verb phrase, precedes interrogative words, and can also occur clause-finally, where it may negate the whole proposition. If bay is final within a noun phrase or relative clause, it negates that constituent, and in some contexts it forms compounds with adverbs, as shown by phonological changes in forms like **asabay** ‘never again’ and **fabay**, while other adverbs remain separate phonological words.

text:
For clausal negation, there is no change in word order and no change in clause constituents apart from the addition of the clause final negative particle. A negative clause asserts that some event or state does not hold. Various types of clausal negation in Moloko are illustrated in ( ex:10:28 -- ex:10:43 ). Each pair of examples represents a positive and a negative assertion for comparison.

The negation of an intransitive clause is illustrated in ex:10:28 and ex:10:29.

Ahəmay.\\
a-həm-aj\\
3 s -run- \\
‘He/she runs.’

Ahəmay bay. \\
a-həm-aj baj \\
3 s -run- \\
‘He/she doesn’t run.’

THe negation of a transitive clause is shown in ( ex:10:30 -- ex:10:35 ).

Amənjar Hawa. \\
a-mənzar Hawa\\
3 s -see Hawa\\
‘He/she sees Hawa.’

Amənjar Hawa bay. \\
a-mənzar Hawa baj \\
3 s -see Hawa \\
‘He/she doesn’t see Hawa.’

Akaɗ awak.\\
a-kaɗ awak\\
3 s -kill goat\\
‘He/she kills a goat.’

Akaɗ awak bay. \\
a-kaɗ awak baj \\
3 s -kill goat \\
‘He/she doesn’t kill a goat.’

Asaw sese.\\
a-s=aw ʃɛʃɛ\\
3 s -please=. meat\\
‘I want meat.’

Asaw sese bay. \\
a-s=aw ʃɛʃɛ baj \\
3 s -please=. meat \\
‘I do not want meat.’

The negation of existentials is shown in ( ex:10:36 -- ex:10:39 ).

Babəza əwla ahay aba. \\
babəza=uwla=ahaj aba \\
children=. =Pl \\
‘I have children.’

Babəza əwla ahay abay. \\
babəza=uwla=ahaj abaj \\
children=. =Pl + \\
‘I have no children.’

Dala anaw aka. \\
dala an=aw aka\\
money = +on \\
‘I have money.’

Dala anaw aka bay. \\
dala an=aw aka baj \\
money = +on \\
‘I have no money.’

The negation of a predicate adjective is illustrated in ( ex:10:40 -- ex:10:43 ).

Ndahan zləle ga.\\
ndahaŋ ɮɪlɛ ga\\
3 s richness \\
‘He/she is rich.’

Ndahan zləle ga bay. \\
ndahaŋ ɮɪlɛ ga baj \\
3 s richness \\
‘He/she is not rich.’

Ndahan gədan ga.\\
ndahaŋ gədaŋ ga\\
3 s strength \\
‘He/she is strong.’

Ndahan gədan ga bay. \\
ndahaŋ gədaŋ ga baj \\
3 s strength \\
‘He/she is not strong.’
summary: Clausal negation in Moloko does not change word order or clause structure; it is marked only by adding a clause-final negative particle. The passage shows this pattern with intransitive, transitive, existential, and predicate-adjective clauses, where the negative form simply adds the particle while preserving the positive clause’s structure and meaning apart from denying the event, possession, or property.

text:
Most frequently, it seems that the element closest to the negative that is under the scope of negation, even though a clause-final negative marker can have scope over the whole verb phrase or even over the entire clause. To negate only one constituent in a clause, the clause is sometimes rearranged so that the constituent that is negated is placed in the clause-final position adjacent to the negation particle. Examples ( ex:10:44 -- ex:10:46 ) show a question ex:10:44 with two responses ( ex:10:45 -- ex:10:46 ) where each of the two ambiguous elements is negated. The subject ( Mana ) is part of the presupposition (marked off by na in the question, see sec:11.2 ). In ex:10:45 the oblique is negated and in ex:10:46 the entire predicate. The clauses were not restructured since the elements in question were already clause-final. In the following examples, the element that is negated is delimited by square brackets and the negative is bolded.

Mana na, olo [a kosoko ava] ɗaw?\\
Mana na ɔ-lɔ [a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava] ɗaw\\
Mana 3 s -go at market in q \\
‘As for Mana, is he going to the market?’

Ehe, olo [a kosoko ava] bay; olo afa bahay.\\
ɛhɛ ɔ-lɔ [a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava] baj ɔ-lɔ afa bahaj\\
no 3 s -go at market in 3 s -go house of chief\\
‘No, he isn’t going to the market; rather he is going to the chief’s house.’

Ehe, olo [a kosoko ava] bay; enjé a mogom.\\
ɛhɛ, [ɔ-lɔ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava] baj ɛ-nʒ-ɛ a mɔgʷɔm\\
no 3 s -go at market in 3 s -stay- at home\\
‘No, he isn’t going to the market; rather he is staying at home (or going to the chief’s house).’

Examples ( ex:10:47 -- ex:10:50 ) show some restructuring when different constituents are negated. Example ex:10:47 illustrates a question and ex:10:48 to ex:10:50 illustrate three possible answers, each negating a different constituent. Normal SVO structure is maintained for all answers. The responses each use two clauses. The first clause expresses the negation of the element in final position, and the second restates the clause giving the corrected information. In each case the first clause is restructured so as to move the element to be negated to the clause-final position. The response in ex:10:48 indicates that the hearer accepts 'that Mana gave the guitar to someone,' but it was not his father. In this clause, kəndew ‘guitar’ is realised as the 3 s pronominal. The response in ex:10:49 indicates 'that Mana gave something to his father,' but not a guitar. In this case, the adpositional phrase ana baba ahan ‘to his father’ is replaced by the indirect object pronominal so that the negated element kəndew ‘guitar’ can be placed next to the negative.

Mana avəlan kəndew ana baba ahan ɗaw?\\
Mana à-vəl=aŋ kɪndɛw ana baba=ahaŋ ɗaw\\
Mana 3 s + -give= 3 s. guitar father= 3 s. q \\
‘Did Mana give the guitar to his father?’

Ehe, avəlan na [ana baba ahan] bay, \\
ɛhɛ à-vəl=aŋ na [ana baba=ahaŋ] baj \\
no 3 s + -give= 3 s. 3 s. father= 3 s. \\

avəlan na ana gəmsodo ahan.\\
à-vəl=aŋ na ana gʊmsɔdɔ=ahaŋ\\
3 s + -give= 3 s. 3 s. mother’s brother= 3 s. \\
‘No, he didn’t give it t o his father, he gave it to his mother’s brother.’

Ehe, avəlan [kəndew] bay, avəlan cecewk.\\
ɛhɛ à-vəl=aŋ [kɪndɛw] baj à-vəl=aŋ tʃɛtʃœkʷ\\
no 3 s + -give= 3 s. guitar 3 s + -give= 3 s. flute\\
‘No, he didn’t give a guitar to his father, he gave him a flute.’

The fourth possible reply to the question in ex:10:47 negates the subject. Moloko clause structure does not allow the subject to occupy the clause-final position; to specifically negate the subject of a clause ex:10:52, a predicate nominal clause structure is used. The predicate is recast as a relative clause (see sec:5.4.3 ) with the presupposed information that someone gave a guitar to his father marked with na. The nominal is the negated subject Mana bay ‘not Mana.’

Ehe, aməvəlan kəndew ana baba ahan na, [Mana] bay;\\
ɛhɛ amə-vəl=aŋ kɪndɛw ana baba=ahaŋ na [Mana] baj \\
no -give= 3 s. guitar father= 3 s. Mana \\
‘No, Mana didn’t give the guitar to his father. (lit. the one that gave guitar to his father, not Mana)’ \\

aməvəlan na, Majay.\\
amə-vəl=aŋ na Madzaj\\
-give= 3 s. Madzay\\
‘The person that gave [it was] Madzay.’

Examples ( ex:10:51 -- ex:10:52 ) show a similar restructuring of a verbal clause into a predicate nominal in order to negate the subject of a clause. A question with a verbal clause structure is shown in ex:10:51. In order to negate the subject, the clause is restructured to put all of the known information in a predicate that is a relative clause delimited by na, and the negated subject becomes the final nominal ex:10:52.

Hawa adan ɗaf ana Mana ɗaw?\\
Hawa à-d=aŋ ɗaf ana Mana ɗaw\\
Hawa 3 s + -prepare= 3 s. millet loaf Mana q \\
‘Did Hawa prepare food for Mana?’

Amadan ɗaf ana Mana na, [Hawa] bay.\\
ama-d=aŋ ɗaf ana Mana na [Hawa] baj \\
-prepare= 3 s. millet loaf Mana Hawa \\
‘The one that prepared the millet loaf for Mana [was] not Hawa.’
summary: The passage explains that in this language, negation usually applies to the constituent immediately preceding the negative particle, though clause-final negation can also scope over a larger phrase or clause. When only one constituent is to be negated, the clause is often rearranged so that constituent appears clause-finally next to the negative marker; if the subject is the target, the clause may be recast as a predicate nominal with the known information in a relative clause and the subject placed at the end for negation.

text: The syntax of interrogative constructions is remarkable in that all interrogative particles except wɛlɛj ‘which one' occur clause finally. In certain constructions, the clause itself is rearranged so that the interrogative particle can remain clause final. Interrogative constructions are superimposed on top of the other clausal construction types. Like the case for the negation construction (see sec:10.2.3 ), the element closest to the interrogative pronoun or question word seems most frequently under the scope of interrogation. Types of interrogative constructions include content questions (see sec:10.3.1 ), yes/no questions (see sec:10.3.2 ), tag question construction, to clarify a particular statement (see sec:10.3.3 ), rhetorical question constructions (see sec:10.3.4 ), and emphatic question constructions (see sec:10.3.5 ).
summary: Interrogative constructions are notable because all interrogative particles except **wɛlɛj** ‘which one’ appear clause-finally, and in some cases the clause is rearranged to preserve this position. These constructions are layered on top of other clause types, with the element nearest the interrogative pronoun or question word most often falling under the scope of interrogation. The passage identifies several kinds of interrogatives: content questions, yes/no questions, tag questions, rhetorical questions, and emphatic questions.

text:
Information questions use interrogative pronouns which must be clause-final. The interrogative pronouns (see sec:3.1.4 ) each fill a slot in the clause according to the element they each are questioning. All elements in a clause can be questioned including subject, direct object, indirect object, verb, oblique, and noun modifier. The clause structure will always be arranged such that the element questioned is clause-final. Three main clause structures are employed in order to achieve clause-final interrogative pronouns. tab:82. shows the interrogative forms used for content questions.

The first clause structure that is employed is the verbal clause structure (SVO), but with substitution of a question word. The verbal clause structure is rearranged in the same manner as for constituent negation (see sec:10.2.3 ) in order to position the questioned element in the clause-final position so that it is replaced by the interrogative pronoun. Information questions in verbal clauses are paired with a response in ( ex:10:53 -- ex:10:65 ) so that the structure of the interrogative clause can be compared with that of the declarative. Examples in this section are given in pairs. The first example in the pair shows the interrogative construction. The second example is the clause with the information filled in for comparison.

The direct object is questioned in ex:10:53. The presupposed information is that the man saw someone. Note that there are no other elements that follow the direct object in the verb phrase. The interrogative pronoun fills the direct object slot (identified by square brackets).

Zar amənjar [ way ]?\\
zar à-mənzar [ waj ]\\
man 3 s + -see who\\
‘Who did the man see?’

Zar amənjar [Mana].\\
zar à-mənzar [Mana]\\
man 3 s + -see Mana\\
‘The man saw Mana.’

A noun modifier is questioned in ex:10:55. The presupposed information is that the woman made some kind of sauce, and the question seeks to find out what kind of sauce. The interrogative pronoun weley ‘which’ is within the noun phrase delimited by square brackets in the example. Even though the interrogative pronoun is inside a noun phrase, that noun phrase is clause-final so the interrogative pronoun is the final word in the clause.

Hor ede [elele weley ]?\\
hʷɔr ɛ-dɛ [ɛlɛlɛ wɛlɛj ]\\
woman 3 s -prepare sauce which\\
‘The woman is making which kind of sauce?’

Hor ede [elele kəlef].\\
hʷɔr ɛ-d-ɛ [ɛlɛlɛ kɪlɛf]\\
woman 3 s -prepare- sauce fish\\
‘The woman is making fish sauce.’

Example ex:10:57 questions the direct object of a subordinate clause, in this case a purpose adverbial clause (delimited by square brackets). The presupposed information is that the listener has come to do something. The interrogative pronoun almay ‘what’ is clause-final since the adverbial clause has no other elements following the direct object. Two possible responses are shown in ex:10:58-- ex:10:59.

Kəlala [aməgəye almay ]?\\
k\`ə-l=ala [amɪ-g-ijɛ almaj ]\\
+ -go=to -do- what\\
‘What have you come to do?’ (lit. you have come to do what?)

Nəlala [aməgəye slərele].\\
n\`ə-l=ala [amɪ-g-ijɛ ɬɪrɛlɛ]\\
+ -go=to -do- work\\
‘I came to do work.’

Nəlala [aməjənok].\\
n\`ə-l=ala [amə-dzən-ɔkʷ]\\
+ -go=to -help- \\
‘I came to help you.’

In ex:10:60, the indirect object is questioned. The presupposed information is that Mala gave a book to someone. The interrogative pronoun way ‘who,’ is located within a prepositional phrase identified by square brackets. That prepositional phrase is clause-final, so that again the interrogative pronoun is the final element in the clause.

Mala avəlan ɗeləywer [ana way ]?\\
Mala à-vəl=aŋ ɗɛlijwɛr [ana waj ] \\
Mala 3 s + -give= 3 s. paper who\\
‘Mala gave the book to whom?’

Mala avəlan ɗeləywer [ana Hawa].\\
Mala à-vəl=aŋ ɗɛlijwɛr [ana Hawa]\\
Mala 3 s + -give= 3 s. paper Hawa\\
‘Mala gave the book to Hawa.’

In ex:10:62 and ex:10:64, an oblique is questioned. The presupposed information is that the woman plans to go to market sometime. The interrogative pronoun is the temporal element in the clause in ex:10:62. While temporal noun phrases can occur clause-initially, the interrogative pronoun is again found in the clause-final position.

Hor olo a kosoko ava [ epeley ]?\\
hʷɔr ɔ-lɔ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava [ ɛpɛlɛj ]\\
woman 3 s -go at market in when\\
‘When is the woman going to market?’

Hor olo a kosoko ava [hajan].\\
hʷɔr ɔ-lɔ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava [hadzaŋ]\\
woman 3 s -go at market in tomorrow\\
‘The woman is going to market tomorrow.’

The elements within non-core adpositional phrases are questioned using the generic location question word amtamay ‘where’ ex:10:64. This generic location question word does not need to be located inside an adpositional phrase, eliminating the possibility that the locational postposition would follow the interrogative pronoun in the clause allowing the interrogative pronoun to be clause-final. The presupposed information is that the hearer is going somewhere.

Kolo [ amtamay ]?\\
k\'ɔ-lɔ [ amtamaj ] \\
+ -go where\\
‘Where did you go?’

Nolo [a kosoko ava].\\
n\'ɔ-lɔ [ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava ] \\
+ -go at market in\\
‘I went to market.’

The second clause structure that is employed for interrogative constructions is the predicate nominal. The predicate nominal structure is employed for questioning an element of a predicate nominal clause. ( ex:10:66 – ex:10:71 ) are example pairs where the first of each pair is a question and the second is a possible response. In ex:10:66 an aspect of the nominal is questioned with the interrogative pronoun in a prepositional phrase. The prepositional phrase is delimited by square brackets.

Mogom nehe [anga way ]?\\
mɔgʷɔm nɛhɛ [aŋga waj ]\\
house who\\
‘This house here belongs to whom?’

Mogom nehe [anga Mana].\\
mɔgʷɔm nɛhɛ [aŋga Mana]\\
house Mana\\
‘This house here belongs to Mana.’ (the house here, belonging to Mana)

In ex:10:68 and ex:10:70, the interrogative word itself is the predicate.

Mogom ango [ amtamay ]?\\
mɔgʷɔm=aŋgʷɔ [ amtamaj ]\\
home=. where\\
‘Where is your home?’

Mogom əwla [a Laway].\\
mɔgʷɔm=uwla [a Lawaj]\\
home=. to Lalawaj\\
‘My home is in Lalaway.’
summary: Information questions require interrogative pronouns to be clause-final, and any clause element can be questioned as long as the clause is arranged so the questioned item ends up last. The passage shows this with verbal clauses, including questions about direct and indirect objects, noun modifiers, obliques, and elements in subordinate clauses, as well as predicate nominal clauses where the interrogative may function as part of a prepositional phrase or as the predicate itself.

text:
Bahay a slala aləkwəye na [ way ]?\\
bahaj a ɬala=alʊkʷøjɛ na [ waj ]\\
chief village=. who\\
‘The chief of your village is who?’

Bahay a slala əwla na [Ajəva].\\
bahaj a ɬala=uwla na [Adzəva]\\
chief village=. Adziva\\
‘The chief of my village is Adziva.’

The predicate nominal clause is also used for questioning the subject in what would otherwise be a normal verbal clause (paralleling the case for the negative, see sec:10.2.3 ). The subject of what would be a verbal clause in a declarative speech act cannot be questioned using the SVO verbal clause construction in Moloko, because the clause can never be simply rearranged so that the subject is clause-final. For example, it is impossible to question the subject in ex:10:72 using the SVO verbal clause construction. Unless the emphatic question construction is used sec:10.3.5.

Hor ede ɗaf.\\
hʷɔr ɛ-d-ɛ ɗaf\\
woman 3 s -make- millet loaf\\
‘The woman is making millet loaf.’

To question the subject ( ex:10:73 – ex:10:74 ), the verbal clause must be reformed into a predicate nominal interrogative construction. The clause is reformed into a noun phrase with a relative clause so that the interrogative pronoun questioning the subject can be in clause-final position.

Hor amədəye ɗaf na way?\\
hʷɔr amɪ-d-ijɛ ɗaf na waj \\
woman -make- millet loaf who\\
‘Who is making millet loaf?’ (lit. the woman that is making millet loaf [is] who?)

Hor amədəye ɗaf na weley?\\
hʷɔr amə-d-ijɛ ɗaf na wɛlɛj \\
woman -make- millet loaf which\\
‘Which woman is making millet loaf?’ (lit. the woman that is making millet loaf [is] which one?)

ex:10:75 and ex:10:77 show two other predicate nominal clauses that question what would be the subject of an otherwise verbal clause. ex:10:76 and ex:10:78 are possible responses to these questions.

Məze amanday aməzəme ɗaf na way?\\
mɪʒɛ ama-ndaj amɪ-ʒum-ɛ ɗaf na waj \\
person - -eat- millet loaf who\\
‘Who is eating loaf?’ (lit. the man that is eating millet loaf [is] who?)

Mana anday ozom ɗaf. \\
Mana a-ndaj a-zɔm ɗaf \\
person 3 s - 3 s -eat millet loaf\\
‘Mana is eating millet loaf.’

Aməzəɗe dəray na way?\\
amɪ-ʒɪɗ-ɛ dəraj na waj \\
-take- head who\\
‘Who will win?’ (lit. the one that takes the head [is] who?)

Mana azaɗ dəray.\\
Mana a-zaɗ dəraj\\
Mana 3 s -take head\\
‘Mana won.’ (lit. Mana took head)

The third structure for content information questions uses a right-shifted na -marked element (see sec:11.3 ). This structure is employed in cases where it is impossible for a questioned verb phrase element to be clause-final. In ex:10:79, the direct object is questioned. In this case the direct object cannot be clause-final since it is necessary to include the information ana məlama ahan ‘to his brother,’ and the prepositional phrase must follow the direct object in the verb phrase ( chap:8 ). Thus in the interrogative structure, the interrogative pronoun replaces the direct object and the rest of the clause is put into a post-posed na -marked phrase (underlined in this example). A possible response is shown in ex:10:80.

Mala avəlan almay ana məlama ahan na?\\
Mala a-vəl=aŋ almaj ana məlama =ahaŋ na\\
Mala 3 s -give= 3 s. what sibling= 3 s. \\
‘Mala gave what to his brother?’

Mala avəlan dala ana məlama ahan.\\
Mala a-vəl=aŋ dala ana məlama=ahaŋ\\
Mala 3 s -give= 3 s. money sibling= 3 s. \\
‘Mala gave money to his brother.’
summary: The passage explains that in Moloko, subject questions cannot be formed with a normal SVO verbal clause because the subject cannot be moved to clause-final position. Instead, the clause is restructured as a predicate nominal interrogative, with the subject questioned in final position, and another strategy using a right-shifted na-marked phrase is used when a questioned verb-phrase element cannot be clause-final.

text:
Yes/no questions are interrogative clauses which can be answered by a simple ‘yes’ or ‘no’ – they are not asking for content in the reply. Moloko uses the interrogative marker ɗaw at the end of what is otherwise a declarative clause to create yes/no interrogatives. Pure yes-no questions can be answered with either yes or no, but in Moloko there is often a degree of expectation to the question. Expectation is a central element in understanding Moloko grammar (see sec:7.4.3 ), as is what constitutes shared information with the hearer (see chap:11 ). Questions are constructed in Moloko with that knowledge and expectation in mind, even when seeking new information. Tag questions are discussed in sec:10.3.3. When a speaker asks a yes/no question ( ex:10:81 – ex:10:83 ), they are usually expecting an affirmative reply.

Zar na ndahan baba a Mala ɗaw?\\
zar na ndahaŋ baba a Mala ɗaw \\
man 3 s father Mala q \\
‘That man, is he Mala’s father?’

In ex:10:82, the speaker expects that Mana is on his way; he is asking for confirmation (but a negative response is always possible). Likewise in ex:10:83, he expects that the referent zar ango ‘your husband’ is well.

Mana na álala ɗaw?\\
Mana na á-l=ala ɗaw \\
Mana 3 s +IPV-go=to q \\
'Mana, is he coming?'

Zar ango ndahan aba ɗaw?\\
zar=aŋgʷɔ ndahaŋ aba ɗaw \\
man=. 3 s q \\
‘Is your husband well?’ (part of a greeting; lit. your husband, does he exist?)

There is often an even stronger affirmative expectation when the question is negated. Compare the positive and negative pairs of questions ( ex:10:84 – ex:10:89 ). Some of the negated questions can be used rhetorically (see sec:10.3.4 ), since the speaker already knows that the answer is yes. In the examples, the interrogative markers and the negative particles are bolded.

Baba ango, ndahan ava a mogom ɗaw?\\
baba=aŋgʷɔ ndahaŋ ava a mɔgʷɔm ɗaw \\
father=. 3 s +in at home q \\
‘Is your father in?’

Baba ango, ndahan ava a mogom bay ɗaw?\\
baba=aŋgʷɔ ndahaŋ ava a mɔgʷɔm baj ɗaw \\
father=. 3 s +in at home q \\
‘Is your father not in?’

Ólo a kosoko ava ɗaw?\\
\'ɔ-lɔ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava ɗaw \\
3 s + -go at market in q \\
‘Is he going to the market?’

Ólo a kosoko ava bay ɗaw?\\
\'ɔ-lɔ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava baj ɗaw \\
3 s + -go at market in q \\
‘Is he not going to the market?’

Məlama ango álala ɗaw?\\
məlama=aŋgʷɔ á-l=ala ɗaw \\
sibling=. 3 s + -go=to q \\
‘Is your brother coming?’

Məlama ango álala bay ɗaw?\\
məlama=aŋgʷɔ á-l=ala baj ɗaw \\
sibling=. 3 s + -go=to q \\
‘Is your brother not coming?’

As is the case for the negation construction (see sec:10.2.3 ), it could be that the entire proposition in the clause is being questioned. However, it is often the case that only the final constituent is being questioned. Often the clause is restructured when a constituent of the clause is questioned so that the constituent is in final position. In ex:10:90 the direct object is fronted and marked as presupposed (it is the topic of discussion) so that the other elements in the clause are questioned (see sec:10.3.2 ). See also ex:10:82 where the subject is marked as presupposed and it is whether or not he is coming that is being questioned.

Awak ango na, káaslay na ɗaw?\\
awak=aŋgʷɔ na káá-ɬ-aj na ɗaw \\
goat=. + -slay- 3 s. q \\
‘Your goat, are you going to slaughter it?’
summary: Yes/no questions in Moloko are formed by adding the interrogative marker **ɗaw** to the end of an otherwise declarative clause, and they can be answered simply with yes or no. The passage emphasizes that these questions often carry an expectation of an affirmative answer, especially when negated, and some negated forms can be rhetorical because the speaker already knows the answer is yes. It also notes that while the whole proposition may be questioned, often only the final constituent is focused, with other elements restructured as presupposed or topical.

text:
Question tags can be attached at the end of what would otherwise be the construction used for a declarative clause to seek confirmation of a particular statement. In Moloko, a question tag is kəyga bay ɗaw ‘is that not so?’ The affirmative response is kəyga ‘it is so.' The negative response is kəyga bay ‘it is not so’ with a statement to explain why the negative answer. Some rhetorical questions have a special question tag esəmey ‘isn’t that so’ (see sec:10.3.4 ). In the examples below, what is under the scope of questioning is put in square brackets.

[Kolo a Marva hajan] kəyga bay daw? 65pt \\
[k\'ɔ-lɔ a Marva hadzaŋ] kijga baj ɗaw 5pt \\
+ -go at Maroua tomorrow like that q \\
‘You are going to Maroua tomorrow, not so?’ 35pt

[Apazan kolo a kosoko ava] kəyga bay ɗaw? \\
[apazaŋ k\`ɔ-lɔ a kɔsɔkʷɔ ava] kijga baj ɗaw \\
yesterday + -go at market in like that q \\
‘You went to the market yesterday, right?’

Nə alməmar na, [avar abay] kəyga bay ɗaw? \\
nə alməmar na [avar abaj] kijga baj ɗaw \\
with dry season rain + like this q \\
‘In dry season, there is no rain, right?’

Other question tags are evaluative. Example ex:10:94 is a question tag asked in a context where the speaker is examining something physically (perhaps at the market as he is considering to buy it) or analysing and evaluating an event.

[Səlom ga] ɗaw?\\
[sʊlɔm ga] ɗaw \\
goodness q \\
‘[Is that] good?’
summary: The passage explains that Moloko uses question tags to turn a declarative statement into a request for confirmation, with **kəyga bay ɗaw** meaning ‘is that not so?’ and **kəyga** and **kəyga bay** serving as affirmative and negative responses, respectively. It also notes a special tag, **esəmey** ‘isn’t that so,’ used in some rhetorical questions. In addition, some question tags are evaluative, asking for a judgment such as whether something is good.

text:
In a rhetorical question, the speaker is not pragmatically asking for information. Rather, the questions can be evaluative, may carry an element of reproach, or may be a mild command. The context gives the rhetorical force. Some rhetorical questions have a special emphatic structure (see sec:10.3.5 ) but many have the normal interrogative structure for a content question ( ex:10:95 – ex:10:96, see sec:10.3.1 ). For example, the speaker is not seeking an explanation when he asks kamay ‘why’ in ex:10:95. More probably he is making a strong statement, ‘the people had no reason to do this bad thing to me.’ Likewise in ex:10:96, the speaker is saying that the listener will listen to no one.

Məze ahay tagaw ele lala bay kamay?\\
mɪʒɛ=ahaj ta-g=aw ɛlɛ lala baj kamaj \\
person=Pl 3 p -do=. thing good why\\
‘The people had no reason to do this bad thing to me.’ (lit. the people did the bad thing to me why?)

Values, 29\\
Hərmbəlom na, amaɗaslava ala məze na, ndahan ese na,\\
Hʊrmbʊlɔm na ama-ɗaɬ=ava=ala mɪʒɛ na ndahaŋ ɛʃɛ na \\
God -multiply=in=to person 3 s again \\
‘God, the one who multiplied the people, him again,’\\

kagas ma Hərmbəlom na, asabay na,\\
ka-gas ma Hʊrmbʊlɔm na asa-baj na \\
-catch word God again- \\
‘[if] you no longer accept the word of God,’\\

káagas na anga way?\\
káá-gas na aŋga waj \\
+ -catch who\\
‘you won't listen to anyone.' (lit. ‘you will catch it [word] of whom?’)

Other rhetorical questions have the same structure as a tag question ( ex:10:97 – ex:10:98, see sec:10.3.3 ). However either there is no expected answer or the expected answer is the opposite of that for a normal yes/no tag question. For example, during the telling of the text from which ex:10:97 is taken, when the storyteller asked the rhetorical question lala ɗaw ‘[is that] good?’ the people in the audience replied lala bay ‘[it is] not good.’ (even though the answer was obvious from the story). Likewise, in ex:10:98, the audience replied səlom ga ‘[it is] good’ to the rhetorical question səlom ga bay ɗaw ‘[is that] not good?’

Kólo kagas anga məze kək, lala ɗaw?\\
k\'ɔ-lɔ kà-gas aŋga mɪʒɛ kək lala ɗaw \\
+ -go + -catch person id:catch by throat good q \\
‘[If] you catch [something] belonging to someone else [and steal it], [is that] good?’

Kólo ele ango, səlom ga bay ɗaw?\\
k\'ɔ-lɔ ɛlɛ=aŋgʷɔ sʊlɔm ga baj ɗaw \\
+ -go thing=. good q \\
‘[If] you mind your own business (lit. go to your things), [is that] not good?’

A particular question tag, esəmey ‘isn’t that so’ carries an element of reproach. There is no expected answer to the question in ex:10:99. The message is a strong declaration that the speaker had already told something to the hearer.

[Nahok ma fan] esəmey?\\
[nà-h=ɔkʷ ma faŋ] ɛʃɪmɛj \\
+ -tell=. word already isn’t that so\\
‘I already told you, didn’t I?’
summary: Rhetorical questions in this passage are not genuine requests for information; instead, they can express evaluation, reproach, or a mild command, with their force determined by context. They may use either ordinary interrogative forms or special emphatic/tag-question structures, but no answer is expected, or the expected answer is the opposite of a normal answer. The tag question esəmey ‘isn’t that so’ is noted as carrying reproach and functioning as a strong declaration rather than a real question.

text:
Emphatic questions do not ask for information, but rather make an emphatic statement or carry imperatival force. As such they are a sub-type of rhetorical questions (see sec:10.3.4 ). The emphatic question construction uses two interrogative pronouns, a reduced emphatic pronoun within the clause in the normal slot for the element questioned, and the other a sometimes reduced pronoun at the end of the clause.

These reduced interrogative pronouns are wa (from way ‘who’) in ex:10:100, ex:10:102, ex:10:103, may and alma (from almay ‘what’) in ex:10:101 and ex:10:104, respectively, malma (from malmay ‘what’) in ex:10:105, and meme and mey (from memey ‘how’) in ex:10:106.

Wa aməgok na way?\\
\ \ wa amə-g=ɔk na waj \\
\ \ who -do=. 3 s. who\\
\ \ ‘ What is wrong?’ / ‘Stop crying!’ (lit. who to do it to you, who)

Kege may ana war ga may?\\
ka-gɛ maj ana war ga maj \\
-do what child what\\
‘What are you doing to the child, what?’ / ‘Stop doing that!’

Cicada, S. 18\\
Náanjakay na wa [amazaw ala agwazla ana ne na] way?\\
náá-nzak-aj na wa [ama-z=aw =ala agʷaɮa ana nɛ na] \\
+ -find- who -take=. =to spp. of tree \\

waj \\
who\\
‘ Who can I find to bring to me this tree for me? Who?’ / ‘ Someone should be able to bring me this tree.’

Wa andaɗay way?\\
wa a-ndaɗ-aj waj \\
who 3 s -love- who\\
‘Who loves whom?' / ‘No one loves him.'

Alma amədəvala okfom na may?\\
alma amə-dəv=ala ɔkʷfɔm na maj \\
what -trip=to mouse what\\
‘ What was it that made that mouse fall? What?' / ‘What else [but a snake] makes a mouse fall?’

Malma awəlok may?\\
malma a-wəl=ɔkʷ maj \\
what 3 s -hurt=. what\\
‘ What is bothering (hurting) you? What?’ / ‘ Nothing should be bothering you.’

Meme ege mey?\\
mɛmɛ ɛ-g-ɛ mɛj \\
how 3 s -do- how?\\
‘ What happened?’ / ‘Why did you do that?’ / ‘Stop the foolishness.’ (lit. how did it do?)
summary:
Emphatic questions are a type of rhetorical question that do not seek information, but instead make an emphatic statement or convey imperatival force. They are formed with two interrogative pronouns: one reduced pronoun appears inside the clause in the normal position of the questioned element, and the other reduced or sometimes reduced pronoun appears at the end of the clause.

The passage lists the reduced forms used in this construction, including wa ‘who’, may/alma/malma ‘what’, and meme/mey ‘how’, with examples showing that these forms can express meanings such as “Stop crying!”, “No one loves him,” or “Someone should be able to bring me this tree.”

text:
There are several types of imperative constructions in Moloko, which are used in different situations, sometimes to express different degrees of obligation. So far six different constructions have been identified, each with a different force of exhortation. They are shown in tab:83. Some constructions use the imperative mood form of the verb (see sec:7.2 ), others use Imperfective aspect Tense, mood, and aspect!Imperfective aspect|( or irrealis mood Tense, mood, and aspect!Irrealis mood|( or are in the form of a rhetorical question (see sec:10.3.4 ). tab:83 illustrates all of the imperative constructions for the verb / lo / ‘go.’ The verb forms are also shown in Perfective and Imperfective aspect (lines 1 and 2) for comparison.

The imperative form of the verb is used for an immediate command ( ex:10:107 -- ex:10:109, line 3 of tab:83 ). The verb is in the imperative mood (see sec:7.2 ) and can be preceded by a vocative. The addressee is expected to carry out the order in the immediate future as opposed to commands that demand reflection before carrying them out. In hortatory texts, imperatives are not usually found in the body of the exhortation since the hearer is expected to wait until the discourse is finished before carrying out the instructions.

Lohom a mogom.\\
lɔhʷ-ɔm a mɔgʷɔm\\
go- at home\\
‘Go home!’

Zəmok ɗaf.\\
\ zʊm-ɔkʷ ɗaf\\
eat- 1 Pin millet loaf\\
‘Let’s eat!’

Cəke.\\
tʃɪk-ɛ\\
stand[. ]- \\
‘Stand up!’

The word etey or ete ‘please’ can be added to other clause types ( ex:10:110 -- ex:10:111, line 5 in tab:83 ) to achieve a milder pragmatic imperative force than the use of the construction without the polite adverb.

Nde na asaw na, gaw na etey?\\
ndɛ na a-s=aw na g=aw na ɛtɛj \\
so 3 s -please=. do=. 3 s. please\\
‘So I want that you do that for me, please.’

N\'ənjakay yam ete ɗaw?\\
n\'ə-nzak-aj jam ɛtɛ ɗaw\\
+ -find- water please q \\
‘Could you please get me some water?’ (lit. can I find water please)

A negated clause in the Imperfective aspect Tense, mood, and aspect!Imperfective aspect|) expresses a negative exhortation or statement of expectation ( ex:10:112 -- ex:10:113, line 5 in tab:83 ). In second person ex:10:112, the negative expectation carries a weak hortative force. The speaker is expressing that he/she expects the addressee not to carry out the action. In third person ex:10:113 the negative expectation is not hortatory, but rather simply expresses that the speaker does not expect that the action will be performed.

Kámənjar fabay.\\
ká-mənz\=ar fá-bàj\\
+ -see already- \\
‘Don’t look at it yet.’ (I don’t expect you to look at it).

Á-mənjar fabay.\\
á-mənz\=ar fá-bàj\\
3 s + -see already- \\
‘I don’t think he looked at it.’ (I don’t expect that he looked at it).

A clause with a verb in the Hortative mood Tense, mood, and aspect!Irrealis mood (line 6 in tab:83, see sec:7.4.3 ) concentrates on the will of the speaker -- the speaker wishes the action done. This form is illustrated for 3 s in ex:10:114.

Mamənjar fabay. \\
mà-mənz\=ar fá-bàj\\
+ -see already- \\
‘He/she shouldn’t look at it yet.’ / ‘Don’t let him/her look at it.’ (I don’t expect him/her to look at it).

An even stronger deontic form is made by the addition of an adverb of obligation ( dewele ‘obligation’ ex:10:116, səy ‘only’ ex:10:115 – ex:10:117 ) preceding the clause, with the verb in Hortative mood (line 7 in tab:83 ). Imperative forms with an adverb of obligation indicate that the hearer is obligated to do something (he/she has no choice, there is no other way). These forms are used to give an order with insistence, a strong counsel.

Səy koogom endeɓ.\\
sij k\`ɔ\`ɔ-gʷ-ɔm ɛndɛɓ\\
only -do- wisdom\\
‘You must be wise (lit. do only wisdom).’

Dewele səy keege na.\\
dɛwɛlɛ sij k\`ɛ\`ɛ-gɛ na\\
obligation only + -do 3 s. \\
‘You are obligated to do that.’ (lit. obligation: you must only do it)

Səy keege anga dewele.\\
sij k\`ɛ\`ɛ-g-ɛ aŋga dɛwɛlɛ\\
only + -do- obligation\\
‘You must do that obligation.’ (lit. you must only do the thing that belongs to obligation)
summary: Moloko has six imperative constructions with different degrees of exhortative force. These include the imperative mood for immediate commands, polite forms using *etey/ete* “please,” negative exhortations in the imperfective aspect, hortative forms expressing the speaker’s wish, and stronger deontic constructions marked by obligation adverbs such as *dewele* and *səy*.

text:
Exclamatory sentences have either an interjection at the initial position ex:10:118 or one of several exclamatory adverbs at the final position ( ex:10:119 – ex:10:122 ). In the examples, the interjections and exclamatory adverbs are bolded.

kaj n\`ɛ-g-ɛ na baj\\

‘Yesterday you said that Moses would come;’

macakəmbay aməlala na ndahan bay nəy!\\
matsakəmbaj amə-l=ala na ndahaŋ baj nij \\

‘but the one that came was not him after all!’

Enje bay ɗeɗen dey!\\
\`ɛ-nʒ-ɛ baj ɗɛɗɛŋ dɛj \\

Gaw endeɓ dey!\\
g=aw ɛndɛɓ dɛj \\

‘Be careful!’ (lit. do brain for me)

Epele epele na me, Hərmbəlom anday agas ta a ahar ava re!\\
ɛpɛlɛ ɛpɛlɛ na mɛ Hʊrmbʊlɔm a-ndaj a-gas ta \\

a ahar ava rɛ \\

summary: Exclamatory sentences in the passage are marked either by an interjection in initial position or by one of several exclamatory adverbs in final position. The examples show these forms used to express negation, surprise, emphasis, warning, or strong evaluation, often with the exclamatory element highlighted in bold.

text:
The default relation between a na -marked clause and the matrix clause in a na construction is that there is a sequence (temporal or logical) and the event/state expressed by the na -marked clause precedes the event/state in the main clause. Examples ex:11:15 and ex:11:16 are both taken from a Moloko legend (from the Leopard story, ) where some domestic animals are fleeing their owners because the owners are constantly killing the animals’ children in order to satisfy the demands of the spirits. A reason-result construction is shown in ex:11:15. It is also an example of tail-head linking, see sec:11.1.3. A hen begins the story with her lament expressing the reason why she is fleeing. She first states, “They have killed my children," then uses a na construction to say that because they have killed her children, she is fleeing in anger. The na -marked clause repeats the information she just declared in the first clause. This now presupposed information (‘they are killing my children’) is followed by the matrix clause containing the assertion of new information (I am fleeing in anger). Connecting the two clauses in a presupposition-assertion construction influences the hearer to deduce a logical or temporal connection between the two clauses; here reason-result.

Tanday taslaw aka babəza ahay va.\\
ta-nd-aj ta-ɬ=aw =aka babəza=ahaj=va \\
3 p - - 3 p -kill=. =on children=Pl= \\
‘They have killed my children.’\\

Nde, taslaw aka babəza ahay va na,\\
ndɛ ta-ɬ =aw =aka babəza =ahaj =va na \\
so 3 p -kill=. =on children=Pl= \\
‘So, [because] they are killing my children,’\\

nəhəmay mogo ele əwla.\\
nə-həm-aj mɔgʷɔ ɛlɛ=uwla\\
-run- anger thing=. \\
‘I am running [in] anger.’ (lit. I am running my anger thing).

Example ex:11:16 shows a temporal sequence (or perhaps another reason-result construction) from a little later in the same legend. The group of animals is joined by a dog. The dog expresses that whenever a person in the family gets sick, the family will be advised to kill a dog, because dog meat is thought to be especially good to help a sick person get stronger. The dog’s speech uses a na construction to express this relation. The na -marked clause indicates the condition for the event expressed in the main clause. In this case the clause marked by na (‘a person gets sick’) is not previously mentioned in the discourse, but rather is a fact of life, a cultural presupposition.

Cəje agan ana məze na, tawəy, “Kəɗom kəra."\\
tʃɪdʒɛ a-g =aŋ ana mɪʒɛ na tawij kʊɗ-ɔm kəra\\
disease 3 s -do= 3 s. person 3 p +said kill[ ]- dog\\
‘[If] a person gets sick (lit. sickness does to person), they say, “Kill a dog!” [for the sick person to eat].’

Examples ex:11:17 and ex:11:18 are from another legend that talks about how God used to live very close to people. However one day, a woman did something that made God angry, and so he moved far away from them. The narrator expresses the relation between God becoming angry and his moving away using a na construction ex:11:17 where the na -marked clause indicates God’s anger (the reason for his leaving) and the main clause indicates the result (he went away).

Hərmbəlom na ɓərav ahan atəkam alay na, avahay ele ahan botot.\\
Hʊrmbʊlɔm na ɓərav =ahaŋ a-təkam =alaj na a-vah-aj \\
God heart= 3 s. 3 s -taste=away 3 s -fly- \\

ɛlɛ=ahaŋ bɔtɔt\\
thing= 3 s. id:flying\\
‘God (for his part) got angry; [and so] he went away.’ (lit. God, he tasted his heart, he flew his thing)

Example ex:11:18 is from the conclusion of the same legend where the narrator uses a na construction to express a counterexpectation. Although people may seek paradise, they won’t find it because God has gone far away (because of what the woman did). In the na construction, the na -marked clause expresses what people seek, and the main clause expresses that they won’t find it.

Mənjokok egəne sləlay mbəlom na, Hərmbəlom enjé dəren.\\
mə-nzɔk-ɔkʷ ɛgɪnɛ ɬəlaj mbəlɔm na Hʊrmbʊlɔm ɛ-nʒ-ɛ\\

There is no connecting conjunction in either of the clauses; however the reader can discern that there is a logical connection between the first clause ‘[If] you will ever accept the word of God' (marked in five places with na, see sec:11.5 ) and the second ‘whose word will you accept [then]?' (a rhetorical question, see sec:10.3.4 ).

Values, S. 29\\
Hərmbəlom na, amaɗaslava ala məze na, ndahan ese na,\\
Hʊrmbʊlɔm na ama-ɗaɬ=ava=ala mɪʒɛ na ndahaŋ ɛʃɛ na \\
God -multiply=in=to person 3 s again \\
‘God, the one who multiplied the people, him again’ \\

kagas ma Hərmbəlom na, asabay na,\\
ka-gas ma Hʊrmbʊlɔm na asa-baj na \\

[káá-gas na aŋga waj] \\

Cohesion!Tail-head linking

In a discourse, the speaker will use several devices to ensure that the hearers can follow what is being said; i.e., to help track participants through the narrative, connect events, and understand logical connections. One of the ways cohesion is achieved in Moloko discourse is by the use of the presupposition marker na to mark presupposed (including previously-introduced) information. Cohesion is also created using a special construction that Longacre calls “tail-head repetition”. In this construction, an element previously mentioned in a discourse is repeated in a subsequent sentence in order to provide a cohesive link between new information and the preceding discourse. In Moloko, a clause on the event line is first asserted and then at the beginning of the next sentence the same propositional content may be repeated almost word for word and marked at the end by na. Several examples are shown below. Example ex:11:21 comes from a different retelling of the Disobedient Girl text than is shown in sec:1.5. The final element of təhaya na kə ver aka ‘they ground it on the grinding stone’ is repeated in the next line and marked with na as the first element of the next sentence tənday táhaya na ‘they were grinding it na.’ In ( ex:11:21 -- ex:11:26 ), the clause containing the element to be repeated is delimited by square brackets and the na -marked clause in the next sentence is underlined. The element that is repeated in both clauses is bolded.

Presupposition-assertion construction: na -marked clausal element Cohesion!Na-marking
summary: The passage explains that Moloko discourse achieves cohesion partly through the presupposition marker **na**, which marks previously introduced or otherwise presupposed information. It also describes **tail-head repetition**, where a clause from one sentence is repeated at the start of the next, often with **na**, to link events and help the hearer track the narrative. In some cases the repeated material is not identical but refers to an expected result of the previous event, and this still serves the same cohesive function.

text:
The second type of presupposition-assertion construction occurs when a single clausal element is fronted and marked with na. Na marks (occurs immediately after): a) presuppositions and b) topics (including contrastive topics). In both cases the clausal element immediately preceding na is part of an understood presupposition. The part of the clause following na is the assertion which contains new information the speaker wants to communicate.

The normal order of elements in a Moloko clause (without na ) is SVO. fig:18. illustrates the constituents in a declarative clause, combining fig:15. and fig:16. so that the verb phrase constituents are also shown.

In a presupposition-assertion construction, one (or more) of the clause or verb phrase elements is marked with na and fronted with respect to the subject noun phrase and the verb phrase. The fronted construction is illustrated in fig:19.

The examples below show the presupposed element can be almost any element of the clause: the subject ( ex:11:27 -- ex:11:28 ), the direct object ( ex:11:29 -- ex:11:30 ), or an oblique ( ex:11:31 and ex:11:32 ). A discourse conjunction or temporal can also be marked as being presupposed ( ex:11:33 -- ex:11:35 ). In each case, the fronted element is presupposed in the discourse -- it is a known or culturally expected participant, location (spatial or temporal), or object. It is noteworthy that neither verbs by themselves, nor an existential word, nor ‘body-part’ incorporated nouns, nor ideophones can be fronted and marked as presupposed. In the following examples, the presupposed element is underlined and the presupposition marker na is bolded. The na -marked element and the assertion are marked in ex:11:27.

The presupposition-assertion construction is also used to mark topic for participant shifts. Called ‘subject’ in. The na -marked element will be the main participant of the clauses that follow it, until there is another na -marked clause-initial element. says,

quote
“what is presupposed in a topic-comment relations is not the topic itself, nor its referent, but the fact that topic referent can be expected to play a role in a given proposition, due to its status as a center of interest or matter of concern in the conversation. It is this property that most clearly distinguishes topic arguments from focus arguments, whose role in the proposition is always unpredictable at the time of utterance…One therefore ought not to say that a topic referent “is presupposed” but that, given its discourse status, it is presupposed to play a role in a given proposition.”
quote
summary:
In Moloko, the presupposition-assertion construction fronted with **na** places a clause element before the subject and verb phrase, marking it as presupposed, while the material after **na** is the new assertion. The presupposed element can be a subject, direct object, oblique, conjunction, or temporal phrase, but not verbs alone, existential words, body-part incorporated nouns, or ideophones.

This construction also serves discourse functions beyond clause structure: it can mark topic shifts, participant tracking, and boundaries between discourse episodes, especially when a conjunction or temporal adverb is marked with **na**. In topic-comment relations, the topic referent is not itself presupposed, but is expected to play a role in the proposition because of its discourse status.

Definite construction: na -marked clausal element

The Definite construction occurs when a non-fronted noun phrase is marked by na. fig:18 (from sec:11.2 ) shows the default order of constituents in a clause. In the definite construction, the na –marked element is in its normal clausal position. In this construction, na functions in the realm of definiteness. Definiteness Deixis!Definiteness|( is defined by as signalling when “the referent of a phrase is assumed by the speaker to be identifiable to the addressee.” While definiteness is a separate function than presupposition, Lambrecht points out that definiteness is related to presupposition in that the definite article is a grammatical symbol for an assumption on the speaker’s part that the hearer is able to identify the definite element in a sentence -- the speaker presupposes that the addressee can identify the referent designated by that noun phrase.

In ex:11:41 from the Cows in the Field story, the na marker is attached to the noun gəvah ‘field’ within an adpositional phrase. This construction is simply identifying the field to be the one that the cows destroyed, definite and previously mentioned in the story, and not some other unidentified field. In the examples in this section, the na –marked noun phrase is underlined and the adpositional phrase is delimited by square brackets.

Presupposition-focus construction: na precedes the final element of the verb phrase Presupposition-focus construction

The presupposition-focus construction in Moloko makes prominent the final element of a clause. define prominence as “spotlighting, highlighting, or drawing attention to something.” Na precedes the final element in the verb phrase. This is the only na construction where the na -marker follows the verb complex but is not clause final. In effect, all of that information that precedes the final element in the clause is marked as presupposed with na. The result is that the final element in the clause is highlighted in the discourse.

Example ex:11:45 is from line S. 20 of the Disobedient Girl text. The placement of na postverbally, just before the final element in the verb phrase ( gam ‘a lot’) functions to highlight that the woman prepared a lot of millet. The fact that she prepared a lot of millet instead of just one grain (as she was instructed) is critical to the outcome of the story. An added effect of the na plus pause before the final element is to slow down the narrative just a bit Focus and prominence!Discourse peak, resulting in heightened attention on the final element gam ‘a lot.’ In the examples in this section, the prominent final element is bolded and the na -marked elements are underlined.

It is also seen in a hortatory text when the speaker is reiterating his or her argument to make an important point. The many marked elements slow down the discourse and build up tension towards the final element in the clause, thus putting even more emphasis on the focused item. In ex:11:46, the fact that the woman’s habit where she came from was to grind a large amount of millet at a time is crucial to the story. The ambiguity is resolved by syntactic position: the presupposition marker normally appears before a final focused element, while the pronominal can occur inside verb phrases or noun phrases. text: In Moloko, clauses may combine in six ways:
summary: The passage states that Moloko clauses can combine in six different ways. It introduces the topic without yet listing or describing those combination types.

text: A complement clause is a clause that is an argument in the matrix clause. Complement clauses in Moloko can contain one of three verb forms: dependent, nominalised or finite. When the complement clause has the same subject as the main clause, the complement clause has a dependent or nominalised verb form ( sec:12.1.1, see also sec:7.6 and sec:7.7 ). When the subject of the complement clause is different than that in the main clause, the verb in the complement clause is finite and the clause has a noun phrase subject ( sec:12.1.2 ).
summary: Complement clauses in Moloko function as arguments of the matrix clause and can use one of three verb forms: dependent, nominalised, or finite. If the complement clause shares the same subject as the main clause, it takes a dependent or nominalised verb form; if it has a different subject, it uses a finite verb and includes a noun phrase subject.

section: Clauses linked by conjunctions and conjunctive adverbs
text:
The verbs in clauses connected by a conjunction or conjunctive adverb are always finite. The conjunction or adverb specifies the relationship between the two linked clauses. Conjuctions can be either subordinating or coordinating. Clauses subordinated by a conjunction can be divided into two types, depending on whether the subordinate clause follows or precedes the main clause (discussed in Sections sec:12.3.1 and sec:12.3.2, respectively). Coordinating conjunctions link clauses that are not syntactically dependent on one another ( sec:12.3.3 ). Conjunctive adverbs also function to link clauses ( sec:12.3.4 ). tab:84 shows the characteristics of all of the conjunctions and conjunctive adverbs in Moloko.

sidewaystable

Subordinating and coordinating conjunctions
sidewaystable
summary: In clauses joined by a conjunction or conjunctive adverb, the verbs are always finite, and the conjunction or adverb indicates the relationship between the two clauses. Conjunctions may be subordinating or coordinating: subordinating conjunctions link a subordinate clause to a main clause, while coordinating conjunctions connect clauses that are not syntactically dependent on each other. Conjunctive adverbs also serve to link clauses, and the table mentioned summarizes these items in Moloko.

section: Clauses linked by conjunctions and conjunctive adverbs
subsection: Adverbial clauses introduced by a subordinating conjunction
text:
When an adverbial clause introduced by a subordinating conjunction follows the main clause, the adverbial clause supplies new information to the discourse. The different subordinate conjunctions specify the relationship between the new information and the matrix clause. Subordinating conjunctions include bəyna ‘because,’ waya ‘because,’ and kəwaya ‘because,’ (all involved in reason-result constructions) and ha ‘until.’ Sentences in Moloko do not normally have multiple subordinate clauses. In the examples, each of the subordinate clauses is delimited by square brackets.

The subordinating conjuction asa ‘if’ intoduces a condition on the realisation of the event expressed by the main clause. The construction is asa plus the conditional clause. The end of the subordinate clause is delimited by the presupposition marker na or the particle ɗəw 'also.' Which marker is employed depends upon speaker assessment. If the presupposition marker na delimits the condition ( ex:12:42 -- ex:12:44 ), the clause is neutral with respect to whether the speaker expects the condition to be fulfilled or not. summary:
The conjunction **asa** ‘if’ introduces a condition on the realization of the main-clause event, with the subordinate clause normally ending in **na** or sometimes **ɗəw**. When **na** marks the boundary, the clause is neutral about whether the condition will be fulfilled, but with **ɗəw** the meaning becomes more concessive, like “even if.”

The **asa** clause usually comes before the main clause, though it can be right-shifted in some contexts, and it is always delimited by **na**. Additional particles can modify its force: **ana asa** expresses a strong expectation that the condition will be fulfilled, while **azana asa** means “maybe if” and gives the clause an almost temporal sense.

section: Clauses linked by conjunctions and conjunctive adverbs
text:
Conjunctive adverbs are adverbs that function to connect clauses within a larger discourse. They include kəlen ‘next,’ nde ‘therefore,’ and macəkəmbay ‘meanwhile.’ With the exception of kəlen, conjunctive adverbs are clause-initial. The examples give some of the surrounding context so that their function can be demonstrated. Many of the examples are from the Disobedient Girl story or the Cicada story. In order to study the larger context for the examples, the stories themselves can be found in sec:1.5 and sec:1.6, respectively. The clauses with conjunctive adverbs are delimited by square brackets.

Kəlen ‘next’ indicates a subsequent mainline event that often follows a digression (often reported speech). This conjunction can either be clause-initial ex:12:57 or follow the first argument in the clause ex:12:56.

The clause with macəkəmbay marks what the toad had done before the race -- he had secretly invited his brothers to line the race route so that there would always be a toad ahead of the giraffe. The giraffe ran faster than the toad, but when he stopped running and called out to see how far behind him the toad was, one of the toad’s friends ahead of him would call to him, making him run so hard that he collapsed, thereby losing the race.

id:sudden start 3 p -prepare= -run- id:run id:run id:run\\
‘ Paraw, they started the race, running birketem, birketem, birketem.'\\

Kərcece enjé təf na, awəy, “Moktonok nok amta?”\\
kɪrtʃɛtʃɛ ɛ-nʒ-ɛ təf na awij mɔkʷtɔnɔkʷ nɔkʷ amta \\
giraffe 3 s -leave- id:far said toad where \\
'The giraffe went far away [along the race route]. He said, “Toad, where are you?”'\\
summary: Conjunctive adverbs connect clauses within a larger discourse and include kəlen ‘next,’ nde ‘therefore/so,’ and macəkəmbay ‘meanwhile’; except for kəlen, they are clause-initial. Kəlen marks a subsequent mainline event, often after a digression or reported speech, nde introduces concluding remarks or decisions, and macəkəmbay indicates information that occurred off the main event line.

Many clauses in a Moloko discourse are independent and are not linked grammatically to a preceding or following clause by a connector or by the presupposition marker na. The semantic nature of the connection between these unmarked, juxtaposed clauses is inferred from the context. The presupposition marker na aids in making a connection between two clauses, because it makes it explicit that the first ( na -marked) clause is known information. Na constructions have already been discussed in sec:11.1. A juxtaposed clause can simply re-express the thought in the first clause. In ex:12:62, the second clause restates in the negative that God is near. In ex:12:63, the second clause makes more precise the general instruction in the first clause. In ex:12:64, the second clause expands on what the speaker sees about the chief. In the examples in this section, each clause is delimited by square brackets and the juxtaposed clause is bolded.

Two clauses linked by juxtaposition can also express a comparison ( ex:12:68 -- ex:12:69 ). The first clause is a predicate-adjective clause (see sec:10.1.2 ) including the attribute being compared. The second clause establishes the comparison by means of the verb dal ‘pass.’

summary: The passage explains that many Moloko clauses are independent and can be juxtaposed without a connector or the presupposition marker na, with their relation inferred from context. Juxtaposed clauses may restate, elaborate, or qualify the first clause, or they may express temporal, logical, or comparative relations; na makes a link explicit by marking the first clause as known information.
